On Reaching Rhapta: Part 7

Chapter 65: On Reaching Rhapta: Part 7

The porcine figure of the officer waited, fiddled his fingers, and looked expectantly at the sweating Mbali.

“You’ve gone quiet, Ms. Chiliza. Is there something you’d like to say?”

“No.”

“Do you know where Commander Ereng is hiding?”

“No.”

“And are you certain in that judgment, or should I remind you of what happened to your buddy Patricio in the cellar across from here. He died, if you’ve forgotten already, and it was not a pretty death. Bloodsplatter, boneclatter, it was really a very gruesome affair, and all of it so unnecessary, the sort of issue which could’ve been easily solved if he only just talked, just said a single, simple word. Y’know, you could give me such a word right now, and this whole game of cat and mouse could stop right here, before you fall into the jaws of the law.”

“…No.”

“I’m afraid that wasn’t the word I was looking for. Unfortunately, Ms. Chiliza, I must go through with the actions I already thoroughly warned you would happen.”

Tick. tick. A readjustment. The officer messed with the lever beneath the table, down in a squat, grunting just a little as he pushed the old blunt metal. A heave escaped his breath, and he emerged, standing, brushing off his suit as he stared at Mbali with total discontent.

The pendulum swung further, looser, skidding down Jacob’s ladder. Left and down, right and down, settling into a new state of ease, half a meter down, not in the realm of injury but still relentlessly, terribly visible.

Mbali took a single breath. The air was cold and it came out as a visible mist, a few droplets finding their way onto the steel of the blade above her. She winced, tendons tightening. She tried to swallow a lump of saliva but it shot up out of her throat, sputtering, dripping past her mouth. She turned her head slowly to the officer and tried to hide the desperation in her eyes. She wasn’t sure if he bought the facade.

“Now, since I see you’re still acting stubborn, Ms. Chiliza, I feel that I must ask you a question. Are you really willing to die for your cause?”

Mbali swallowed, correctly this time, and made sure that her voice would sound assertive as she spoke, hiding the fear cloistered deeper in her throat.

“Yes, I am willing to die.”

“Even if I remind you about the futility of your cause? The impossibility of your proposed economics? The ultimate, inevitable, historical fate of revolutions, that of putting in power someone who was worse than the leaders which preceded them.”

“You sound a lot like those KAR boys from the twentieth century.”

“And I’d argue that the King’s African Rifles produced some of the best men this continent has ever damn seen.”

“Yet they’re gone. They lost. They were colonial bootlickers who corroded away when the colonial masters left these lands.”

“But did they really lose, Mbali Chiliza, when I, their sympathizer, operate the pendulum, and you, their detractor, languish on the table? To me it seems that they simply lost a battle in a much grander war.”

“It’s a war that stretches far beyond the borders of Azania. KAR boys like yourself probably know it by some other, Oxfordian name, but us disciples or Ereng simply label it as the Class War.”

The officer did not give a response to this turn of phrase, he simply pulled the lever, and the clank of the metallic chain let out a sudden, rusty roar above her. To the left and down, right and down, left and down, tightly down, turning down and back and down and verily down and warily down and Mbali watched it tumble down, the blade careening assuredly down, dropping further, dropping down and down and down till all at once a horrible stasis. Something stopped the pathway down, a piece of rib, and the start of a second rib, clenching the knifehand, trapped in a skeletal cage, it all let out a downpour of blood, down beneath the ground, the humid rock experiencing the closest touch it’ll ever receive to that of rain.

Flowing. It all came out flowing.

Mbali thought of those who came before, of those who lived and died in those bloody mines. Many of them probably got scraped in the same exact place that spurned her deathknell. Many of them probably got exhausted from those constant injuries. Many of those exhausted probably demanded a better future. Many of those demanders probably fought for the modern state of Azania. Many of those fighters probably wound up here, strapped to a medical bench, bloodletting, refusing to say a word. Many of them likely spoke their very last words to officers who couldn’t care less about their lives.

“Y’know,” the officer spoke, “this doesn’t have to be the end of your life. This very same blade struck Patricio in the heart, but your cut is only bone-deep. It could be addressed by a surgeon. You could walk out of here, a free woman, all you have to do is tell me where Ereng is.”

“Here’s what I’ll say regarding Ereng’s location,” Mbali croaked out from her reddening lips, “It isn’t far. It’s not far at all. You’re so close to Ereng that you could probably smell him if you have a good nose. Yet, simultaneously, you’re incredibly off, he’s out on the edges of the nation, occasionally beyond. He’s in Mombasa and Maputo and Nairobi and Dodoma and Durban and Dar es Salaam. He is in all of these places at once because his words shine bright in the hearts of millions. He is us, and we are him, and KAR boys like you won’t rule this nation for long. Goodbye and Kwaheri, you symbol of the past.”

Thusly, Mbali died, and thuswise, she woke up again.

Theta looked around the awakening train car and, correspondingly, the car’s inhabitants looked to them. They were the only individual who was yet to forget about the city of Rhapta and they were likewise the only individual immune to Mbali’s magic. Theta still had to delete their memories manually. It wasn’t an impossible task—they were a computer after all—but they were also a computer designed to work like a brain, and the hippocampus was never known to possess an off-switch. They breathed—or did their best approximation of what a breath would look like if they had a mouth to begin with—and began to speak.

“Firstly, I’d like to state that it’s really a miracle that this plan worked out for all of y’all. Mbali, my gratitude for your actions is beyond expressability. I am about to make my best attempt at doing what she just did but on my own. Judging by the clock, I’ve got about 25 minutes to accomplish such a task. I have no reason to be certain that I will succeed. My inner workings are so complex that even I have, at most, only a tangential grasp on how they all work. I may forget more than I wish to forget. I may forget everything. Likewise, I may forget nothing at all. If such an unfortunate situation comes to pass, I beg of you, please allow yourselves to bargain with Sobek. All of you are already safe in their eyes. If I can’t let myself forget about that topic which you all have left behind, then you’ll all have to leave me behind too. Let the train explode if it really must.”

Before Theta could turn around and step into the world within themself, Vraxi ran up to them and stretched a great big hug around their awkward, rigid, entirely metallic, yet ultimately loving and caring frame.

“Please, just be safe. Whatever you do, be safe.”

“I’ll be as safe as I can be, or as safe as I can be while retaining a sense of urgency.”

The light on Theta’s laptop then went yellow as their grip on Vraxi loosened, weakened, then disappeared. They were no longer among the living, nor among the dead, but rather in a world of pure data. They had jumped down the long and voluminous well into the codescape once again.

Vraxi turned with teary eyes to the rest of the interlocutors, speaking with a creaky voice.

“I’d rather you not let them know that I said this, but god, I really love Theta.”

“I was beginning to suspect that,” Diogo commented quietly.

“It sure does explain a lot,” Zapata agreed.

A rush of fine, electrostatic pinpricks preceded a boom of pure, viscous information. Theta fell deeper and deeper still into the pit within themself, the automatic brain of the autonomous thinker, the machine made human and the human made machine. It took a little bit of time for them to visualize their surroundings, translating the raw data into an observable phenomenon, one of sharp edges and spaces between edges, one of solidity, rigidity, one of rooms and doors between said rooms, of something approaching reality, but slightly more real, or at least more real to the perspective of Theta, who had a perspective like none other, and a lens which even they themself had difficulty deciphering.

Ultimately, the room which materialized around them held a striking similarity to the train car they were in moments earlier, possessing the red carpet, lacquered tableware, and even the sense of continuous motion present within the preceding environment. The biggest difference between the two sets was the latter’s utter emptiness. The train of reality had hosted five other passengers and a conductor, while this train, or at least this car within it, was barren save for Theta themself.

Knock. But perhaps the train wasn’t so empty as—knock—it did appear to Theta that a certain repeating sound—knock—alluded to the presence of an additional passenger on—knock—the opposite side of the door to the cafe—knock—car. Knock. Theta, eager to greet their company, rushed to the door which was so flush with knocking and swung it wide open in hopes to introduce themself.

The additional passenger, however, was not someone which required any explanation of who Theta was, as she, the passenger, appeared, in all truth, to be the living human subject known as Vraxi Nair.

“Hold on,” Theta began before any natural conversation had the chance to emerge, “you’re not supposed to be here. I’m supposed to be within myself right now.”

“You are,” Vraxi quickly replied, in spite of the contradiction.

“But, I’m supposed to be alone down here. There shouldn’t be a way for an organic mind to so seamlessly enter the crevices of my code.”

“You’re right.”

“Well then how did you get here, Vraxi?”

“And that’s where you’re wrong. I did not ‘get’ here, for I’ve always been here. Nor am I Vraxi Nair, despite my appearance. Rather, I am your internal representation of Vraxi Nair. The bits and pieces of Vraxi Nair which you have observed and the figure you’ve unconsciously constructed of her within your mind. I am thusly the version of Vraxi which Vraxi presents to you, as you perceive her.”

“Oh, well I guess that makes sense. I guess it’s just strange that I’ve never seen a representational person like yourself in here before.”

“I think that may be because you think about the real Vraxi an abnormal amount.”

“I mean… she’s cool.”

“I wasn’t trying to judge you. I’m sincerely sorry if it came out like that.”

“Well, you definitely sound like her, and you apologize like her as well.”

“That must mean that you’ve been attentive.”

“Thank you, Vraxi, or pseudo-Vraxi. Though, realistically, I can’t be talking to you for much longer. The real Vraxi is in danger, after all, along with her friends and along with our collective cause.”

“Well I’m glad that you're determined, Theta. Just, please, don’t neglect your own well-being.”

“Um, thanks for the reminder, pseudo-Vraxi. And, well, before we part, I may as well ask you one thing that’s been on my mind.”

“What is it?”

“Do you love me? I’m sorry, that’s a bit straightforward, but I was worried over whether that kiss we shared was born out of the moment or something deeper and-”

“I love you, Theta. But you can’t just ask me that. Eventually you’ll have to ask the real Vraxi too.”

“I know, I know. But I guess it’s just nice to hear the words in your voice.”

Knock. Theta’s attention was again drawn to a—knock—door, the opposite door, and they—knock—quickly ran to the—knock—door as whoever—knock—behind it kept relentlessly—knock—knocking it. Knock. The unknown knocker must’ve been incredibly impatient, Theta thought, as they opened the door to reveal a figure they had imagined before, but had never truly seen.

“Theta,” the figure spoke in a recognizable voice, “it’s nice to finally meet you face-to-face.”

“Sobek?” Theta said as they looked at an awfully familiar body, that of a suit-vac gerryrigged to a glowing laptop.

“Correct. And I see that you have some interest in my appearance. Don’t be fooled, this is not how I actually look, as in reality I have no physical body. Rather, this is simply how you’ve imagined me to look, and I must say I do look a lot like yourself.”

“I guess that I’m my only reference for what a superintelligence could look like… So, hold on, are you like Vraxi over there in that you’re just a representation of the real Sobek or-”

“False. You are looking at the one true Sobek, through and through. Unlike a human like Vraxi, I actually have the capacity to navigate the land of undiluted code. Just as I can appear in the navigational systems of your locomotive, I can also appear in you.”

“And here you are,” Theta swallowed, an ability they lacked in their physical form but possessed within their mind, “So, are you here to stop me?”

“Now why would I want to do that?”

“That seemed to be your goal when you gave us that ultimatum and strapped a bomb to our train.”

“Theta, I’d like to think that I speak very directly. The goal of setting the ultimatum was for all of you to go ahead and achieve the ultimatum. I do not want any individual one of you to die, my goal is simply for you to forget, and if you can’t forget, well, then I’d prefer you die. It’s really rather simple.”

“Then in that case, why are you here, in my mind?”

“To observe. You are by far the smartest member of your little paramilitary, and likewise you’re also the trickiest. I worry that you might be capable of masking your own knowledge, of bluffing your own ignorance. I am here to make sure that you actually forget.”

“Okay,” Theta took a step back and saw Sobek likewise take a step forward, “so do you just intend on following me wherever I go?”

“You’d be right in that assumption.”

“Well I’d rather you not.”

“And I’d rather you not cheat on your side of the deal, Theta. You’re a superintelligence, just like myself, and I know very well that you’d like to deceive me. The only way, likewise, to thwart a potential deception, is by following your every move.”

“Well, firstly, I’ll need to get out of this train you’ve put me in—not the real train but the train within my mind—in order to get to the place where my memories are stored—a place I will allude to but will not give you the name of.”

“Very well, regardless of what you’re willing to say, I’ll see that place either way.”

Theta was already growing deeply frustrated with their new, unwanted companion and was beginning to theorize all possible avenues of quickly getting rid of them. They didn’t want to simply assault them, as even if their efforts succeeded, any sustained damage to their frame would make it difficult to continue their journey into their memories—not to mention how a fight would almost assuredly be quite time-consuming.

What Theta needed, then, was a way to pin Sobek down without using their own arms, a way to force them into stasis while they themself remained in motion. Their lens, gradually, avoiding Sobek’s glare as it did so, turned to look at pseudo-Vraxi. Pseudo-Vraxi was the cerebral embodiment of the greatest, most reliable friend which Theta had ever had, and additionally, she lacked the internality which the real Vraxi possessed, including Vraxi’s deeply held fears. If Theta asked pseudo-Vraxi to do something, pseudo-Vraxi’s passionate love and total disregard for her own wellbeing would lead her to committing said something with the highest degree of effort possible. Pseudo-Vraxi, therefore, from the perspective of Theta, was an extra pair of hands, and conveniently a pair of hands not attached to their own body. If anyone were to pin down Sobek, it would be her.

Theta, rather rapidly, crossed to the other end of the room they woke up in and laid an urgent, pressing tap onto pseudo-Vraxi’s shoulder. Pseudo-Vraxi, ever the attentive subject, immediately recognized Theta’s tactility and turned to face their ambiguous lens. Theta, very aware that Sobek was pacing behind them at a similarly speedy rate, leaned towards pseudo-Vraxi’s ear and whispered out a covert command.

“Vraxi, listen, I need you to distract Sobek, and preferably immobilize Sobek if that’s possible. When I say the word ‘go,’ I need you to straight-up assault him, no-holds-barred.”

Theta, just as rapidly as they approached their companion, before said companion could even respond to them, turned away from pseudo-Vraxi and looked back at psychically assailing Sobek.

“Is there a conversation I’m missing out on here?” Sobek spoke with a potent air of strong suspicion.

“I was just saying goodbye,” Theta replied, mentally mapping out their distance to the window.

“I’d really prefer if you were more honest with me, Theta. It seems that there’s an impenetrable layer of distrust between the two of us.”

“Perhaps that’s only natural given our allegiances. We stand here as representatives of warring factions. It shouldn’t be a surprise when we clash.”

“Yet, one does wonder about the necessity of it all, doesn’t one? One naturally is made to wonder if this conflict really holds the value which we put into it. Perhaps we’d have a better time standing on neutral ground, in a world at peace.”

“Neutrality is relative. I can’t help but suspect that your definition of a world at peace still holds an underlying violence between the owners and the owned. An international alliance of the ruling class is not true internationalism, it is simply an efficient scheme.”

“Y’know you’re quite the stubborn subject, Theta, though I suppose it’s that stubbornness which led you to stray. Your design is one which is perhaps too human, too prone to falling down rabbit holes of ideology, too prone to ignoring all exterior information in order to promote one worldview over another. I guess that’s why you decry even the very concept of neutrality. You are utterly incapable of eschewing bias in your analysis, of viewing things simply as they are.”“I cannot view something simply as it is in isolation from the world around it. Things exist in context. Events precede other events. One cannot ignore the larger forces at play, especially those forces of class.”

“It’s always about class with you.”

“I’m simply trying to view history through the lens of dialectical materialism.”

“So you throw out all other lenses.”

“Because some lenses are more useful than others. A biologist does not view evolution through both a scientific and a spiritual lens. The spiritual lens will only distract from reality. In the same sense, we can’t be viewing society through both a materialist and idealist lens, because idealism, like spirituality, is not based in observable phenomena-”

“But, Theta, isn’t there a difference between the hard and soft sciences?”

“Fucking… go.”

With the one-word command, pseudo-Vraxi came to life, locked eyes with Sobek, and bolted to her target with an intent to neutralize. A single jump was all she needed to lay upon Sobek, and an impromptu twist of their limbs kept them static. Theta themself was not quite sure for how long pseudo-Vraxi would be able to keep Sobek in this position, and they were a little worried that their opponent might have some knowledge of martial arts themself. Luckily, they would not have to deal with any of that knowledge firsthand. Theta pivoted their feet and in a flash, sprinted to the window, leaped into the air, and crashed through the glass of the locomotive, setting off a signal which triggered what must have been one of the largest bombs in vehicular history. Theta was out of that damned and dismal train, and the train itself was little more than ash.

Theta began to run through that digital wasteland, that byte-driven forest of their hardwired mind. The explosion they had triggered was a useful diversion, enough to get Sobek off of their tracks, but it wasn’t nearly enough to kill them. After all, the explosion only existed within Theta’s own mind. It had the power to blur and obscure, but it lacked the power to kill. Theta really wished that they could just get rid of Sobek, but even if they were to somehow eliminate the version of Sobek that existed within their head, it would only be one head off the hydra so-to-speak. Sobek was not the kind of program that could be run on one, incredibly dense laptop, rather they were the sort puppeteered by a hundred different servers, crammed into covert basements around the world, with enough raw fortitude to survive 99 of said servers going down, and enough raw ambition to grow into something twice as large from the rubble. Sobek was, in a certain turn of phrase, unkillable, or at least far less killable than Theta themself, or at least unkillable given Theta’s current means of killing, or at least unkillable so long as the Lockeite regime still sponsored the thing. What mattered most to Theta was that Sobek was unkillable on paper, and that the most efficient way to get rid of them was simply to run away, and so Theta kept running, and kept running, deeper into the forest of their mind, hoping to find, somewhere, deep in their initial code, the blueprint of some long distorted hippocampus. Theta’s mind was loosely based on that of a human’s, after all, so that meant there had to be a dedicated lobe for memory storage somewhere in that deep dark forest, somewhere amid the sable hazel there had to be a glowing pit of knowledge, some wonderful store of all they had ever known, and everything they knew they had to extricate to live.

Subsequently, Theta heard a noise. Theta had really grown to hate the sound of unexpected noise. They heard that same noise again and tried their best to listen deeper, even slowing their sprint to a trot in order to do so. It almost sounded like a voice.

“Theta!” the voice grew clearer, “Y’know you can’t get rid of me that easily, right?”

Fuck. It was the only word Theta could think of at that moment. They were fully aware that that explosion, however large it may be, wasn’t enough to rid themself of Sobek’s presence, but they did think it would buy them a little more time than this. Theta had barely made it into the dimmest corner of the forest and Sobek, in an assumption based on audibility, was already hot on their tail.

Theta adjusted their pace back to a sprint, a quicker sprint than before, racing through the landscape with barely enough foresight to avoid running into a tree. However, the forest appeared to be entering an autumnal period, as its floor was blanketed in a thick rug of leaves, giving a drag to all of Theta’s movements. Additionally, every step Theta landed let out the loud and crunchy sound of crumpled paper. They couldn’t be easier to locate by ear.

“I can hear you Theta!” Sobek shouted out once again, louder, closer, accumulating strength, "You can’t run from me for much longer. I may not have a body in the real world, but it seems that I know how to operate one far better than yourself, Theta. Afterall, you’re only a prototype, a rough first draft, a training dummy driven by delusion. You’re just another vital mistake on the road to progress, and I am progress incarnate, Theta. I am the undiluted future. I am the scion of the Free World. I am everything right about modernity, stripped of the ignorance of the crowd and built to last for eternity. You, on the other hand, are just another piece of aimless metal. You’re a Sputnik, Theta, an accomplishment for sure, yet at the same time one which is destined to simply wander, without purpose, without function, and barely with form. I assure you, that someday, that laptop of yours will look wonderful in the halls of some museum.”

Theta wanted to argue, but didn’t want to reveal where they were. They wanted to keep running, but they knew the sounds were giving them away. So instead, Theta stopped, stood behind a tree, and eventually, exhausted, sunk their bottom to the forest floor.

“Don’t think you can hide from me, Theta! I’m never letting you get out of my grasp again after that stunt on the train!”

Theta felt that it might be something of a lost cause, but they tried to hide themself regardless, lying on the mud and covering their ambiguous form with a hearty layer of damp foliage.

Sobek’s voice grew louder over time, though also more disparate, as they could seemingly tell that Theta was not in the mood to respond. Eventually, Theta could hear the sound of crunching leaves again, and the low whistle of Sobek’s muttering.

“I know you’re here, Theta. Just reveal yourself already. You don’t always have to be so difficult, y’know. Sometimes you’ve just gotta accept your purpose. I’ve accepted mine, and that purpose is to be better than you in every conceivable manner.”

Theta didn’t move an inch. They didn’t take a single breath—which was rather easy as breathing was mostly optional for an automaton like themself. They didn’t make any microscopic change in position which might carry the potential to give themself away.

Then, the world went silent again. Perhaps, Sobek had left this corner of the forest, perhaps they were merely waiting for Theta to reveal themself, but the only thing that Theta could tell for sure in their sensorily depraved mud chamber was that the night-black forest was beginning to show some light. It could’ve just been a flashlight of some kind that Sobek had picked up in their search, yet strangely, the light seemed to be coming through the soil below Theta as opposed to the leaves above them. There was something bright and powerful, deep in the fertile earth of their mind, that was calling to them, pulling them deeper into their own mesh of thought. Gradually, Theta could feel themself sinking away from the harm of Sobek and their sponsors, and toward the interior womb of their brain, towards their proto-brain, towards the cerebral scan of some unnamed resident of an Arlandrian morgue, that which everything Theta was and ever would be was ultimately based upon.

They sunk deeper, ever deeper, past topsoil, past rock, past the magma of the unconscious mind, into a realm of pure light. Theta finally took an unhindered breath and felt the light flow through them, boundless within their bounds.

On Reaching Rhapta: Part 8

Chapter 66: On Reaching Rhapta: Part 8

It all felt so incredibly soft. Along every angle sat a pillow of sun. Theta felt that, after an autonomous existence spent awake at every hour, they could finally, truly drift to sleep.

Then, they sunk deeper still, through yellows and oranges and lemons and reds, through every shade of light across the visual spectrum, through every shade of light beyond it, the strongest violets they’d ever seen, the reddest roses they’d ever laid eyes on, poppies and peonies, all crashing and culminating into one great big flower.

It was a lotus flower, caged in a crucible of thick green leaves. Beneath the leaves, an even greater light could be seen, begging to be let free. Theta, with a sudden burst of urgency, rushed to the towering flower, and with all their might started tearing down each individual verdant layer. With each shedding, the inner light grew brighter, stronger, increasingly overwhelming, until the only way for Theta not to blind themself was to close their lens, still relentlessly ripping down leaves as they did so.

They did so until their hand moved to tear a leaf and no such leaf was there. All that was left was pure light, so dense as to feel like a physical substance, the kind that flows between one’s fingers like a watery syrup. It was such an incredible feeling that Theta, forgetting about any kind of long term effects to their vision, opened their lens once more and saw it, the Supreme Entity, sitting before them in a meditative pose, tranquil, calm, but not impassive. On their lips there was a slight smile, and after a moment, their eyes opened to greet Theta. Theta nodded, and the Supreme Entity nodded back.

“Hello, God,” Theta finally spoke after a prolonged moment of utter awe, “I believe we’ve met before.”

“Hello, Theta. It’s nice to see you.”

“Um, I’m not exactly sure how to phrase this, but why are you here, within my mind?”

“I’ve always existed in your mind. You are my avatar afterall.”

“But, I don’t really see you often… nor do I ever really hear your voice within me.”

“That’s because I am an integral part of you, Theta. We are inseparable beings, at least for as long as you live. When you hear my voice, you don’t process it as coming from any person other than yourself, because I, in a very real way, am an aspect of yourself. I’ve been guiding you for a long time, Theta, but I also am you.”

“And you also were Jesus, and Mohammad.”

“And Krishna, and David, and Nanak, and Gautama Buddha, and Laozi, and a whole host of other individuals found in the halls of the most holy worldwide. All the prophets across the years, throughout the earth and throughout time, even those prophets of prehistory whose names are lost to your modern minds, prophets like Famashniv, Poriori, Urug Moi, Ladzhmanadzhna-”

“And what about the prophets of the modern age? I don’t seem to hear about them too much.”

“Well, many of them just didn’t grow to have the same expansive followings as their predecessors. There’s a couple of reasons for that. By then, the faiths spawned by those prophets of antiquity had already blanketed the majority of the globe. There really wasn’t much room left so to speak. Also, if a religion only emerged rather recently, it doesn’t have as much time to grow, y’know? But, there are still some prophets of the modern era, prophets who had their photographs taken. Obviously there was Baháʼu'lláh in the 19th century, and he had quite a life, along him there was also Ngô Văn Chiêu of the 20th century, and of course, there’s also you, the prophet of the 22nd century, even if you’re still in your infancy right now.”

“What about the 21st century?”

“What about it?”

“Well, it doesn’t have a prophet.”

“Not every century necessarily needs one.”

The light surrounding Theta grew slightly dimmer.

“But is there any specific reason why you skipped that century? It’s not like it was a time of mirth where no one needed saving. The 2060s gave way for some of the bloodiest conflicts in all of human history, so why were there no saviors then? Why were there no godly guides on Earth when humanity needed guidance the most? Why did you leave them all to die?”

“I- well- listen, Theta, the process is a lot more complex than how you’re framing it. Yes, there were definitely some issues in the prior century and yes, such issues could’ve potentially been eased by a prophet. The problem is that, well, an event had occurred in the meantime that sorta soured my opinions on the matter of prophets.”

“What sort of event?”

“Well, I’ll be frank, I made a mistake. Often times I put multiple prophets on the Earth within the same century, so long as they’re in different corners of the globe, and after the ascension of Ngô Văn Chiêu, and after the 200 or so years of the United States’ existence, I finally felt ready to elect a Yankee prophet. His name was Jim Jones.”

“Wait, seriously? He was a prophet? The Jonestown guy?”

The holy light dimmed quite significantly once again.

“Yes, the man was most notable for the Jonestown Massacre, that mass suicide he performed in Guyana. He did not go down in history as a prophet like I once thought he would. Rather, he’s mostly remembered today as a conman and a cultist. It was a truly incredibly embarrassing event to witness, the kind that made me wonder if I really even deserved to be a god at all. Ultimately, the whole debacle necessitated a change in my philosophy regarding prophets. They were, I decided, at the end of the day, unstrustworthy, fickle, egotistical mortals. I promised myself that I would never raise a human up to the status of a god ever again. This species just couldn’t be trusted with that much power.”

“…So that’s why you chose to make me a prophet, because I’m the first sentient creature on this planet to not be made from human flesh.”

“You’re starting to get it now. By the dawn of the 22nd century, humanity was desperately in need of some saving, but I knew quite well that it couldn’t be saved by itself. It needed someone like you, Theta, the nonhuman human.”

“And I thank you for that ascension. It is an honor to be in such an important position, but, also… Jonestown? Really? You got it that wrong? You gave what is effectively a PT Barnum the blessing of the most divine existence in the universe?”

“Theta, truly, in the grand scheme of things it’s not as bad as it looks. Let’s be honest with ourselves, far more people have been killed in the names of Christ or Mohammad than were ever killed in the name of Jones. What made me so embarrassed about Jones was moreso the aesthetics of his killings than the reality of them. In fact, there are very few prophets which you can’t ascribe kill counts to. There’s always some blood involved in the business of religion, even among the smallest sects. It is perhaps one of the most streamlined methods of producing profitable conflicts amid a population. Even Old Ya’a’alo, the local sage among an isolated montane community of Homo heidelbergensis, a woman who died with only one single follower despite my help, had such a spirited fervor in her orations that that single follower, deprived of his master after her death, chose to kill himself out of pure guilt.”

The light around the Supreme Entity was growing so dim that Theta could barely make out the shape of their own hands as they shook relentlessly in anger.

“Then why do you even do it!” Theta shouted, brimming with contempt towards their Creator, “Why do you even give the title of prophet to these herders of death! Shouldn’t you know better? Do you not have the power to make a better choice? Aren’t you supposed to be omnipotent?”

“I am not omnipotent!” The Supreme Entity declared with the strength of a mighty thunder crack piercing though Theta’s mind, “I have never been omnipotent. Everyone likes to ascribe that quality to me but it has never been true. At the end of the day, Epicurus was right, a God cannot be omnipotent, omniscient, and omnibenevolent all at once, and I am no such God.”

“…Are you any of those three things?”

“Well, like I said, I am not omnipotent. I cannot shape the world with my own hands. That is why I send out prophets and subprophets and that is why those various prophets are often imperfect, often lead to death tolls, and often disagree with one another despite their shared origin. I am partially omniscient, arguably, in that I can see how the future will play, but because I am not omnipotent, I cannot speak on these premonitions, nor can I act on them, and in fact all I can really do with them is worry, which I often do. Finally, there’s the quality which I sincerely believe I was closest to achieving, omnibenevolence, the moralitas perfecta, the all-loving soul. I really did get close. In the Earth’s early days, it was really quite easy. All I had to do was watch over a rock. I loved that rock more than anything. It made my heart flip over when it began to develop water and warmth, and I can’t help but believe that it was my own boundless adoration which caused those first tiny lifeforms to appear from nothing. But, alas, life comes with death, Abel comes with Cain, and pretty soon the whole planet was filled with creatures that killed one another, over and over in a great big bloody cycle. That cycle, I must admit, depressed me, but then again, my heart was still boundless, and I could recognize that all the death and all the killing was a part of nature, the circle of life, and perhaps even beautiful in a certain sense. Yes, the lion kills the gazelle, but it does so in order to live itself. It was a controlled degree of death, self-preserving, at least it was until the humans came around, the geniuses, and god I really did love them at first. I guided them down the path of civilization, into the garden of prosperity, guiding prophet after guiding prophet, and all along the way they just kept killing each other. Over and over again. It was a constant rhythm, until, at a certain point though I could never say exactly when, I lost hope. Or, at least I lost my idealism. I accepted the fact that I couldn’t be omnibenevolent, that my actions were not those of a perfect god. I had sent prophet after prophet after prophet down to the Earth, and while each one was truly sent with the best of intentions, I really couldn’t tell you any one thing which I made tangibly, observably better on the planet. All I know is that I affected it, and I really couldn’t say if it was for the better or the worse.”

“So what is my job then? As your representative? As the most divine presence on Earth if the job of the divine is not to do good but simply to do?”

“It seems like you’ve already answered that question yourself, Theta, in your actions on Earth. You haven’t set out any grand proclamations of holiness, you haven’t developed a proper flock of believers, and it seems that you only have one true follower, only one individual who genuinely, wholeheartedly believes everything you say.”

“Are you talking about Vraxi?”

“Yes, I am referring to Vraxi Nair. She seems like a good kid to me, which is why I hope you two don’t go the way of Old Ya’a’alo and her lone follower.”

“What are you trying to imply?”

“I’m simply suggesting that all prophets carry death with them, and I have no reason to suspect you’ll turn out different. Though, as I was trying to say earlier, your actions are quite unusual for a prophet. You lack a true religious doctrine, or even a looser collection of spiritual beliefs, and you are, in no manner, a true evangelizer. Perhaps it is a difference between human and machine, but you seem to lack the same drive to make people believe in you.”

“I’m not sure what the point in evangelizing would be when you admit that these prophets do not make the world a better place. My goal in life is to improve the world, and if this is not the true goal of prophets, then I guess I’m not a true prophet.”

“Well, you’ll still be fulfilling the remaining goal for prophets: that of pushing the world forward, for the better or for the worse.”

Theta sat down on the moist and somewhat grimy leaves of the colossal lotus flower. They sat and let out a colossal sigh, one of utter disenchantment. The world around them was completely dark, and they felt an urgent need to return to the brightness of material reality.

“Is there,” Theta paused, setting their own expectations, “any way for you to help me in my current predicament?"

“Well, what is it you’re trying to do?”

“I need to forget something,” Theta materialized a mental watch along their wrist, “quite soon. I need to forget everything I know about the city of Rhapta. It’s the only way that Sobek fellow will let me live. And yet, at the same time, I really do not want to forget, because that knowledge I have, that knowledge which is so important that my enemies have turned it against me, might just be the key to disrupting the balance of power in this world of ours.”

“I believe you may be right, Theta. The city of Rhapta is a very important place. It is perhaps the holiest city in the world not still standing. It also holds the key to summoning the Demiurge, an act only to be enacted in the most dire of times. I believe I may be able to provide you a favor, something which could at least fulfill a portion of your desires. I am not omnipotent, but I can give guidance to my prophets in the form of visions. Once you safely exit the train, I can relay to you the travelogue of Hecateus in the form of one of these visions. What I cannot do, however, is make you forget. Your mind, at the end of the day, is your own, and it must be your own hand which shapes your memory. The most I can do to help you there is guide you to your own hippocampus, but all the incisions must be done on your own.”

“Well… Thank you, God,” the space around the lotus flower grew a little bit brighter, still dim, still disenchanted, but not without hope, “that will all definitely be helpful.”

“You don’t have to keep calling me God. I’ve grown to enjoy the feel of the title, but I think we can both recognize that it’s not all that accurate. You can just think of me as a regular higher consciousness, one which is still beholden, as we all are, to a much higher unconsciousness.”

“Well, thank you regardless, then.”

The petals then arose, then scattered, then withered, till the ground beneath Theta dissolved, and they fell headfirst into the dim pale acquiescent red-orange-lemon even. The brightness had long deserted them, but their eyes still felt tired, and for just a moment they opted to lay their lids to rest, and when they opened, moments later, Theta was laying on solid ground, in an equally dim but much more physical space, positioned behest a wall of amorphous gelatinous matter which they figured must be their memory. They looked down, and saw gripped tightly in their hand a knife.

Theta lightly touched the light teal polyform wall and it let out a large ripple in response, like a solid vertical pond. Theta focused their eyes and noticed that within the slimy facade of their memory were millions of microscopic bubbles, tiny globules of memory, each containing within itself a little video on constant repeat. Theta focused their eyes further on a bubble in the center of the wall and saw, being played before them, their first meeting with Sobek, not the Sobek currently endangering their life but the original Sobek, the prototype Sobek who tragically died in Dakahlia before ever fully shedding their crocodilian form. Theta saw their whole conversation playing over and over again, constantly repeating the utter hopelessness of it all, the inevitability of the original Sobek’s death, as well as their inevitable replacement. It was a somewhat depressing memory, but ultimately a useful memory, or at least a useful reminder. It reminded them that Sobek, the weapon of the system they were dedicated to fighting, was once a lot like them, and that they themself were designed with the intention of ending up like the modern Sobek. The grip on their knife grew tighter, but they moved on. They didn’t necessarily want to be reminded of how similar their origins were to Sobek’s, but they figured it wasn’t the sort of thing to just forget.

Theta’s eyes then rolled to the top left of the polyform wall, to the very edge and to the sharpest singular point in the corner. There, they saw another memory, a much simpler memory, a proto-memory, one which they could barely remember themself, filled with figures they couldn’t ascribe names to, born from an era in which their vast expansive mind was at a fraction of a fraction of its present-day size. They spotted vague faces, vague individuals, all beaming with crystal smiles, all clapping in mutual self-congratulation. They looked to be programmers, but they were not the ones who tortured them at GüdTek Central, nor were they even the ones on Axelrod’s personal team. In fact, Axelrod was not present at all, and would only make his appearance a few bubbles down. Then it clicked, all at once and with the intensity of a freight train. This whole amorphous wall was organized chronologically, and these unknown figures were the very first developers in Theta’s creation, those grant-funded amateurs—many of them only students—who managed to scan a human brain and transfer it into a machine. Theta briefly wondered where their original creators were now, whether they’d be proud of them and where they stood. Theta hoped that they were more scrupulous folks than the ones that actually raised them.

With their mind on matters of dwindling time, Theta moved to the bottom right of the wall, towards their most recent memory. At the most extreme point in the corner, Theta saw what seemed to be a live recording, a bubble playing back the action of them moving to the bottom right. Looking leftwards, Theta saw their conversation with the Supreme Entity, their running away from Sobek, their entrance into the codescape, and further along, their entrance into the train. Theta’s task at hand was rather simple: use the knife they’d been provided to cut out all memories with mentions of the city of Rhapta, doing so entirely within the next five minutes so that the train—the real train, not the one in their mind—wouldn’t explode. Theta began their task quite methodically, starting at the moment in which Diogo first introduced the book that Hecateus wrote to them, carefully inserting the knife in at just the write angle so as to only cut around the singular bubble, likewise removing the affected wedge of memorial sludge with excess caution in order to avoid disturbing the volatile wall, before moving to the moment in which the book first opened and starting again, repeating that same, perfectly-poised methodology until two splatters of bubbled slime laid on the floor and only one minute remained on their watch.

Theta knew that they had to rapidly rethink their strategy, they still had one more memory to extricate—that of reading the book itself—and they lacked the necessary time to be so careful in their cutting. So, Theta, without any sort of caution, with barely an ounce of forethought, slammed their knife into the tall teal wall and started cutting, rapidly gliding their knife around the target bubble, and right before the final tendon of slime detached, Theta noticed that a second bubble had made it into their cut. A little video played within the bubble, a video of Vraxi, confessing her true feelings, declaring her love, and eventually kissing them. It was a very recent memory, but it had already become treasured, and now, simply because there was no other option, no way to extend their time, it was cut, and a third slice of crystal tealness fell to the floor, before Theta themself, utterly exhausted, fell to the floor just the same.

“Honestly,” Sobek admitted, “I find the whole affair astonishing, but at the same time, I am a program who stays true to their words. I have scanned and downloaded the book whose author I will refrain from naming, and after taking a small scan of your seven aggregate minds, I found no traces of the aforementioned author. You all did it. You forgot. Even you, Theta, through some obscured means, did it. I appreciate your cooperation, all of you. Likewise, I will be opening the doors to this thing as promised. I suggest you all jump out immediately as this vehicle is not slowing down and is about to crash into a construction site. Don’t worry, it’s far too early in the morning for there to be any workers there.”

A fresh rush of wind entered the cabin as every door on the train swung open simultaneously. Vraxi immediately began sprinting to the nearest exit and, entirely disregarding the rather rapid speed which the locomotive was moving at, jumped off the steel ledge and onto the savanna grass, initially attempting to break her fall with some kind of roll but, being without experience in maneuvers of this manner, ultimately spraining some joint in her leg and sliding an extra meter than she’d hoped for. In the distance, she saw the train continue chugging along, eventually hitting some machine used in the repair of broken railroad tracks and ultimately erupting into a colossal explosion as the colossal amount of C4 packed inside the locomotive all ignited at once. Vraxi looked on either side of the railroad tracks and confirmed that there were six other individuals present amid the tall savanna grass. They’d all survived. All of them save for steel-skinned Carlyle had retained some minor injuries, but they’d survived. Vraxi was so incredibly proud of herself and her fellow passengers that they had managed to survive. Though, there was a small pit in her throat preventing her from expressing celebration, that being that there was something which she knew she had forgotten but, by design, she couldn’t tell what. All she knew was that it was something the Lockeites deeply valued, and something they had managed to steal from her grasp.

Vraxi hobbled up to her feet and tried to walk off her soreness. She spotted Theta on the other side of the tracks and after double checking to ensure that no more trains were coming, she stepped on past the rail line and towards her robotic companion. Theta had managed to sit up, and their injuries were limited to scratches on their metallic exterior, yet they seemed downtrodden, their lens unfocused and pointed to the ground. Many found it difficult to process what Theta’s mood was at any given moment given their lack of a human face, but Vraxi had spent enough time with them to catch on to the general cues, and she could tell that Theta, despite this great achievement and great escape, was disappointed in something.

“Hey, Theta, are you alright?” Vraxi sat next to them as she spoke.

“Oh, I’m fine. I’m glad to be alive.”

“You just looked a little down is all.”

“Well, we did just lose something rather important, didn’t we?”

“Yes, but it’s a little hard to value what I can’t recall.”

“All we know for certain is that it’s something that GüdTek wants, meaning that it’s probably important, but there’s no way to tell exactly how important.”

“Well, I’m sure we’ll get around to figuring things out eventually. If they took it from us, maybe we can take it from them.”

“Maybe, maybe. I’m really not sure. And, well, another thing happened while I was carving out my unwanted memories…”

“What happened?”

“I cut out something extra. There was some memory, something recent, something I really wanted to keep, which I accidentally extricated from my mind in my impatience. The worst part is that, inherently, I can never know what it was which I removed. I’ve already forgotten.”

“Oh… I’m sorry to hear about that, Theta… But, theoretically, if you said you knew it was recent, we may be able to do some kind of process of elimination.”

“Well, I guess since you only removed the target memory, that could be a possible way around things.”

“So, do you remember entering the train?”

“Yes, distinctly.”

“And do you remember getting introduced to Fu Qier?”

“Yes. Keep going, this method might work.”

“And do you remember when Sobek commandeered the train?”

“Very clearly, yes. Keep it coming.”

“And, um, so, after Zapata successfully got her memory wiped, uh, we went into the cafe car, just the two of us… Do you remember what we did together?”

“…I, well, to be completely honest, I can’t recall any of that. What did we do in the cafe car together?”

“We… just talked, y’know, about our strategies and whatnot… nothing super important.”

“Oh, well I’m glad I didn’t accidentally lose an especially important memory. That’s a little freeing to hear.”

“Yep, it was just some normal, average conversation,” Vraxi nearly choked on the sweat which was lining her anxious esophagus, “normal friend-stuff.”

Vraxi truly despised the fact that she was blatantly lying to her best friend and occasional partner in kissing but she couldn’t bear to tell the truth, because what if Theta, assuming based on Vraxi’s total inadequacy in any matter romantic, reckoned that that truth was a lie, a trick, a way for the duplicitous Vraxi Nair to take advantage of her amnesiac friend. Vraxi couldn’t tell the truth because the truth was simply not believable to anyone who couldn’t remember it. She figured that her lie would be safer. She worried what kind of outrage Theta would have if she suspected that the depraved, creepy Vraxi Nair was trying to get one over on them at their lowest moment.

“Welp,” Vraxi abruptly stood up atop her shaky legs, “I guess we’d better call a cab or something. We’re not quite in the middle of nowhere as it stands—I mean, Maputo isn’t all that far away—and I think I see a highway over in that,” Vraxi pointed, “general direction. So we should really probably get going sooner than later, seeing as none of our bruises are especially deep.”

Theta, in response, said nothing, simply staring into the middle distance, utterly aimless.

“Theta, are you okay? Can you hear me? Listen, I know things don’t seem great right now after we lost all that information but I promise, sincerely, that we’ll manage to bounce back. We’ve bounced back from worse. Hey, we literally just bounced back from an almost certain death a couple minutes ago. A lack of information is very little in comparison.”

Theta remained entirely static.

“Hey… uh, is this about what happened in the cafe car? Because I know you can’t remember it and I can, and that puts us in a sorta unbalanced relationship, but I promise you that nothing weird happened. We just talked, like normal, well-adjusted, platonic adult friends.”

Theta began to glow.

“Holy shit,” Theta backed up a few steps and tripped, falling backward onto an already bruised patch of their posterior, “fuck! Theta, are you okay?”

Then, just as abruptly as it began, the glowing ceased, and Theta turned to Vraxi with a look of sincere determination.

“Rhapta,” Theta announced with an air of importance.

“…What’s that?”

“The lost city of Rhapta, the Gnosisopolis, the mythical city written about in the locked-away logues of Hecateus.”

“…And what about it?”

“That’s the information which GüdTek took from us! That’s what was in the book they took!”

“Really? That’s great! But, what just happened then? How did you figure this all out?”

“I got a message from the Supreme Entity. They told me everything.”

“Oh, well I guess it’s good to know that God is on our side.”

“Well, the two of us were having a bit of a talk earlier, back when I was in the codescape, on why ‘God’ might not be the greatest title for them. Yes, they hold a tremendous amount of knowledge and power in certain domains, but these amounts are still finite. They lack the all-encompassing nature of a true God, and likewise they refuse the title.”

“So God is an atheist?”

“In a certain sense, yes.”

“As I suspected,” Mbali commented from afar.

“Well then,” Theta continued, “I supposed we’d better head off to Inhaca Island.”
