On Reaching Rhapta: Part 9

Chapter 67: On Reaching Rhapta: Part 9

Dawn had finally made its way to Azania by the time Vraxi Nair exited the ferry to Inhaca. The town on the port was rather quaint but—as Mbali would explain to her—had grown quite significantly since the revolution. The town, however, was not a place to be explored for any degree longer than necessary, for it was on the south side of the island and the highest point—the point which Hecaeteus pointed to—was firmly set on a hillock in the north. Mbali had made some calls to her friends in the Azanian government and had managed to hire a handful of local construction workers to help with what was officially deemed an ‘archeological dig.’ In a certain sense, there was no falsehood in that title, but Vraxi knew that beneath the soil was something far more important than bones and pottery. There was a world down there, trapped beneath the surface, and that world was the key to unlocking the forbidden aspects of the world held above. For a moment, in the loud and crowded truck to the digsite, Vraxi prayed, not to God, not to Ayyuppan, not even to Theta, but to Humanity at large. She prayed that the people of the world would be able to harness that power which was beholden to those of the highest strata—the means of production and means of ascension—before the Lockeites, those clerics of the dollar bill and scions of the past, seized that power for themselves.

When Vraxi saw the digsite empty of any meddling, absent of any trace of Sobek, she let out a breath of relief, but in the deepest part of her esophagus, a knot remained, the fearful knot of hope.

Vraxi gazed at the busy pair of excavators on the top of the hillock, and turned to Theta, who was staring at the dig with a tangible sense of wonder.

“So do you really think it’s down there?” Vraxi started.

“What? The city?” Theta took a moment to respond, enraptured by the view of the uncovering.

“Yeah, Rhapta. I think we can both admit that it’s a bit of a far-out concept. A grandiose city, one of the greatest in the world during the times of antiquity, nearly entirely stricken from the historical record, destroyed in some great disaster of biblical proportion and buried under its own demise.”

“It’s happened in degrees in other places. Ur was abandoned. Cahokia was abandoned. Honestly, the practice of not abandoning cities when things get rough is really rather recent.”

“But all of those cities have since been rediscovered. Archaeologists have matched up the historical accounts of the abandoned cities with the real-life remnants of their abandonment.”

“But Rhapta was a very secretive society, and while it kept its own historical record, it did not share its record with those from afar, with the single exception of their chance encounter with Hecateus. So with Rhapta fallen, its libraries destroyed, and the single account of Hecateus locked with a magic seal, there was no history for archaeologists to start with, and they likewise had no interest in the island of Inhaca. Sure, there have been some casual, often unintentional archaeologists over the years. I’ve found some old articles about locals finding strange coins on the beaches here, but when they sent those relics to Western museums, the historians scoffed at the idea that the origins of those relics could be found on the island they emerged from. ‘There must have been a shipwreck here, assuredly chartered in a faraway port,’ they would say, disregarding the locals. ‘Perhaps the Greeks left it there,’ and those Westerners would applaud. ‘Yet another achievement to record in our history books, and yet another foolishness of the Southern side of the world, to ever think that their riches might belong to their own hands.’ Rhapta was never discovered, because according to those in charge of history, this is a land without any, so there wasn’t any reason to look.”

Vraxi paused for a long moment. Azania was rising into the position of a global power. It was challenging the capitalist hegemony. It had a very real chance to wipe out the remnants of American empire for good. Even after America’s death, its scions remain, in the chairs of every major power’s cabinet, as the chairs of every major corporation. People like Josephine Bran still walked the world, preserving their long dead doctrines, penned by Monroe and engraved into the open veins of the planet. But it didn’t have to stay that way. The Yankee Frankenstein was not immortal. Azania still had the chance to soar, and to do so, it needed to rediscover itself. The world had stripped Young Azania of her history. It had killed and enslaved her ancestors and erased their names, but regardless, unchangeably, deep in the fertile earth, an echo of those ancestors remained. The very first humans were born in Azania, and the memories of them would not go ignored, their children would be excavated from the prison of the soil and their grandchildren would peer into that deep dark hole and sense a long, distant, yet overwhelming feeling of homecoming. Azania’s past could not go buried, for Azania present was still very much alive.

“Vraxi! Theta!” A voice from the top of the hillock declared, an ecstatic, astonished voice, the voice of Mbali Chiliza, “We’ve found it! It’s real! Rhapta is real!”

Vraxi stared at the faraway figure of Mbali, hands waving wildly in the dawn-soaked air, and turned to Theta, hoping to catch some emotion from their expression.

“You were right,” she stated to them bluntly, “it’s real.”

“Hecateus wasn’t lying,” Theta lifted up their chin and widened their lens, “and a new day is dawning over this long-wronged land, a day of recollection. Now, I suggest we check this city out, before some GüdTek drone prevents us. Remember, they know just as much as we do. Maybe even more.”

The rope wrapped around the torso of Vraxi Nair was well-secured, yet she still felt rather nervous. The seven survivors of the train wreck had all drawn straws to see which one would be the first to descend into the deep dark sinkhole. Vraxi had pulled the longest straw. She swore that it was the very first time she had ever pulled the longest straw and it just so happened to be at a moment where she’d really rather not. While she was honored to be the first rediscoverer of the long lost metropolis, she was also somewhat scared of heights, and there was quite a fall between the top of the hillock and the point down below where Vraxi could just make out what looked to be a washed-out cobblestone street. The construction worker beside her activated the light on her helmet and tightened her harness one last time.

“Are you ready?” the worker spoke with a genuine curiosity and a pinch of concern.

“I believe so,” Vraxi swallowed, “as ready as I’ll ever be.”

“You’ll do great,” Theta assured her, “we all believe in you.”

The machine attached to the other end of the rope began to turn, unwinding the tether. In response, Vraxi stepped into the chasm, and felt herself suspended in the damp cave air. Slowly but surely, her body drifted downward, further and further into the voluminous earth, into this great unseen, unnatural cavern. As the light on her helmet illuminated the underground walls, she saw her first glimpses of all that Hecateus once wrote about. A grand, almost Corinthian facade faced her down, of carefully carved limestone with cerulean pigmentation. Holding up every pillar was a statue of an elephant head. ‘There aren’t elephants in this part of Azania,’ Vraxi briefly thought, ‘but before the common era, their ranges were wider.’ After staring at the grand, somewhat ruined and assuredly abandoned building, Vraxi delved back in her memory and realized something. According to Theta’s recitation of Hecateus, this building must be the Library of Rhapta. It was one to one. This was truly the same Rhapta written about on those ancient maps, the most far flung city which the Greeks ever reached, unfolding before her in tremendous beauty.

Then Vraxi’s feet touched the ground, and the scariest part of the descent began. Vraxi carefully removed her harness and pulled on the rope. Wordlessly, the harness started rising into the air, as somewhere in the overworld, a machine started turning in the opposite direction. She was alone in a city untouched for millennia, and until the rope came back down, she had lost all connection to the world of what was known.

So Vraxi waited, and saw the harness steadily ascend to the sky, until it was out of her eyesight, and she waited further, hoping to see another person gradually drift down.

About ten minutes passed, ten minutes since the harness had left her vision and ten minutes of total silence. Vraxi knew that it shouldn’t take this long. The process of actually applying the harness to a human abdomen didn’t take all that long and the machine designed to assist in the descent appeared to turn quite quickly. Perhaps, she considered, there had been some sort of minor setback. What if they realized that they were out of helmets and didn’t think it safe to let someone down without one? Well, then they’d have to travel all the way to some kind of establishment which sells that sort of thing—a clade of establishment which Vraxi herself had no experience in and one which she wasn’t sure would be present on the meagerly populated island of Inhaca—and then they’d have to travel all the way back before they could start the process over again. It was a believable story, and Vraxi began to believe it, as it was a much more comfortable outlook than the sort which her fears intended her to glimpse, that of some horrible, deadly accident which would not only endanger her companions but leave her to rot in a pit for eternity.

But perhaps eternity was a bit of an overstatement, Vraxi considered while attempting to calm herself down. She still had Ayyuppan’s sword, afterall, and while it likely didn’t fit the same safety regulations as the harness she came down on, she imagined that it would still give her the ability to head back to the surface if needed. Just to comfort herself—as she did not intend to head upwards right away in case the delay was just a misunderstanding—she materialized the sword in her outstretched palm. She attempted to grip onto the hearty hilt and felt it fall like sand through her fingers. She tried again, and once again, her blade of the righteous was transfigured into dust. She began to realize that while Rhaptan civilization was long dead, its traces still remained. The ancient magis of this city must’ve laid some protective runes, the sort that made Vraxi’s foreign magic instantly warded and nulled.

Vraxi was quickly overtaken with fright. She was at the bottom of a large hole with no method of exit, entirely reliant on a group of people who were nowhere to be seen. It was possible, still, that that group was just embroiled in a minor-to-medium setback, but because Vraxi had no way to observe or perceive them, it was equally possible, at least in her mind, that all of them had suddenly died via an unexpected car bomb. There was simply no way to know. Every possible possibility was laid out on the table with absolutely no separation on the basis of plausibility. Vraxi might as well be stuck in the past, transported in some miraculous—now broken—machine to the ancient gnosisopolis, just days after the fall, with no known method of returning to the present.

Vraxi waited for another ten minutes, sitting on top of a rock which she later realized was a broken column, and attempted to control her breathing, though she inevitably resorted to a sort of hyperventilation. It was the only method of breathing which seemed apt in a situation as catastrophic as the one she was living through. Eventually her legs got so shaky in unrequited panic that she had to stand up from her seat so as to avoid a static spasm. She began walking in circles, an effective way to relieve stress on the mind but also, she later realized, a method which involved the exhaustion of calories, and if she had to stay here for much longer she would eventually need a source of food. She briefly wondered if the Rhaptans, clearly well-versed in manners of the mystic, were able to derive some method of food-preservation which could last for a couple millennia. While considering this subject, she eventually realized that her gait had only widened, pace only quickened, all as the circle around which she walked had only spiraled out greater. She realized that if she continued walking along this particular ring, she would eventually walk directly into the facade of the library. She figured instead that she might as well walk through the entrance to the library in order to learn a little more about Rhapta before it starved her to death.

The interior to the library was rather grand, but its grandiosity was tempered by five half-millennias of rot and decay and gradual water damage. There had once been books here—that was very clear as there even remained some remains of shelves—but the books themselves were unable to persist through the natural processes of erosion. Occasionally, Vraxi would run into fragments, snippets of beaten papyrus, some even containing glyphs which she assumed represented the ancient Rhaptan tongue, but when she tried to touch one of these fragments and hold it up to the light on her helmet, it dissolved within her palm. While she was presently playing the role of one, Vraxi Nair was not an archeologist, and she didn’t know the proper techniques for the preservation of artifacts. To avoid accidentally destroying all evidence of this ancient civilization, she stopped touching the fragments, and simply hoped that someday, someone might be able to decode them.

As Vraxi walked away from a large collection of said fragments, she nearly tripped on the ground’s masonry. Looking down after nearly falling, she saw that carved into the stone were a series of concentric circles, rings around rings around ever-growing rings. She almost immediately correlated the structure with that of how Hecateus had described the city of Rhapta’s layout, that of an increasingly rural ripple around a metropolitan core. Looking back upon the masonry, she saw a star etched into the space between two rings and realized that must be representative of where she’s standing now, a marker for the library within a map of the city. Her eyes then gazed to the center of the concentric circle, which was marked with one of the unknown glyphs she had seen repeated on the fragments. That was where she needed to head, Vraxi figured, that was where the mysteries of the Demiurge would finally be uncovered. She didn’t want to make the trip alone, but she figured that if she was going to starve down here, she may as well uncover the secrets of the universe while she still had the strength to move.

When Sobek informed her of the knowledge which Hecateus had written about, of the great and buried city of Rhapta, as well as of how those who once held the knowledge had now all forgotten, Dr. Gabriella Badden responded with a rather ecstatic expression and immediately chartered a stealth jet to the Azanian coastline. Badden had had to travel to Azania a handful of times before on diplomatic missions, and while she could, in a certain sense, admire the nation, at least through its infrastructure and incredible rate of growth, she sincerely despised the spirit of the nation which allowed for such a growth to occur. She found the Azanian people pretentious, and still too poor to earn the level of pretension which she herself admitted to possessing. She really just found the whole concept of the country bloated and obnoxious and she couldn’t help but dream of a future where the entire landmass was divided into an array of minor, powerless nation states, all lacking the political power to resist Western influence and the sheer power of the free market. But, alas, it was only a dream, and the Azania she would have to enter under this rather covert mission was an Azania still united, and worse for her, an Azania united by the hand of the proletariat. She would have to endure it, despite her disgust with the entire concept, because buried beneath the Azanians’ noses was a goliath of an artifact, the sort which, if utilized by the right hands, had the potential to bring Azania to its knees.

Badden then proceeded to load herself into a jet from the nearest storage silo, alongside some excavation equipment and a small platoon of Gibson troops. She was glad to hear that Inhaca Island, the place where she’d be digging, had a rather small population and seemingly no consistent presence of the Azanian military, but regardless, she wanted to have some troops with her just in case. Perhaps, she considered, the local villagers, caught up in their communal delusions, might attempt to attack her and thwart her vital mission, believing her groundbreaking to go against the sacred and perceiving her presence as one of a foreign invader. Thusly, she made sure to keep a healthy assortment of hired guns by her side, to dissuade any townsfolk from fighting against progress.

The jet was able to reach the island in quite a minute period of time—with jets of that caliber being one of the fastest possible modes of transport—and Badden, on hitting the ground, immediately exited the vehicle and started climbing up the hillock where Hecateus predicted the city would be stored under, her own troops flanking her on either side.

On reaching the top of the hillock, Badden was met with a rather unignorable setback, that being that another group had found the site of Rhapta first, and worse, that they had already started digging. In fact, this group of amateur archaeologists was amalgamated from the same individuals which Sobek had assured her had forgotten about such things. She noted that down in her mind as an imperfection on the part of the machine, and assured herself that Sobek would face consequences for this bout of ignorance.

Regardless, Badden did still have a minor army on her side, albeit one who had prepared to fight villagers as opposed to professional terrorists, though also one which was assuredly over-equipped to deal with villagers without causing some kind of massacre. Badden was very willing to utilize this battalion as a hammer to deal with these stubborn nails, and decided to enter a negotiation, with her pointed guns as the bargaining chips.

“Hello, terrorists,” she waved and got their attention, “I am here on behalf of the GüdTek corporation. I’m afraid that we have already secured the rights to this dig site and that your current activity is against the law.”

“As a representative of the Azanian government,” Mbali began, taking a few steps back but refusing to back off, “I find your mention of the law to be utter bullshit. And besides, the Azanian government doesn’t sign contracts with GüdTek to begin with, just on principle. The lie you're spouting could never come to fruition.”

“Perhaps you would be correct if I was referring to Azanian law, but international law is a very different beast. In fact, if you look at the legal record, you’ll find that back in 1949, a certain Brit by the name of Captain Wheeling sold this plot of land to an American firm named Pilcher and Dunham International, who attempted to form a mining operation only to discover that this particular plot held no valuable minerals. The land then went dormant for over a century and Pilcher and Dunham’s scale continued to shrink until, just this morning, GüdTek bought Pilcher and Dunham, for quite a low price, and by extension, bought this land as well.”

“But that purchase was made all the way back in the colonial era! And after the land reform policy was enacted during the revolution, this plot was made public!”

“So what this all sounds to me is that the Azanian communists, in a total affront to the god-given right of private property, stole the land which had been rightfully purchased by Pilcher and Dunham, a firm which had done no wrong by the local law and was simply maintaining an interest in the region, violently clawing the plot from their innocent hands to be redistributed to peasants who, judging by the lack of farmland in eyesight, haven’t even attempted to improve the land in any observable manner. Personally, and this is me speaking in an entirely neutral manner, I do not think that sort of argument will stand in international court.”

“International is a funny word to use when three quarters of the judges come from Lockeite regimes.”

“The selection of the judges is made by merit.”

“A metric of merit which is decided exclusively by Lockeites.”

“You can continue to argue about biases within the court for however long you want. Personally, I admit that it is an imperfect system, but it is also the only system we’ve got, and it is one we must abide by, no matter its decisions, in order to quell the fires of chaos within this tumultuous world. Accordingly, I’m afraid I must arrest you all if you continue to resist the court’s orders, and judging by the presence of my little army on either side of me, I think it would be wise of you to back off right now.”

“We will never-”

Before Mbali could even finish her sentence, Badden made a hand symbol to her battalion and a barrage of bullets began raining out from each of their weapons. Mbali, predicting the carnage which could unfold if she was slow to act, immediately pushed the three construction workers to the space behind their car and instructed them to drive away from the hillock with as much haste as possible.

Meanwhile, Zapata Tochihuitl, who was barely prepared for the present onslaught but had managed to summon her scythe, began, with a certain finesse unexpected by even herself, deflecting a hefty portion of the oncoming bullets. It was also, she quickly surmised, not nearly enough. There were about 25 Gibson troops in all and all of them appeared to possess automatic weaponry. The amount of bullets being unloaded at any given moment was uncountable, and while there was a certain distance between them and her companions, Zapata could easily recognize that there was a very limited period of time before one or more of these hunks of artillery ended up lodging itself into the flesh of a friend.

Zapata began thinking of workarounds. She did not believe that there was a world in which she and her companions could succeed in this shootout through standard means. For one, none of them had guns, while the opposing side seemed to possess countless guns. While she herself did hold in her hand a rather incredible piece of weaponry, it lacked the required range to actually attack at those attempting to mow her down. Transitively, if there was no way to shoot any of the soldiers, and the soldiers intended to keep on shooting, then there was no way to thwart the inevitability of being shot—at least, if one sticks to the traditional means of ending a shootout.

Perhaps, Zapata thought, there could be a way to stop the enemy’s shooting without actually having to shoot the enemy herself. Surrender, she thought, could potentially be one of those ways, but there was no way to ensure it. GüdTek might continue viewing her as a threat and attempt to kill her even as she raises the white banner. Instead then, Zapata considered, perhaps she could utilize a hostage. It was a tried and true method of getting authorities to stop shooting at those they viewed as terrorists, with the only issue in the plan being that she had no one which she could effectively turn into a hostage. The construction workers, who were all regular civilians, had already left the area, and even if they had remained, Zapata wasn’t sure if Gibson would stop shooting to protect a nameless innocent.

It was presently obvious to Zapata Tochihuitl that the GüdTek corporation did not care for the nameless. They did, however, care quite a bit for those with well-known monikers and investments in the company. There was only one person in eyesight who fit that description, and it just so happened to be Badden herself. If she could somehow apprehend Badden, she could easily get the Gibsons to cease their shooting, potentially even allowing her to continue with the archeological dig as planned. The only issue in this plan was therefore its premise, the underlying concept of actually grabbing Badden to begin with, which seemed rather impossible. It was true that Badden herself was standing, effectively, out in the open, but there were formations of soldiers on either side of her, and no one would be able to pass through that grassy corridor without getting trapped in a pincer movement and shot at repeatedly and brutally. Or, to be more accurate, Zapata considered, most people would not be able to pass through that corridor, but, potentially, if there were to exist a theoretical individual who could withstand an infinite onslaught of battery, then that theoretical person might be able to work through the task of abducting Badden.

Zapata, rather naturally, allowed her eyes to wander, specifically towards a single point, the point where Carlyle Flanders stood. Zapata, in all honesty, did not particularly enjoy the presence of Carlyle Flanders. He was generally an awkward guy to be around, whose sensibilities and sense of humor seemed to be universally stuck in the 1800s. Additionally, he was something of a face-down card, a man who was nominally on her side but whose true intentions were always up in the air. He was a man who worked for whatever side he thought would win, and to stay on his good side, Zapata always tried to project a facsimile of order and power when near him. Regardless, Carlyle was the obvious choice when it came to the prospect of getting someone to quickly kidnap Badden, seeing as he was a man with impenetrable skin, and Zapata hoped that ordering him to do so would give him the idea that she was in charge and that she would never surrender to the opposing side, that side which might start to seem enticing to him.

“Carlyle!” Zapata shouted across the field of gunsmoke, leaning behind a rock which was rapidly eroding due to the constant barrage of bullets.

“Yes?” Carlyle responded in a rather nonchalant tone, at least considering the circumstances, sitting behind a smaller and less protective rock.

“Do you think you could run over there to where all the gunmen are and abduct Badden?”

“There are quite a lot of people there, and they don’t seem to be interested in stopping their shooting anytime soon. I might get hurt.”

“Aren’t you supposed to be immortal, Carlyle? I think you can manage that!”

“All things considered, yes, I am immortal, but I can still get hurt in the short term.”

“Carlyle, if you don’t allow yourself to be hurt, the rest of us will die. If you truly believe that our side has the capability to win, I need you to do me this favor.”

“Fine then,” Carlyle sat up, “but I would appreciate it if I was given a little more respect around here.”

After wiping the dust off his khakis, Carlyle Flanders immediately engaged in a rapid sprint towards the battalion. Noticing the lone runner, the soldiers all began focusing on mowing down Carlyle specifically. A countless amount of bullets were shot at him, and while none were able to actually pierce the skin, he couldn’t help but think about the bruises he was bound to wake up with the next day.

As the bullets proved ineffective at actually halting the raging comet of a man, the troops surrounding Badden seemed to panic, though their masked visages made it a little difficult to tell exactly what was going through their heads. There was increasingly less shooting as Carlyle got closer and increasingly more erratic movement of the feet, with some troops even fleeing from the battalion entirely, until eventually, before a retreat to the jet could even be considered, Carlyle made it to Badden, and the two stared into each other’s eyes.

“I am here to apprehend you,” Carlyle stated to her plainly, “please don’t make this difficult.”

“Wow,” she replied, “I really never thought you’d turn on me so brazenly.”

“Well that just seems like a poor prediction. I remember the little talk we had when you hired me and I think that I pretty clearly stated my motives for joining your paramilitary. I openly explained to you the inconsistency of my allegiance, and that I would only remain on your payroll for as long as I thought that you might be on the winning side of history. Things have changed since then, and I have changed with them, but none of this should come as a surprise to you.”

“To be clear, Mr. Flanders, I am not surprised that you utilized the stipulation baked into your contract. I was fully aware of its presence and I believe that I took it seriously. What I’m surprised about is how you think that the Lockeites have the potential to lose.”

“I guess I had an innate feeling. There are larger societal factors at play, political mechanisms, material conditions, but all of that theory gets melted down and solidified after passing through the sieve of my mind. I would never call myself an intelligent man, but I do have a rather interesting brain which, if provided with enough instances of observation, can transmutate aimless optic feedback into incredibly accurate predictions regarding the political future of the world.”

Carlyle then grabbed Badden’s arms and flung her over his back to be carried. Badden could’ve tried to fight this maneuver but she had very little confidence that she’d be able to run away without Carlyle eventually catching up to her and beating her into an amorphous pulp. Naturally, she opted to comply. As she passed down the aisle between either half, she saw the various Gibson troopers lay down their guns, obviously not wanting to bear the wrath that would come from corporate if they accidentally shot their own boss. Badden had to admit to herself that she made for a very good hostage.

By the time that the two made it to the top of the hillock, Theta had already managed to set the rope lowering mechanism up and running again, and despite the fact that up until a few moments earlier they had all been under fire, there was a layer of calm overseeing the interlocutors.

“Well,” Theta spoke up, “I’d reckon that now is the time for someone else to head down there. I really don’t like the idea of Vraxi being trapped alone down there with no way to communicate with the world above. Does anyone remember who drew the second longest straw?”

“That would be me,” Fu Qier declared, looking somewhat weary from the recent barrage, “though I’d appreciate some help in putting on the harness.”

“Oh, sure, I can help you out with that. This is exactly the kind of issue which the suit-vac was designed to solve. Though, I must ask, Ms. Fu, if you’re certain you would like to do this. I know we sorta dragged you along here after that explosion but I want to make it clear that you are under no obligation to participate in this dig. You are a civilian train conductor and it’s in entirely possible that there may be some rather potent dangers down there.”

“I understand that, Theta, and I’m glad that you thought to give me the option, but regardless, I am going to go down there. I stand here as a woman who was kicked out of history. I sincerely believe I had the potential to achieve true greatness back in Chengdu, but the Lockeites prevented me from realizing those dreams. This uncovering, at least in my eyes, is a way for me to enter history once again.”

As Vraxi left the Library of Rhapta, she had already assured herself that no help was coming and that she was very likely to starve to death in this city lost to time. Perhaps those people who were supposed to come down with her had all been killed, or arrested, or in some way apprehended. Perhaps they had simply all decided and agreed that they really didn’t like Vraxi and that it would be for the best to just leave her down there. There was really no way to know for certain, but regardless, a little slimy segment of Vraxi’s brain kept suggesting that this abandonment was in some manner, or perhaps entirely, her own damn fault. She should’ve been better. Perhaps then her friends wouldn’t’ve all collectively agreed that they actually kinda hate her and wouldn’t mind seeing her die. It really was an unfortunate thought, but she increasingly began to believe it as the most likely option. She really just hoped that Theta wouldn’t feel too guilty about leaving her down here, and that they’d be able to move on and do real good with a clear mind, cleared of her presence.

Then, in a direct contrast to every thought in Vraxi’s mind, she watched as the distinct figure of Fu Qier lowered from the ceiling and landed on the cobbled ground.

“You’re alive?” Vraxi gasped in an almost embarrassing degree of amazement.

“Yes,” Qier responded plainly, “We just ran into a little disturbance is all. Everyone is fine, physically speaking.”

Qier removed her harness and pulled on the rope to send it back to the surface.

“Oh, phew,” Vraxi’s face was visibly reddened, “that’s all good to hear. I thought that you’d all abandoned me for a second there.”

“Now why would you think that?”

“No reason. I just get a little nervous sometimes,” Vraxi faked a laugh “sorry.”

The sound of the harness descending again could be heard amid the silence of the cave, creating a subtle echo which extended the presence of the machinery within the soundscape. Vraxi could just make out the shape of Theta from where she stood, and her heartbeat finally began to approach a healthy rhythm.

Vraxi led the way to the center of the Gnosisopolis. Theta, Zapata, Diogo, Mbali, and Qier followed suit, while Vraxi was informed that Carlyle had been tasked with staying above the hole in order to keep an eye and a grip on the recently abducted Gabriella Badden. Vraxi was surprised by this development, but continued walking at a steady pace, through the wide streets of Rhapta, and further through the narrow halls of Rhapta’s old royal palace. Deeper and deeper, the sextet barreled through, on a path to the room which Hecateus long ago described and sealed with magic. Through corridor and passageway, they ventured to the spiritual center of the Earth.

The throne stood empty, yet still pristine, as if erosion never made it to this obscure curiosity, as if every droplet of sublimated water fell out of the way of its indomitable aura, allowing it to persist for multiple millenia, good as new and never used. Vraxi almost felt tempted to sit on it—and surely nothing bad could come from such a minor act—yet she felt that she would somehow be disrespecting some subtle spirit, that same wisp of vestigial life which had allowed for the throne to remain usable for so long. Vraxi, tossing the thought away, looked down, and in doing so found a strange sight plastered on the floor in front of the throne. It looked like a large wheel, some alchemical pattern, split into ten segments around an interior circle and with each segment possessing writing in a handful of different languages. Most of that language was incomprehensible, written in scripts forgotten to time, but one of the languages, she quickly recognized, was seemingly just Greek.

“Diogo,” she spoke with an air of urgency, “you can read ancient Greek, right?”

“I’m not great at it,” he replied, scratching his neck, “but I guess you could say I’m passable.”

“Can you read what’s written in these glyphs?”

“Sure, starting clockwise, it reads, ‘Ayuppan, of the righteous, Lucifer, of the wretched, Aldar Kose, of the living, Santa Muerte, of the dead, Inkosazana, of love, The Unknown Soldier, of war, Israfil, of art, Orunmila, of wisdom, Vasundhara, of the land, and Mazu, of the sea.”

“Well,” Zapata said, “I think that leaves us all with one question: Who the hell is Vasundhara?”

“It seems to me,” Theta said in response, “that they may be the final puzzle piece.”

As Theta spoke, in a land far away, a tremendous fire was rising.

Revolution on High: Part 1

Chapter 68: Revolution on High: Part 1

King Yutthisathian II was an awfully particular master. He was the sort that wished for every observable element of his life to possess the utmost degree of presentability and he was further the sort that believed that all his wishes were ordained by the divine right of kings. Some say that kings do not deserve the level of opulence they receive from birth, but Yutthisathian believed that he had climbed a long and perilous spiritual ladder and conquered Yama’s wheel in order to reach that lauded position. Those who lived among the peasantry should’ve simply been better in their previous lives, and perhaps be a bit more thankful that they didn’t get birthed into the world as crickets.

Yutthisathian was currently preparing for a particularly important gala, the sort which would be chock-full of Western business executives all chomping at the bit to be embraced by a highly idealized yet believably authentic portrait of the nation of Siam and its people. It was the sort of event that required an ungodly quantity of champagne—as the Westerners appeared to drink that stuff like water—and a level of performative neatness and poise which would paint such an appealing picture as to convince those businesspeople that Siam was an attractive locale to deposit their investments.

Yutthisathian himself, however, was not an especially competent decorator, and this was a fact which he was first to recognize. He could observe what Western guests seemed to be impressed by and seemed to gloss over, but the actual process of designing a fully realized vision of the perfect event was such a taxing effort on his mind that he had to offload most of the actual work of coming up with it all on his rather larger cast of servants. One of his most trusted maids, a woman by the name of Patcharee Ratnaporn, was tasked with both the design, acquisition, and actual creation of various floral arrangements which were expected to be hung up around the palace before the guests arrived tomorrow night. With all temporal things considered, Yutthisathian II couldn’t help but notice a lack of flowers. If this lack continued, his guests would surely comment on the barrenness of color within the estate, and perhaps even assume that it’s due to the royal funds secretly being utterly destitute, possibly even leading them to actively withdraw investments in the country, a motion which he simply couldn’t allow to occur.

“Patcharee!” Yutthisathian yelled into the reverberant halls of the royal palace.

“I’m on the way, your majesty!” a smaller voice reverberated back, followed by the sound of hurried footsteps and the appearance of a slight visage through a nearby door, that of a winded maid.

“Ah, Patcharee, I’m glad you came to see me. Now, I must admit, there has been a certain curiosity running through my mind as of late which simply demands an immediate answer, an answer I sincerely hope you have.”

“And what would that curiosity be, your majesty?”

“Well, simply put, I gave you the quite simple instruction of putting up flowers, yet I see no flowers, no matter which room I enter within this home of mine. Surely, you understand the importance of the flowers, right? The gala tomorrow night is of the utmost significance in regards to our nation’s prosperity and every observable aspect must be perfect.”

“I understand, your majesty,” Patcharee bowed, “and I sincerely apologize for the delays,” she bowed again, “but there are certain logistical issues which have made certain aspects of your requests, well, functionally impossible.”

“And what would those issues be?”

“Well, firstly, none of the flowers you requested actually grow in Siam-”

“That was on purpose, Patcharee. We don’t want to be overloading our guests with tropicality. They want things that they can recognize, topics of conversation where they feel they have expertise. If we introduce flowers which are entirely unfamiliar to them, they’ll feel less intelligent, act more reserved, speak less often, make fewer connections, and ultimately invest a below-ideal amount of money towards our nation’s future,” Yutthisathian paused a moment and took a breath, “Do you have children, Patcharee?”

“No, nor a husband, for that matter.”

“Nephews, nieces?”

“Many.”

“And wouldn’t like you for them to grow up in a Siam greater than that of your own childhood.”

“…Yes, I would like that.”

“Then you’ll have to put some more effort into the flowers! Their futures depend on it!”

“Yes, your majesty. I apologize, your majesty. But, unfortunately, your majesty, I just have one other issue in regards to the flowers, one even greater than that of where the flowers can be found, and that is that most of the flowers you suggested are entirely out of season. There simply isn’t any manner for me to acquire something like garden phlox, especially not in the needed quantities.”

“Now, Patcharee, I have a very simple question for you. How many hemispheres are there?”

“…Two?”

“Two! So when it’s winter in one place it’s summer in another. Every flower I listed grows somewhere. I don’t know exactly where to find it—that’s your job—but I know with certainty that they exist. I know you have access to a large number of suppliers. I know that this is an entirely doable task, but if you really believe it is, as you say, ‘functionally impossible,’ then I can always hire someone else. It’s not like there’s an absence of people who would like to be hired by a king.”

This was not the first time in which Yutthisathian II had threatened to fire one Patcharee Ratnaporn, and in fact, due to her frequent proximity to the man, she was perhaps the person who had been threatened by him the most. While the king tended to threaten all of his employees at least once, those threats were typically followed by an actual firing, but partially due to Patcharee’s usefulness and partially due to her skills in the art of diffusing his anger, she managed to avoid ever actually witnessing the object of those threats bombarded against her.

“I sincerely apologize, your majesty,” Patcharee spoke in supplication, knowing that one of the best ways to diffuse the king was to constantly restate his majestic nature, “truly, this was all my fault,” she continued, knowing that the king found great joy in seeing others insist that they themselves were in the wrong, “but I believe you’ve opened my eyes, and I will do better,” Patcharee concluded, knowing that Yutthisathian enjoyed it when all metrics of improvement were attributed to his own words and actions.

“Patcharee, there is no need for you to worry, and I will accept your apology with dignity and grace. Now please, think things over, perhaps even meditate a little over all my instructions, and recognize the achievability of the task at hand.”

With those parting words, Yutthisathian II left the room, with a grin of a job well done painted across his face.

Upon her master’s departure, Patcharee began to enter an immense state of panic. While she had avoided having her job taken away from her many times over in the past, the importance which Yutthisathian has prescribed upon this gala meant that, if she were to leave the walls barren and flowerless, she would assuredly not only be fired but be put on the royal blacklist, forced to disclose to any future employer that she had severely disappointed the king. Being placed on the blacklist was, in all truth and honestly, effectively a one-way ticket to destitution, prison, and oftentimes murder within those prisons. It was not a fate which Patcharee wished to be beholden of but the process of actually avoiding such a fate was entirely unknown to her. Many of the flowers which Yutthisathian demanded were not available anywhere at this time of year, not even in the most prestigious international markets. If Patcharee had known about this gala beforehand she may have been able to send a special order to some boutique cultivator, but she had only been informed of the gala’s existence three days prior. Likewise, it was all beginning to seem like she was on an unchanging railroad towards total ruination with no way to exit the train car.

Subsequently, Patcharee walked into the palace garden. Theoretically, said garden was only meant to be occupied by royals and nobles, but Patcharee was on such a high position within the hierarchy of the maid staff that people tended to assume that she was allowed to enter areas which, officially, she was forbidden from. Accordingly, the cousin of a cousin of the king who sat in the garden, lounging in the shade, took no careful notice of Patcharee’s presence. As she sat down in a secluded corner of the garden, she thought the whole thing rather funny, for she never abided by the often given and rarely useful advice of King Yutthisathian II but his suggestion to try some meditation seemed offly apt for her present conundrum. In order to contain that raging whirlwind of unknowable flowers storming and shaking within her skull she needed to allow herself a modicum of calm. She stared at a statuette of the goddess Vasundhara positioned in front of her for a moment, before eventually, gradually, laying her eyes to rest.

A shock. A raging, rising, roiling tempest. A sudden inflammation, followed by rapid exhaustion, followed by rapid surges of uncontainable energy. A bodily rejection, ultimately resulting in a prolonged period of reddish vomit, followed by a lasting sting, a continuous buzz which placed her head in an almost intoxicating stupor and her body below in a tremendous looseness.

Following all of this, Patcharee started to panic further. Disregarding the fact that she had assuredly wound up with some horrible illness, she was also now responsible for an incredibly unattractive stain which terrorized the overall look of the otherwise peaceful garden. However, simultaneously, nobody had seen her. The cousin of a cousin was asleep and out of view, meaning that she could leave the mess to be dealt with by whatever maid might be next to observe it. Typically, she would avoid such actions, not believing it right to pass the burden of work down to those who were assuredly less experienced, but she still possessed a tremendous amount of work to do in regards to the flowers, and this sudden bout of illness had her feeling far too weak to engage in any sort of custodial duties. Just this once, she figured, she could kick the can to someone else. Maybe, after this whole gala problem is over, she can find whatever maid was tasked to clean the vomit and give her a gift of some sort.

After finally making the decision that she would not clean the mess she had made, Patcharee was then left with the task of actually lifting herself off of the ground. Whatever bad piece of food she’d eaten to cause her sudden malady had made it so that every minor movement of the torso gave way to a bracing, stringent pain which demanded to be recognized. After gradually carrying her back into a plank position, the heavy degree of shaking her nerves had instinctually ignited subsequently led to her losing all balance and falling face-first onto the ground again.

While she didn’t want to openly admit it, she was beginning to lose hope. The idea of somehow obtaining the impossible flowers in this weakened, embarrassing state seemed laughable, and the prospect of actually leaving the garden without collapsing into unconsciousness seemed increasingly less likely. Her vision began to grow blurry, and she opted to rest her face atop the pillowy grass, if only for a moment. She just needed a few moments of shut-eye, and perhaps after that she’d be ready to pick herself up and dedicate herself entirely to the task at hand. She very rapidly drifted into the land of dreams, though her mind was too tired to dream up anything other than an inky blackness.

Patcharee woke up again and immediately checked her watch. A full thirty minutes had passed. She was incredibly frustrated that she had overslept so much and at the same time incredibly thankful that the minor prince hadn’t decided to stop his sunbathing and wander near her. She tried to lift up her torso with her wobbly arms and discovered that, though shaky, they had recovered some strength. However, before she could start moving from a kneeling to a standing position, something on the grass laid before her caught her eye. Patcharee, as one of the garden’s most frequent maintainers, had a nearly encyclopedic knowledge of every flower which bloomed there, and she could state with the utmost certainty that nowhere in the garden was grown the exuberant purple of the garden phlox. Yet, despite this knowledge, and despite her knowledge of the environments in which the garden phlox grows, she clearly spotted a single, beautiful, exuberantly purple flower of that species amid the grass laid before her.

It was all incredibly strange. She hadn’t seen the flower before her nap, and in fact had never seen one in person, yet, like magic, one of the most important components of Yutthisathian’s impossible arrangements materialized from out of thin air. Slowly and carefully, she removed a clipper from her apron and pruned the singular flower from its stem. It was a very small start, but at least she could now say that she had begun work on her assignment.

Once Patcharee managed to steadily support her body weight with nothing but her two feet, she heard a rustling in the nearby bushes, and not the kind of rustling often produced by the garden’s resident peacocks, but specifically the rustling of a rather clumsy, perhaps a little daydrunk, human member of the Siamese nobility. It was assuredly Prince Vajirananavarorasa, the cousin of the cousin of the king, someone who Patcharee, admittedly, was quite unprepared to greet. Not only was there a patch of bloody vomit on the ground, but also various splotches of the stuff on her apron, shirt, and chin. It would be very easy for the noble to correctly assume who was responsible for the mess, and the creation of such a tremendous mess in the most harmonious and spiritually significant garden in the entire kingdom was not a crime to be taken lightly. While Yutthisathian himself understood Patcharee’s importance as an employee, to the royal peerage she was just another maid. Vajirananavarorasa would hold no qualms in punishing her to the fullest extent of the law, and from her occasional interactions with the man, she knew with quite certainty that he was not the kind to forgive.

It increasingly became clear to Patcharee that there was no way to explain the mess without facing punishment nor any way to clean the mess before her potential captor could glimpse it. Her mind then produced two methods which could allow her to avoid facing confinement: either hide in the nearby shrubbery and hopefully not get pricked by the thorns, or kill the prince. She obviously could not go through with the latter choice both due to her lack of appropriate weaponry and as-stated wish to avoid any jail time. Accordingly, she jumped into a nearby conflagration of frangipani shrubs and attempted to conceal herself with the glossy leaves. Seconds later, she spotted the visage of Vajirananavarorasa through the greenery, looking confused at first and then quite upset after spotting the unfortunate puddle on the ground. He seemed to look around a bit before eventually giving up on the task of finding whoever might be responsible, turning around, when, right before he would’ve left the area, Patcharee’s mysterious illness flared up, causing an audible sneeze to erupt from the shrubbery.

“What was that?” Vajirananavarorasa asked, “Whoever made that noise, reveal yourself!”

Patcharee remained completely silent. However, gradually, a heap of hot and urgent air began to float up through her esophagus, pushing up against her nasal cavity and begging to be shot out into the world. She tried to delay the inevitable, at least until the prince left, but he refused to move his feet, and her own body refused to wait any longer.

“Achoo!” The sound reverberated around the boughs of frangipani and filled the garden with an easily triangulatable cacophony.

Vajirananavarorasa immediately discovered Patcharee’s hiding spot and grabbed her by the collar through the stubborn branches and onto the open grass.

“You utterly insolent servant,” he spoke, “how dare you create such a disastrous disorder in this most pristine of places, and further, how dare you refuse to respond to your ruler. You are a subject of the Siamese crown and you will listen to its prongs with the utmost respect. As should every good civilian and especially a direct employee of the royal palace. This little stunt you just pulled is absolutely unbecoming of our institution and I will assuredly be filing a request for your permanent removal from the palace staff.”

“I apologize, your majesty.”

“And what is your name? I need to know it in order to file my request.”

“Your majesty, please, just give me a chance to explain myself. I assure you that there are circumstances out of my control which can justify my unusual actions.”

“I asked for your name, maid. Continuous disrespect of a noble as respected as myself can lead to consequences far worse than losing one’s job. Please, maid, think before you say your next words. They may be very important in regards to your future.”

“Your majesty, I swear, I can clean this all up, I can perform any task you ask of me in apology. Just, please, your majesty, I really need this job.”

“I will ask you one more time. What is your name?”

“P- P- P-”

“Go on now. What comes after the P?”

It was in that brief moment of inquisition when, even if only slightly, Vajirananavarorasa’s grip on Patcharee’s collar loosened. Patcharee grasped that golden opportunity, and began to sprint as fast as she could possibly manage. The fabric on the back of her uniform tore off as she made her sudden move, and the prince, so determined in his quest of finding out her name, was momentarily wholly dumbstruck. However, he was only actually stunned for a few seconds. After which point, he was overcome by rage, rage for being so thoroughly disrespected, as if he were an old crone and she a meddlesome youngster, dashing off while he was left helpless. But Prince Vajirananavarorasa was not old yet. He still possessed some spryness in his step and the object of his anger was still in eyeshot. He began running after that damnable maid. As he did so, he fiddled for an object in his sleek, satin pocket, a plasticine knob chock-full of electrodes, and pressed down hard upon a central red button. Suddenly, and at quite a quick rate, the many sliding doors which connected the walled-in garden to the rest of the palace all simultaneously began to close.

This rapid and total removal of all possible ways out was quite the frightening sight for one Patcharee Ratnaporn. She very quickly turned around to make sure she wasn’t missing any exits, and in doing so spotted the reason for escape, the gradually approaching visage of that wicked, horrible prince.

“You can’t run any longer, maid! All you’ve done is doomed yourself! Don’t expect to get off with a simple letter of discharge! You’re going to jail no matter what! So please, maid, surrender now and avoid granting your future self an even longer sentence.”

Patcharee had no escape route. She had no tricks up her sleeve. She had no friends she could call in to settle the situation. She didn’t have many friends at all. She had no social techniques to convince the horrible prince that she was actually quite useful and deserved to retain her position. She still lacked the level of rapport with the Yutthsathian II needed to have him vouch for her. She was stuck, completely and utterly, with absolutely no means for distraction or delay, and despite all of that, despite all of these mounting threats and concerns, her mind could not fully focus on the total state of terror presented by the prince. She just couldn’t stop thinking about that lone, impossible phlox. That tiny, beautiful, utterly foreign flower which she continued to store in her pocket. She imagined that she’d have to depart with it once she was arrested. She imagined that, without her, there would be no possible way for those floral arrangements to be ready for the gala. She also imagined that, in the grand scheme of things, the presence of those flowers probably wouldn’t have much of an effect on the nation as a whole, or at least not to the degree that the king purported. So, ultimately, she imagined what the palace would be like without her, and she imagined that it would do fine. Someone would be promoted to fill her absence, some rookie would be hired to some dirtier position, and the nobles would be just as dissatisfied as usual. Some of her coworkers would probably miss her, but they’d be busy enough with their own issues and the act of molding their fate to be different than her own. Ultimately, she finally figured, they would manage, while most of the royals wouldn’t even notice that she’d left.

Once again, her thoughts drifted to the phlox again, even as the prince drew closer. She thought of every individual petal, every windswept leaf, that white-pink-purple gradient which tracked its maturity, and most often and most immensely, she thought of the stem, that mighty base which greatness grew out from. She wished, albeit for only a moment, that one such stem would spring up from the ground before her, so as to provide a moment of beauty in her final few seconds of freedom.

Prince Vajirananavarorasa was subsequently impaled.

It was not a sword which pierced his flesh, nor any blade of human making for that matter, but something else entirely, the stuff of dreams, specifically the stuff of Patcharee’s dreams.

An unnaturally large stem, resembling, albeit without leaves or flowers, that of the juvenile phlox, had sprung from the ground and in a rather Vladian fashion impaled the persnickety prince. Stepping slightly closer, Patcharee could see that a bit of the stem was peaking out from the prince’s mouth, and judging from where the stem seemed to enter the body, she presumed that it had cut though his entire digestive system. On seeing this, Patcharee cast away all suspicions that the prince might still be alive. She breathed in and breathed out. There was a dead man in the garden. The only other person in the garden was herself. The dead man had died under unusual circumstances. These three facts regarding the potential case at hand rapidly whirled around her mind and very quickly began to trouble her. It was true that she had avoided arrest, and she was very thankful for that recent development, but at the same time, she couldn’t help but feel like anyone investigating the case of Prince Vajirananavarorasa’s untimely death was bound to look at her, Patcharee, the disloyal maid, the only one present at the moment and location of his death, with a healthy serving of suspicion.

Patcharee, rather gradually, began to walk away from the crime scene. One aspect of this case which could potentially be in her favor was the fact that the garden, intended to be a place of the utmost holiness, did not permit the presence of any electronic signals, including those which would be produced by security cameras. This meant that no one could be certain that she was adjacent to the prince at the time of his death so long as she quickly left, but it also meant that she couldn’t prove that the prince’s death was really just an act of god. Before she could fully leave that area of the garden, however, she remembered something else, there was still a pool of her vomit, and subsequently her saliva, and subsequently her DNA on the ground. She would be involved in the case no matter what at the moment they discover that the prince was no longer living. If only, she wished, she could delay that discovery.

The sound of someone entering the garden was then emitted.

Patcharee could not run away. There wasn’t enough time to run away, and every door other than the one which was just opened was still locked. The only way to reach that door would require her first passing the person who just entered and therefore revealing that she was in the garden at the time of the murder. She could, however, still rely on an old classic, she could still go and hide in the frangipani bush. As the footsteps came closer, she jumped into the shrubbery, and wished to all the gods and especially Vasundhara that whoever was entering the garden wouldn’t notice that the prince was dead. He did, afterall, still stand upright, though perhaps at a slight angle. If one were to only briefly pass by, especially if they weren’t the type to be all that aware of their surroundings, they might just come to the conclusion that Prince Vajirananavarorasa was just a little bit tired. It wasn’t likely but it was possible.

Peeking through the greenery, Patcharee saw King Yutthisathian II pass by the corner, presumably on some recreational walk.

“Good afternoon, Vaji,” the king declared as he waved at the cousin of his cousin, seemingly unaware that the prince’s heart had long stopped beating.

Patcharee truly felt that there was a chance, a chance that her king was just stupid enough to mistake a dead man standing for a member of the living. She just wished that, if only for a second, she could pilot that upright corpse, make him respond in some passably believable way. She wished that she could grow roots into his veins and puppet his limbs just to give some kind of plausible ambulation to the whole facade.

Immediately following this impossible wish, the corpse of Vajirananavarorasa began to wave back at the king. The king, fully fooled, continued along his walk. Patcharee could no longer deny the fact that something incredibly strange had happened to her during her blackout. She once again imagined a system of roots in the prince’s veins, and once again, he began to wave.

Patcharee seemed to possess complete control over the unusual plant which piloted the corpse of the prince through his veins. She imagined the roots shifting clockwise, and Vajirananvarorasa turned around, facing her. The blank expression on the prince’s face frightened her, and she decided that this strange power, even if it did save her from the king’s suspicion, was not the sort of thing which a mortal like her should have her hands on. She reached into her apron again and grabbed a pair of pliers. She then crouched under the upright corpse and snipped the stem between where it left the ground and where it entered the body, giving the prince what looked like a small green tail. Strangely, however, the prince did not fall down. Despite his objective lack of warm blood, his feet were somehow able to keep him standing. Without much purpose, she thought of the bodily roots raising and lowering. Subsequently, the prince began to walk.

Even when disconnected from the ground, Patcharee could still direct the body to move. This was an incredibly frightening concept, but also one, Patcharee considered, which might allow her to prove her innocence. If she could get the prince to walk, it wouldn’t be difficult to walk him to his room. From there, she could simply claim that he was sick and that he’d decided to cloister himself within his locked chamber. Perhaps she could even have the prince ‘die’ from his illness to cut off the loose ends, or maybe she could walk him onto a train and have him ‘move to the countryside.’ There was a plethora of manners in which this newly acquired boon could help her avoid a false punishment, but the mechanics of it all began to lead her to a new line of inquiry. If she had complete control over the plant, does that mean she was the one who initially impaled the prince, making her genuinely guilty of the murder of royalty, a crime which was universally punished by death?

No, she thought in response, guilt is not a quality determined by actions. It is a quality determined by the court. She was an innocent woman, and she would remain an innocent woman for as long as she possibly could. It wasn’t worth her time to fret over some divine concept of innocence, as the legal form was the only form which held power over her.

Accordingly, with a relatively clear mind, she grasped the prince’s cold right hand, got the both of them walking, and strolled through the palace with a face of total innocence. She dropped him off in his room and locked the door with his key, and when a fellow maid asked her why his face looked so flushed, Patcharee told her that he’d been feeling very ill, and that she’d held his hand to help with his balance.
