Revolution on High: Part 2

Chapter 69: Revolution on High: Part 2

Patcharee sat on the cold damp dirt beneath a moonlit sky. It was past midnight and she was out in the garden, not in the same garden in which her thoughts had led to the death of the prince, but in the garden of the maids, the one which grew plants for the kitchen and not just for the eyes and nose. There wasn’t nearly as much space in this utilitarian garden as opposed to the one dedicated to lounging, but she had found a small plot of fertile-enough dirt behind an outcropping of cassava plants which she figured would be adequate for her experiment. She took the single phlox flower out from her pocket, its color already somewhat leeched from stewing in her anxious sweat all day, and placed it on the ground before cupping her palms and creating a mound of dirt above and around it, fully concealing her chance at retribution.

Of all the events of the day leading up to this night, none, not even the killing of the prince, had intrigued her more than the sudden appearance of that flower. That flower, she figured, was her singular ticket to avoid an otherwise inevitable firing, she just needed to find a way to somehow make it multiply. Normally, she would consider such a task impossible. She had a general idea of how long it took for plants to grow and couldn’t expect this lone, dead, buried flower to sprout into a thousand more bursts of purple in the matter of a day. However, the rules of normalcy, it was beginning to seem, no longer really applied to her. Her entire life had been governed by a consistent set of rules, a series of constraints placed upon reality, perhaps by a god, perhaps by pure circumstance, perhaps by herself in another life, long ago. Regardless of their origin, she knew these restraints to be immutable, except, as the events of the preceding day had shown, their immutability was far more flexible than she had once suspected. If it was possible for her, with the snap of her fingers, to cause a gargantuan plant to grow through a man’s body in one gruesome second, then it would be idiotic to constrain any of her future endeavors on the teetering convention of logic.

She prayed.

“Oh Vasundhara,” she spoke beneath her breath, trying to avoid being heard by any stray maid who might be committing some nightly duty, “Oh lady of the land. I’ve observed what you have done for me before, and I wish to observe these feats again. Please, grant me the power to work through you, grant me the power to shape your word into life, grant me the power to weave this singular flower into a fertile field, grant me the power to live another day, and grant me the power to forever remember your name. I thank you, Vasundhara, for your honest guidance, and your generous gifts, and your ears in this time of trial.”

Patcharee, kneeling, bowed forward, bringing her head to the ground and letting it sink ever so slightly into the malleable earth. She breathed, and caught a whiff of stewing compost. It wasn’t a pretty smell, but in this moment she could not plug her nose, she simply had to view the decaying, condensed plant matter as yet another segment of a much greater natural process, of the creation of life through life, which was really quite beautiful in the grand scheme of things, and when she took another breath it was not compost she smelled but the concentrated scent of a field of blooming flowers. She opened her eyes and saw that the little plot of dirt was absolutely brimming with phlox. Patcharee was overjoyed. She wouldn’t be fired. Perhaps she would even be promoted for nailing such an impossible task. Perhaps, and this was potentially a long-shot concept but she couldn’t help but consider it, she would one day no longer be just a maid of the palace, finally graduating to the coveted position of ‘palatial administrator.’ She would have an office and everything. To her, that practically sounded like becoming royalty. It was truly a wonderful dream to consider, and she couldn’t stop considering it as she fished out her clippers, started cutting the flowers, and heard, seemingly out of nowhere, the sound of an approaching figure.

She wasn’t sure exactly what to do. The sudden, unexplained presence of these flowers would likely confuse any fellow maid who might pass by her, but at the same time, the average maid would have little interest in accusing her of suspicious behavior and little power to do so if they actually cared. Now, if a noble were to pass by, that could spell some larger problems, however, the average noble spent very little time in the garden of the maids. The garden of the maids held a purely utilitarian purpose and really did not smell too great, which resulted in any curious noble who peered in almost immediately peering out in order to head to the proper, royal garden. So, as a result, in the grand scheme of things, Patcharee really shouldn’t’ve been too stressed about whoever might see her cutting these new flowers, yet, despite this reasonable analysis, she had been so on edge for the entirety of the preceding day that she felt as if she was already on trial.

The figure passed by her, and it was just another maid, a rather young maid, one of the newest ones, a girl named Naphat, who Patcharee had always thought to be a bit strange, rather unusual for her tastes, a girl who always seemed jittery when one of the noble passed by, though Patcharee retained a face of politeness with the young maid while avoiding, as she did with all of the maids, any unnecessary conversations. One thing that Patcharee was quick to learn about the job was that regularly talking with one’s fellow employees about matters unrelated to work was one of the easiest ways to get fired. She realized that this behavior of hers might make her seem stuck-up to the other maids, but she was only doing it to preserve her own livelihood, a defensive instinct which maids like Naphat seemed to lack. Naphat was always talking with the other maids and actively trying to forge connections with those she didn’t know. Not only that, but Naphat’s conversations were barely ever about work, and for that matter barely about the palace, and for that matter she often suggested that she and others should meet outside of the palace. Patcharee had honestly begun to worry that Naphat might be trying to start a union among the maids. It was a fairly admirable idea, but sadly quite unlikely to ever be achieved. The job of being a maid at the royal palace, despite the really rather shallow conditions, was one of the most in-demand occupations in all of Krungthep, simply due to the honor of working with royalty. Even if every single one of the maids united, the king would have no qualms with firing every one and hiring a new cast of eager workers. It just wasn’t a job where a plan like that could work, but in a certain sense, she was fond of the younger generation’s willingness to try.

Naphat, to Patcharee’s surprise, did not simply walk by her. Rather, she stopped, looked at her, looked at the flowers, and then looked at Patcharee once again with a face that seemed to expect a proper answer.

Patcharee, who had not been asked any verbal question, did not feel the need to respond. If Naphat really wanted some information from her, she’d have to raise her voice to do so.

“It’s a nice night tonight,” Naphat casually began talking.

“A lot better than last night,” Patchare responded, expectant of what was to come, “all the rain’s cleared up.”

“That’s for sure. The lack of modern lighting fixtures in this ancient, constantly decaying palace, combined with the rain, can make it really hard to see at night. But tonight’s a lot better. I can see everything completely clearly.”

“That’s right,” Patcharee said, continuing to clip the flowers while ignoring Naphat’s implications, “my vision is unimpaired.”

“Alright,” Naphat crouched to Patcharee’s level, “I’m just gonna be straight with you. I saw what you did.”

“And what was it that I did?”

“You just made a patch of flowers bloom from nothing in a matter of seconds. That sorta thing is hard to ignore.”

“Alright then,” Patcharee responded, relieved that Naphat hadn’t observed the death of the prince, “I guess you’re not lying then.”

“And how’d you do it?”

“To be completely honest with you, Naphat, this is my first time trying. I’m not exactly sure as to how it all works.”

“Do you think you could do it again?”

“Probably. I’d hope so.”

“Y’know, it’s a very useful ability you’ve got here. The kind of ability which might be wasted in this particular position.”

“And why do you say that?”

“You have the power to make stubborn plants bloom. That power could prove to be extraordinarily useful in a drought. You could ensure the consistent production of food in our nation’s poorest regions, and maybe even abroad. But flowers, well, I’m not trying to argue that there isn’t a purpose for flowers—I actually quite like flowers—but we can both admit that they don’t hold quite the same utility, especially when they’re only really visible to royal eyes. I don’t think that an ideal Siam would be without your admittedly rather beautiful arrangements, but they wouldn’t be cloistered in the palatial halls, they’d be out in public for all to admire.”

“And does your ‘Ideal Siam’ involve the royals at all?”

“Well,” Naphat looked over her shoulder and across every sightline she could track within her eye, attempting to ensure that absolutely no one was listening in on what she was about to admit, “Patcharee, you seem to me like and intelligent woman, so I’m just gonna be completely honest with you, and if you find my honesty repulsive, I simply ask that you keep whatever information I say to you to yourself. Can you promise me that?”

“Sure, I can promise you.”

“Good. Now to answer your question, no. The royals are total leeches on society and so are the bourgeois class they uphold. I want their crimes against the people tried in a revolutionary court, their property seized by a proletarian government, and generally to spark a total dissolution of the old order. I am a card-carrying member of the People’s Army of All Siam, though I’m not carrying my card with me at the moment because the PAAS instructed me to take a fake identity in order to infiltrate the royal palace. Judging by my presence here, you can argue that I’ve succeeded in that particular goal.”

“I see. And is your attempt to conscript me into your party?”

“Well, I wouldn’t mind. I’m always down to induct others into our organization. In fact, I’ve already managed to get a handful of other maids involved. And it goes without saying that your particular set of skills would be of the utmost use to the party.”

“I appreciate your enthusiasm, Naphat, but I think I’ll have to think this offer over. Regardless, I’ve still got to get to work on these arrangements and I only have so much time before the gala starts.”

“Alright then, Patcharee. At the end of the day this is all up to you. But please, don’t forget about anything I’ve told you. Keep it in the back of your brain at all times. Let yourself be reminded of it whenever you witness injustice, whenever you witness the devaluation of your labor, and whenever you witness the truly evil views of the ruling class, as I’m sure you’ll see plenty of tonight.”

Then, once again, the sound of someone walking interspersed the air of the garden of the maids. In response, almost instinctually, Naphat hid in a nearby bush, while Patcharee, not sensing the same alarm, stood entirely still. Patcharee then saw who it was that was walking into the garden, and quickly understood the reason for Naphat’s line of action.

“Hello, your majesty,” Patcharee greeted King Yutthisathian II.

“Hello to you as well, Patcharee,” the king responded in a gentle voice, “I see that you’ve gotten your hands on some phlox. Like I said, if you just meditate on the task, you’ll quickly find that it’s actually quite easy.”

“Once again, your majesty, you were right and I was wrong.”

“Oh, Patcharee, you praise me too much. Though, admittedly, I do appreciate the praise. God knows I don’t get enough of it these days. Have you seen what those guerillas in the north have been doing lately?”

“I heard there were attacks on some police stations. And I imagine they haven’t stopped setting fire to the houses of certain landlords.”

“I’m afraid it’s gotten even worse. They seem to have burned down part of the Chiang Mai palace. Obviously it’s not nearly as important of a palace as this one, but it’s still a rather beautiful one. I can fondly recall spending many a childhood summer over there. I just hope that the flames didn’t reach the stables. Some of our nation’s fastest horses are stored there. Ah, it’s all a grand shame, Patcharee, what those PAAS bastards are doing to this country. I just hope their name won’t be uttered at the gala. I hope our investors can forget about our nation’s most shameful individuals.”

“I’m sure it won’t be on their minds. We’re far, far away from any of those involved in those attacks.”

“Ah, I’m sure you're right, wise Patcharee. It really is something of a northern phenomenon. The mountain soil doesn’t have quite the same number of nutrients as what we possess down south, so their brains never achieve the same complexity as the average resident of Krungthep. Truly, the soil quality can explain a lot about our nation’s regional differences: the North’s improper dialect, the North’s low school attendance, and yes, the North’s idiotic tendency to revolt. It’s all a matter of nutrients. If this whole great country was flooded with floodplain soil, if we all ate onions grown in similar conditions, then none of these violent disruptions would be plaguing us as they increasingly are now.”

“So you think this whole conflict is a consequence of the Northerner's brain?”

“Not all of them. No, plenty are plenty intelligent. But if we’re to look at averages, in a completely detached, scientific manner, then it would be impossible to make any other conclusion than that the brain of the northern Siamese is less developed than that of their southern counterpart. I’ve read many articles on this, and while at first I didn’t believe it, I simply can’t see any better explanation to the grand present issues gnawing at our nation’s foundation.”

“Alright then. I must admit that it’s an interesting theory-”

“Not just interesting, it is very much the truth. I plan to publish a study on the matter in the Royal Journal of Science.”

“Well, I’ll make sure to give it a read. Now I better start getting to work on these arrangements before the guests start rolling in.”

“I appreciate your drive for hard work, Patcharee. I’ll see you at the gala,” and with those parting words the king exited the garden of the maids and, slowly but surely, Naphat peeked her head out from the bushes.

“I really fucking hate that guy,” she stated very bluntly, “but the garden here clearly isn’t a safe place to be speaking about confidential matters. I’ll see you sometime in the future, Patcharee, and I really hope you consider my offer.”

The gala began at around 6 PM. The flowers had all been arranged rather haphazardly, but they were present, and that was enough to make Patcharee proud. She even saw a couple of those Westerners, those which the king spent so much time gushing about, stop to take a prolonged glance at one of her creations. She knew that it was empty praise, that it was utterly unimportant flattery that wasn’t even directed towards her but to her superiors, but with all the words of grandeur Yutthisathian II had applied to these flowers, she couldn’t help but feel a little warm inside.

Briefly, she saw Naphat pass by her, and she wondered what she might be thinking about all of these visitors. Naphat never talked kindly about the West, which was really rather understandable considering the stories she told about that corner of the world’s history. It was a different history than what Patcharee had been taught in school, but then again, she knew from first-hand experience that the Siamese government liked to appease the West. It made sense that a school system ultimately governed by a man like Yutthisathian II, who so admired everything Western, would have a positive bias pertaining to the Western world.

“Hey Patcharee,” Naphat spoke, interrupting Patcharee’s thoughts.

“What is it? If it’s about what we discussed last night then now really is not the time.”

“It’s entirely unrelated. I just wanted to say that I really find your floral arrangements to be quite beautiful.”

“Oh. Well, thank you. I was sorta on a time crunch but I think I managed to make something that I’m rather proud of.”

“And you usually give these arrangements names, right?”

“I do, generally speaking.”

“Does this one have a name?”

“Well, once again, I was in a bit of a time crunch. I only got ahold of the all-important phlox at the last minute, so naming conventions weren’t really at the front of my mind, but regardless, I do think I like the name Vasundhara for the piece.”

“Vasundhara,” Naphat paused, as if sensing something special about that name, “like the goddess?”

“That is what I had in mind.”

“Interesting. Well, I’d better go now. These Westerners really seem to be fucking obsessed with their deviled eggs and we’re already running low.”

Naphat proceeded to depart from Patcharee and she wasn’t again faced with the implications of her coworker’s questions until about an hour later. Dinner was being served, and all of the important guests had been shuffled over to the dining hall, leaving the rest of the palace rather empty. Despite this, as Patcharee was making her rounds around the venue, assuring that there wouldn’t be any dust after the meal’s end and during the masquerade, she ran into what seemed to be one of the many estimable guests, seemingly just wandering the palace halls, potentially lost.

“Ma’am?” Patcharee called out to her, “Would you like me to show you the way to the dining hall? Dinner has already begun to be served and my master was really hoping to fill every seat.”

“Oh, well, I appreciate the consideration,” the guest—who was strangely already in their masquerade costume—tersely replied, “I’m afraid that I wasn’t feeling of the greatest health this morning and the many hors d’oeuvres have entirely sated my appetite to the point where I can’t even possibly think about food without feeling a little bit ill in my stomach. Nevertheless, I feel good enough to dance, so I’ve opted to change into my costume early.”

“Well, if that’s how you feel, then I have no reason to try and change your mind, even if the food is quite delicious,” Patcharee paused for a moment and figured that she wouldn’t mind engaging in some polite conversation. Many of the guests whom the king invited were wholly unwilling to hold any pleasant speech with a woman of her standing, but this guest seemed approachable enough to do otherwise. She accordingly continued, “May I ask for your name?”

“You can call me Ms. Gambheeram. And what should I call you?”

“Oh,” she hadn’t expected for her question to be applied to her as well, “I guess you can call me Patcharee.”

“Patcharee Ratnaporn?”

“…Yes. I am Patcharee Ratnaporn. How did you know that that was me?”

“I didn’t know. I simply knew that there was a woman named Patcharee Ratnaporn in the building and extrapolated from your first name. It’s nice to meet you, Ms. Ratnaporn.”

“And it’s nice to meet you too, Ms. Gambheeram, but I guess I’m a little confused as to why you would know of my name at all. You understand that I am not a fellow guest, right? I am just a maid here.”

“I am fully aware of that, Ms. Ratnaporn. And I was not informed about your existence due to any particularly important occupation you might hold, but rather due to the fact that you seem to possess a very useful ability. Are you familiar with a woman by the name of Naphat Nantasri?”

“…Yes. Yes I am. And I have a feeling that I know what ability you’re alluding to.”

“And would you say that you have a certain connection, be it direct or merely ephemeral, to the goddess Vasundhara.”

Just hearing the name sent a small shockwave through Patcharee’s capillaries.

“Yes, I would say that I do.”

“Well I must admit that that is a very exciting thing to hear-”

“But can I ask you a question before we go any further in this little conversation?”

“Sure, please, go ahead.”

“What side are you on in all of this? And is Naphat okay? I’m assuming that you’re either in regular contact with her or you’ve actively captured her if you’re speaking about knowledge which should really only be known to me and her.”

“I can answer your question, Ms. Ratnaporn, but I’m going to do so quietly, and I sincerely wish that you also keep quiet about this whole conversation. Currently, I am loosely working for the Azanian government, in covert collaboration with the PAAS, which, within its lower ranks, includes a member by the name of Naphat Nantasri. Typically, the kind of information she would be conveying would not be of the grandiose sort to lead to international involvement, but the fact of the matter is that your collaboration with the goddess Vasundhara is of a much greater importance to the world at large than even you yourself seem to suspect. As a result, people like me have had to get involved.”

“And you're of the belief that I’d be willing to betray the royalty to help out with your cause.”

“That’s at least what Naphat suspected when she first conveyed her information to us. If that isn’t the case, then I’ll be out of here, but in all likelihood, you’ll probably see me sometime again regardless.”

Patcharee began to think very pensively. It was true that she hadn’t developed the greatest of bonds with the royal class. While she likely held a more cordial relationship with the king than any other lowly maid, every interaction she had with him was held with the constant threat that she may, at any moment, be summarily fired. Likewise, her actual opinion of the king was rather low, but still, the idea of acting against the king’s interests was incredibly frightening, because he was the most powerful man in the entire country, the one man who could, without any need for jurisdiction, without any real remorse, call for her execution at a moment’s notice—and it’s not like he hadn’t used this power on others who he’d deemed as traitors. It was a scary thought, and not a thought she liked to ponder and especially not one she liked to act on, but then again, inevitably, her mind drifted to the topic of the prince. She had murdered Prince Vajirananavarorasa in cold blood, a full-on landed noble, a great friend of the king, in an act which could absolutely be perceived as total treason. She would not be able to hide this crime for much longer. She could only keep his dead body stewing in his room for so long. His death was bound to be discovered, and she was bound to be a suspect, and the king was bound to be disappointed, and his disappointment was bound to result in execution. If Patcharee was bound to die either way, regardless of if she painted herself as a perfect citizen or an inimitable rebel, then what was the point in binding herself to a system she knew to be unjust? She didn’t know too much about Azania, but she knew it was a place where the workers were valued, and she knew that the PAAS were trying to bring about that same kind of society back home, and it really seemed to her like a beautiful concept, so finally, with a conflicted mind but a passionate heart, she announced to the masked figure:

“Sure, I’m willing to betray them.”

“Thank you, Ms. Ratnaporn. I cannot understate how much your help will be appreciated.”

“But I do have one more question before we proceed with this idea of yours. If you work for the Azanians, how did you even manage to get invited to an event like this?”

“Simply put, because I wasn’t invited. And I’m using a fake name, and due to the rather convenient nature of the masquerade, I’m able to wear a fake face as well.”

“Well in that case, if you're roping me into this whole facade, I think it’s only fair that you tell me your name first.”

“Alright then,” the masked figure paused, clearly evaluating whether Patcharee was trustworthy enough to be provided with such covert information, before eventually, a smile drew subtly onto her face, and the truth spilled out her lips, “you can call me Vraxi Nair.”

“It’s nice to meet you, Ms. Nair. May I ask what’s first in store in regards to my objectives?”

“Right now? Nothing really. I just need you to blend in. Here,” Vraxi handed her a tiny piece of nearly transparent metal, “stick this thing into your ear. It’ll let us give you commands when the time comes for action.”

“Okay,” Patcharee nudged the device into her auditory orifice, “but I suggest you hide yourself away again. Dinner is nearly over and you don’t want people to walk out of there and wonder why you were staying in the hall.”

With very little delay and an inaudible response, Vraxi headed back to some shadowy corner. Patcharee was once again alone, and she tried to stay calm. Her days had only been growing stranger, but she needed to retain some sense of order. She patrolled the ballroom and ensured that every piece of furniture was well-dusted. She breathed and breathed out. She thought of the corpse she had left in the prince’s locked room, and she thought of Naphat, who always seemed to materialize in her mind in the form of a corpse.

Then suddenly she heard the band start to play, some brassy ensemble, all Western instruments, whose melodies were decidedly not classical yet simultaneously refused to dip into jazz. It was decidedly inoffensive music, and to the rhythm of that established beat, the various party-goers all started flooding into the ballroom, all cloaked in different masks, some extravagant and some lazy, clapping their hands and whistling in a manner which was distinctly off-tempo. More food was served, small plates, expensive plates, Canadian caviar and Champagnois champagne, all served in tempered glass, set atop tempered discs, held by the careful fingers of her fellow maids. The music was quite loud, and every single guest seemed to believe that their personal conversation was the most important and needed to be heard above all others, so the whole room was saturated with the cacophonous noise of arguing Westerners. Patcharee attempted to navigate the mess as she had been tasked with the job of constantly perfuming the area with the aroma of cinnamon and clove. Yutthisathian II thought it would give the party a festive feel, so Patcharee had been provided with a sort of glass spray bottle which she constantly emitted fragrant fumes from while weaving around the many bumping elbows of the increasingly intoxicated guests. In her opinion, the perfume was far too strong to be used at this scale and made the whole room smell like some Teuton pie after only about ten minutes or so of constant spraying. She even had guests come up to and tell her to stop but she figured that the decrees of the king overruled all their requests. Ultimately, though, she wasn’t really focused on either of their opinions on the matter. Her mind was set nearly unanimously on one gnawing subject: the chip in her ear. She couldn’t stop thinking about what Vraxi might ask her, and when she finally heard a voice come rolling out of that little machine, she ignored the task of perfuming entirely, fully rapt.

Revolution on High: Part 3

Chapter 70: Revolution on High: Part 3

All at once, cutting through the cacophony like a hot knife through an ice sculpture, Patcharee heard a command ring through her ear. It went as follows:

“We know about what happened to Prince Vajirananavarorasa. We have a pretty good idea as to how your actions led to his death. The maid who you communicated with on your way to his room was in contact with Naphat, and in the grand scheme of things, in contact with us. Don’t worry, we’re not mad. If anything, we’re a little glad that he’s done with the whole living thing. What’s important is that the palace officials are not aware of his passing, and further, that it seems like your encounter with Vasundhara has given you the ability, at least to a degree, to reanimate the dead noble. This is a very useful thing to know, Patcharee, and it is integral to our first ask of you. We want you to speak to the king, to isolate him from the crowd to the best of your abilities, and in that moment of relative privacy, inform him that his cousin is hopelessly sick and could die at any moment. We’ll then need you to bring him to Vajirananavarorasa’s room, and we’ll need you to puppet his limbs around in the manner of a deeply ill individual. You do not need to make him speak. Just tell the king that the prince told you that he wanted to have his funeral at the central shrine in the city of Roi Et. Just trust us on this. Have the cadaver nod to affirm that your words are the truth and, no more than a minute later, puppeteer his peaceful death. Also, for your own sake, do whatever you can do to avoid a proper autopsy. It shouldn’t be too hard though, because, at least from what I’ve read, the prince was never the biggest fan of modern medicine.”

Patcharee nearly dropped the glass bottle when she heard those words. Her legs began to shake a little. Perhaps, she began thinking, she had dug herself into a rather large, rather inescapable hole. Lying to the king, so objectively and about such a grandiose and criminal affair, was a truly unforgivable act, the kind which, if discovered, she sincerely believed would lead her to a death upon a flaming pyre. It would be a public execution, and people would travel from all across Krungthep, all across Siam for that matter, to observe in simple celebration the death of the duplicitous traitor, the wicked woman who killed the prince and attempted to lead the king to the same fate, though the king, a paragon of morality and knowledge, detected the wicked woman’s schemes at a glance and immediately proved her guilt to the whole palace. He would surely force the entire troupe of maids into the audience, making them watch what happens to those who disrespect the crown, and all the PAAS sympathizers would quietly snuff their inner flames of hope, and Naphat herself, well she would be so dejected that she might go ahead and hang herself. It would be an endlessly depressing affair, a gruesome blow to the efforts of the revolution, perhaps even a deathknell.

But it was possible that her thoughts were racing ahead of herself, for how difficult would it be, really, to puppeteer the movements of a man on his deathbed? It would only be a handful of movements in the arms and neck. The face muscles could stay static, the fingers wouldn’t have any real need for articulation, and obviously the legs would be entirely bedridden. It didn’t sound the least bit impossible, and in fact, as Patcharee rushed across the ballroom, attempting to locate the king, occasionally spritzing the perfume as she did so, she increasingly began to believe that Vraxi’s idea just might work. It just might actually function, and whatever would be done in the city of Roi Et she truly had no idea, but it would assuredly be something of revolutionary significance. Perhaps, and in this thought she was really getting ahead of herself, she might even end up in the history books herself for her vital role in this all-important scheme.

While it was a little difficult to identify him when he wore a mask that made him look like some sort of toucan, Patcharee did eventually find the king. Unfortunately, he seemed to be engaged in a deep—or at least superficially deep—conversation with some opulent and bemonacled Westerners. Patcharee attempted to just wait for the talk to reach a natural end, but after about ten full minutes of sticking to the sidelines, she heard yet another message in her earpiece.

“Patcharee, we really need you to isolate the king as swiftly as possible. If we wait much longer, Vajirananavarorasa’s room is going to smell like a dead man the moment you two walk in.”

This order invigorated Patcharee’s resolve, encouraging her to do the unthinkable, encouraging her to interrupt the king. He was currently speaking on some topic of agriculture but she just needed to butt in.

“And that is why,” Yutthisathian orated, “the quality of a nation’s soil is so integral to its success. Even if one is a true carnivore, they cannot escape the prison of their ecosystem, and the issues in the dirt, all the low-grade minerals, will inevitably rise up to even the smartest of minds. And that is also why I refuse to eat Siamese cuisine. While the crops grown in the south are leagues greater than their northern counterparts, they are both outclassed by the seeds freely planted along the French Riviera. To keep my mind sharp, I have all of my personal foodstuffs imported directly from Paris. Afterall, if I want the mind of a Napoleon, it only makes sense to eat like one, and furthermore-”

“I apologize, your majesty,” Patcharee interrupted and watched as the king and all the Westerners turned to look at her with expressions of disgust, “but Prince Vajirananavarorasa’s illness has grown much more severe in the past hour. He would like to see you right now,” then Patcharee dropped her voice so that only Yutthisathian could hear her, “he says it’s about his funeral.”

The king’s expression shifted, and he attempted to hide his countenance from his guests as his annoyance rapidly dropped into an expression of total grief and panic. It was hard to see his eyes through the mask, but his mouth spelled total despair.

“I apologize, gentlemen,” he quickly spat out, “but I’m afraid I have an important family matter to deal with. I’ll be back soon. Please, enjoy the champagne.”

Vraxi Nair, wearing a mask that hid her entire face behind the visage of a jackal, standing on the second floor interior balcony, looked down on the king as if he was an ant, shuffling past human obstacles, following the scent of death, with Patcharee trailing behind him, presumably apologizing. She was glad to see her plans come together, and a smile began to form upon her hidden face, but an undercurrent of unease still penetrated her every movement. She constantly felt the need to look behind her, to check if she was being watched.

Just as that exact thought of worry crossed her mind, Vraxi looked directly to her right, and she saw that with one hand leaning on the banister and the other slung in a cast, the one and only Joey Axelrod was standing right next to her. He had a mask which occupied the space around his eyes, but it had to be him, Vraxi was certain that it was him, yet, based on his expression, he didn’t seem to have any suspicions regarding the identity of the person stood next to him. After Vraxi stared at him for one too many seconds, Joey began to speak.

“So have you been enjoying the gala,” he asked casually, presumably without a second thought as to who he was speaking to.

“The food has been nice,” Vraxi casually replied.

“Do you have any favorites from tonight’s menu?”

“Well,” Vraxi hadn’t attended dinner and couldn’t name a single menu item, “I quite liked the champagne.”

“I wouldn’t quite call that a food, but I do agree that it’s been nice. Very authentic. Truthfully, I wasn’t expecting the meal to be so French-forward. I was kinda hoping for some pad thai.”

“That’s fair. So on whose behalf are you here tonight?”

“Oh I’m just a GüdTek representative. Josephine Bran herself actually almost attended, but then she said she was busy, so she got me to come here in her stead. I must admit, it’s been much more enjoyable than most of the events she makes me attend on her behalf. Usually I end up at some conference or convention, scrounging the local food trucks for something palatable, but tonight has really just been a party. It’s quite refreshing.”

“May I ask about the cast?”

“Oh, this?” Joey pointed to his bound arm, “well,” he then decided not to tell the truth about his altercation with Carlyle that had led to the injury, “I fell down the stairs a few days ago.”

“Oh. That’s unfortunate.”

“Quite. And it hasn’t helped that GüdTek has been enduring some really stressful times as of late.”

“Is that so?”

“Well, I mean, don’t let that comment adjust your stock profile, it’s just that, to tell the truth, well, I mean, Sobek’s been doing great, this isn’t about Sobek-”

“What is it about, then?”

“…You know those people who stole the Singularity, the original one?”

“I’m tangentially aware of them.”

“Well, they’re still on the run and they’re growing more powerful. And the worst part is we almost caught them. We used Sobek and Gibson and everything, but they managed to escape alongside some very important information.”

“What sort of information?”

“The kind that’s too important to just disclose willy-nilly.”

“Well that’s understandable. Anyways, I think I’d better go down to the main floor-”

“Hold on, before you leave, I think I recognize your voice from somewhere. What’s your name?”

“Oh, you can just call me Ms. Gam-” Vraxi then realized that alluding to Gambheeram wouldn’t be helpful to her cause in the slightest seeing as how the real Gambheeram wasn’t on GüdTek’s good side either, “bini.”

“Ms. Gambini? Is that an Italian name?”

“Correct,” Vraxi then took a brief glance at her own skin, “I’m adopted.”

“Oh, well I guess that explains things. Have a nice night, Ms. Gambini.”

“You too, Mr. Axelrod,” and as Vraxi spoke she waved and turned around and started walking and realized that Joey had never introduced himself all simultaneously, resulting in her twisting and falling through her own confusion, ultimately landing directly on her face and creating a large fracture in her rather fragile jackal mask.

“Are you okay, Ms. Gambini?” Joey said as he rushed to help Vraxi up off the ground, and in doing so he spotted a face only half-covered, with the other half of the jackal laying on the ground in disarray, and in that parallel half of the face, that which had lost its facade, he saw a skin he had witnessed many times before, in many angered configurations, and a current of rage began to form beneath his own face when he saw with unfettered eyes the woman he had just been talking to.

“Vraxi Nair,” Joey uttered with a new timbre, “why the hell have you followed me here?”

“Well I must admit,” Vraxi scooted backwards and wobbled into a standing position, “it was never my intention to meet you.”

Joey then wordlessly pulled out a gun and pointed it directly at Vraxi’s forehead.

“Joey,” Vraxi raised her hands in a position of surrender, “please put your gun down. We really don’t need to cause a scene here, especially when you’re supposed to be representing your boss’s interests.”

“It would be in the interests of my boss to just kill you, right now, right where we stand, right away. The only thing that she wouldn’t be interested in is the noise that the gun is bound to make.”

“Well, then, I guess you could say there’s a conflict of interests in the matter. Maybe we can come to some sort of verbal agreement instead of disrupting this entire party with a terrible murder. If you’re so determined to kill me, then surely there’s also something you want from me.”

“…Are you trying to offer GüdTek something?”

“I’m trying to offer you something, Joey Axelrod.”

“Listen, Vraxi, I know I tried to go independent for a while and attempt to form a team with Shui, but none of that worked out for me, as is apparent by the presence of the cast. I’m back at GüdTek, and every action I take is in service to GüdTek. Alone, there’s really only so much I can do, but with Bran on my side, I’m quite unstoppable.”

“But unstoppable to what goals? I know there are things you want from me, Joey, and even if those things are not in the interest of your company, that doesn’t at all temper your desires.”

“…Be specific. I want to know exactly what you’re willing to offer me. I don’t want to be tricked by you yet again.”

“It’s Theta. You can take them. Truthfully, I’d rather not hand them over to you, but if it’s the only thing that’ll stop me from getting a bullet through my head, then I have no choice.”

“Are you really telling the truth, Vraxi? Do you really mean it?” Joey lowered his gun slightly but didn’t stop pointing it, “You know this would mean the world to me.”

“Of course I know that. That’s why I’m offering them to you. Theta is literally sitting in a van just outside the palace, and all you’ve gotta do to earn them back is put the gun down.”

Gradually, with globules of sweat forming along his arms, Joey Axelrod pointed his gun to the ground, though he didn’t ease his finger off the trigger.

“Alright, Vraxi,” he continued with an uneasy voice, “I can give you an ultimatum. All I need you to do is lead me out of this party, out of this palace, and out to the exact spot where Theta is located. I’d also like to take the van they’re in with me and drive away with both it and Theta in tow. If you do all of this without complications, I promise I will not shoot. Alright?”

“Understood.”

“Good. Now-”

And before Joey Axelrod could even begin his next sentence a full champagne bottle was smashed into his skull, shattering on impact and pushing him to the ground, his gun flying out of his hand as he crashed.

Vraxi, in response, was quite astonished. She looked up to see the masked figure who had done such a thing and saw a familiar jackal face strapped onto the familiar body of Zapata Tochichuitl.

“Why the hell would you do that?” Vraxi immediately chided her companion.

“What?” Zapata had expected more thanks, “He had a gun pointed at you! Did you not see that? You could’ve died!”

“I saw the gun, Zapata. I had already compartmentalized the presence of the gun. I was in the process of leading him down a path of trickery which would ultimately save me from getting shot without drawing attention to ourselves.”

Zapata peered out at the crowd surrounding her and, go figure, she did indeed see many partygoers with faces of concern, all feeling a bit violated by the sudden act of terrible violence within a supposedly peaceable event.

Then, one lone guest with a face wrapped in discontent pointed an accusatory finger at the unmasked Vraxi and shouted at the top of their lungs:

“That’s Vraxi Nair! That’s an international terrorist! Somebody, call the police!”

Vraxi and Zapata looked at one another, and with little delay, jumped into a sprint. Vraxi understood that suddenly running could potentially lead to even more eyes getting drawn to her, but at the same time there was really no longer any safety found in staying static. She had been discovered. The ruse, one which she was quite proud of establishing in the first place, had been crushed into a million tiny glinting pieces, just like that bottle of expensive champagne whose shards were now partially lodged into the neck of Joey Axelrod. Now, her main goal was just to leave the palace as quickly as possible, hope that her getaway car was still where she’d left it, and hightail it out the city’s center out of the view of the royal police. This all meant that, rather sadly, her mission had been cut short, but it was at least paired with the fact that her most urgent objective, contacting Patcharee, had already been achieved. Now she just hoped that the mission she’d assigned to Patcharee wouldn’t end in disaster, a fate which could be avoided entirely so long as she made sure to remain incredibly careful.

The room containing the corpse of Prince Vajirananavarorasa had a certain smell to it. It wasn’t the most pungent of smells, not the kind immediately noticeable as being that of a dead body, but it was present, and it was, to Patcharee’s chagrin, impossible to ignore. She just had to hope that, with the impending death of his cousin on the mind, the king wouldn’t think too much about aromas.

“How is his condition?” Yutthisathian asked urgently.

“I suggest you just look at him,” Patcharee replied, as the two turned a corner and saw the sickly prince splayed out on his bed.

Patcharee made sure to ambulate the roots inside the corpse’s body ever so slightly, making them enter and exit the body’s lungs metronomically, creating an illusion of faint breathing.

“Thank God,” the king muttered after seeing his cousin’s chest rise and deflate, “he’s not yet dead.”

The king moved closer to his cousin’s corpse and attempted to hold his hand. Patcharee wasn’t expecting the king to actually touch the body, so she had to rapidly dig some roots into the prince’s hands, permitting the cold fingers to gently cling onto the hand that grasped it. It wasn’t the most human of movements, but the king still seemed convinced.

“I’m sorry for being so late,” Yutthisathian whispered, “I would’ve cancelled the whole gala if I knew how dire your state was. I can’t believe the maids would let me believe you were recovering when the truth was so grim. I’ll have to fire a handful of them.”

Hearing this, Patcharee tensed up a little, once again fearing for her job, and decided—even though it wasn’t necessarily a part of her instructions—to instigate the prince’s head into shaking a negative response.

“You don’t want me to fire them?” Yutthisathian seemed surprised, “Well, I guess it should be your decision in the end. But, Vaji, I just want to let you know, I don’t intend on allowing your funeral to be the kind that slips quietly out of memory, even as you now slip quietly into death. I want it to be extravagant, truly fantastic, so that anyone who was not yet aware of your name will hear it, be made aware of it, and be made aware of your status as a national hero.”

Patcharee figured that now would be the perfect time to insert her addition, to just casually mention the location in which the prince would like to be buried. Patcharee still wasn’t entirely sure why Roi Et had been chosen, though she had her suspicions, seeing as the PAAS was much stronger up there in the north than down in Krungthep.

“Um, your majesty,” Patcharee gathered the courage to interject, “When he was still able to speak, Prince Vajirananavarorasa communicated to me that he would like his funeral to be held in Roi Et, at the central temple.”

“…Really?” Yutthisathian asked, perplexed, “Typically we try to keep all the royal funerals in and around the royal cemetery. It obviously makes burial a bit easier that way—less transportation and whatnot—and it’s also really just tradition. I can’t recall any funeral being held in Roi Et—it’s quite far and a bit obscure and it’s not like he spent his final days there.”

Despite the king’s confusion, Patcharee ambulated the head of Vajirananavarorasa to make it look like he was awkwardly nodding.

“Wait,” the king did not seem any less confused, “are you nodding in response to what I said or what the maid said.”

Patcharee really did not want to engage in this song-and-dance. The more she moved around the limbs of the dead prince, the more obvious it became that he was a puppeted dead man. His motions were all janky, disjointed, and just generally unbecoming of a living person. Even on the death bed, people move with a certain verve that the festering corpse of the cousin of the king simply lacked. Regardless, the king had asked his cousin’s corpse a question, and the only way for it to be answered was to spur the dead man’s arm into clumsily pointing at Patcharee herself. If the king had known that the act of puppeting a dead man was possible, he would’ve immediately suspected that that was occurring. Luckily, that theoretical had not yet come to pass, and the king, though a little flummoxed, was convinced.

“I don’t quite understand your reasoning, Vaji, but I trust that there is logic to it, even if it is logic I will never be able to decipher. Your funeral will be held in the city of Roi Et. I will attend it, I will speak at it, and, almost assuredly, I will weep.”

Patcharee was about to suggest that the prince might be dead for good when, before she could get her words out, the king proposed one final question to his brother.

“But, surely,” the king proposed, “while I understand that you’re on the way out, there must be a way for you to give me one last message, your final word on Earth. All I request is one word, one simple explanation for that choice regarding your funeral. I get that you may be losing your speech, but I’m not asking for an entire message. I’d just like to hear one word from your lips.”

Patcharee should’ve predicted this. She should’ve predicted that Yutthisathian II, a man who always expected everyone to serve him, would request the impossible from a man on his death bed. Vraxi Nair had specifically warned her about this. She had specifically told her to at all costs avoid speaking to the king in the voice of the deceased prince, to at all costs avoid ventriloquism. But what other choice was she left with? She could theoretically move the roots within the body in such a way as to make the prince’s mouth and tongue look alive, but she couldn’t make them speak, she couldn’t strum a voice within that empty vessel. Her only option, truly, was to move around the mouth with the roots while attempting to imitate the voice of the prince. It seemed like the kind of plan which would inevitably get her executed.

Perhaps, she started fretting, the king could tell that he was being duped. Obviously, the prince’s sudden illness was rather inexplicable, though it wasn’t entirely unheard of given the prince’s aversion to medicine. Regardless, the circumstances of the death were strange and suspect, especially, she presumed, from the perspective of the king. The king had heard that his cousin was sick, had spent a day and a half without seeing his cousin, and was now being told that his cousin was about to die, his cousin who was strangely unable to speak or make complex movements. Any mind even only trivially curious could look at the circumstances of Vajirananavarorasa’s sudden departure and ponder the possibilities of murder, a murder which Patcharee would naturally be the prime suspect of. It was then entirely possible that the king had already suspected the truth that his cousin was already dead and merely being maneuvered around by some unseen mechanism. If the prince were to speak, this suspicion would be disproven, but the prince, by his nature, would never be able to do such a thing.

Patcharee, in total disregard for the ways she’d been instructed, carried on. She had to make an attempt. She had to ply her trade in the art of ventriloquism. Firstly, however, she had to set some expectations.

“I’m not sure if he’ll be able to say much, your majesty. He’s been refusing to speak with me, and even before then he was only mumbling, nearly inaudibly and barely comprehensible. Even if he does speak, you may not be able to understand him.”

“Patcharee,” the king said solemnly, “me and Prince Vaji are connected by a line of royal blood. It is not the sort of thing that a lowborn like yourself could ever completely understand but, to be succinct, it is a familial bond stronger than any other. No matter what he says, I will understand him. No matter how he says it, I will understand him. Even if you yourself find the noise he produces impossible to hear, I will understand it. Me and him have the essence of the gods freely flowing through our veins. There is an indescribable divinity connecting us.”

Patcharee gulped. She never liked to see the king so passionate as he often became when speaking about the importance of lineage. Lineage was the foremost concept which ruled over Yutthisathian’s sense of right and wrong, and whenever he was reminded of its power, he tended to grow crueler to those peasants that surrounded him. It seemed like at that moment a gulf was suddenly formed between the king and the maid, and Patcharee was once again reminded of pitiable social strata she held in comparison to those she worked for. It was an incrossable line, that invisible barrier which separated her from the royals, and she knew that imitating a royal was the one crime adjudicated worse than that of killing a royal. Nevertheless, she pressed on. She let her roots creep down into the dead man’s jaw. She let sprouts form and flourish in the space beneath his tongue. She lined his inner lip with the thinnest bark, just out of sight. It was all to create a convincing dummy, and in the end, she felt it was as convincing as could be, save for the one remaining volatile factor, the problem of her voice.

“Come one, Vaji, speak to me,” the king once again demanded of the dead man, “just one last word, just one little word, just tell me why you’d like to be buried there, and if you can’t, just tell me anything at all.”

The corpse’s lips began to quiver as Patcharee prepared it to speak, but no matter how much the king begged for a word, she couldn’t bear to open her mouth. It just wouldn't work. She knew there was no way it could possibly work. At the instant in which she would open her mouth, the king would immediately discover her. Her voice just wouldn’t match up, in both sound and location. It would only make her death come sooner.

But the king did not give up. He started getting closer to the body. He started placing his hands on the body. At a certain point he started pressing on the body’s abdomen, and a pocket of air, probably the byproduct of some gas-producing bacteria, started shooting up from his stomach and up along his esophagus. Patcharee could feel this swift wind forming against her deepest roots, and she quickly realized this was her best and potentially only chance to make the body speak. She quickly altered the phonetic positioning of Vajirananvarorasa’s tongue and lips, and when that puff of air emerged past his throat, he very softly, rather faintly, but still quite clearly spoke:

“You…”

“Me?” Yutthisathian asked, “What do you mean by that, Vaji?”

But Prince Vaji’s eyes then finally closed and would never be opened again. The body had been preserved a good while after death, but now it was gone for good. The king was no longer teary, he was simply left confused, preparing himself mentally for a trip to Roi Et.

Revolution on High: Part 4

Chapter 71: Revolution on High: Part 4

Shui Hailang could never get themself to enjoy prison food. The life of a demon hunter had always been one of relative opulence and that opulence extended to the food they purchased. Without their daily intake of salmon caviar, Hailang began to grow melancholic—and this wasn’t even touching on the matter of clothes. In an instant, Hailang’s incredibly extensive wardrobe was replaced with a plain, uniform orange, very much unfashionable and very much a testament to their total lack of freedom behind bars. Hailang spent nearly the entire day within the concrete confines of a Sichuanese prison they had never been told the name of. Starting at 2 PM, they were given 45 minutes of courtyard time. Most of the inmates played basketball, but Hailang themself had never picked up that sport in their youth and was too embarrassed to start trying as an adult. Instead they simply watched the amateurs all collectively hone their art. Every day, they could sense that their fellow inmates were getting a tiny bit better at the sport, and everyday, in unison, Hailang felt themself grow even more behind.

One day, while watching their cohort pass balls in the courtyard, a guard approached Shui Hailang and told them that a visitor had come to speak with them. This was quite odd, as when Hailang had been sentenced—in a sham of a court case that was done in under an hour—they had been given the specific stipulation that they would not be allowed to have any visitors over. Perhaps this guard was unaware of that stipulation, but Hailang felt no need to correct him.

The guard led Hailang to a room full of chairs and glass dividers. On the other side of the divider, Hailang saw a face they recognized. The guard then left the room, closed the door, and Hailang rushed over to the glass to stare at the unusual figure sat on the other side. It was very clearly the visage of Aisha Abdulaziz.

“Hello, Shui Hailang,” Aisha spoke into the microphone, “It’s rather nice to see you again.”

“Aisha? I’m confused. Why are you here? And how did you get past the no-visitor clause?”

“Well, to answer the latter question first, it was actually quite simple. I simply played a soothing song on Israfil’s trumpet, letting down the guards’ guards, and from there it was easy to inform them that I had some document which overrode that clause. They were all so out of it that they never actually asked for the document and I strolled into this room as if I wasn’t doing anything wrong.”

“I guess that explains things partly, but my first question still stands. I still find it quite odd that you would go through all these hoops to meet with me of all people. We’ve never really had a positive relationship before. When I was on Nair’s side, you were against them. You did eventually make amends, but that was around the same time that I realized Nair’s treachery and we parted ways. So it really shouldn’t be odd why I find this whole thing hard to believe.”

“Well, the answer is ultimately rather simple. Theta is trying to gather every avatar into one place, and you, naturally, are one such avatar.”

“Okay. I’m not sure why they think I would ever join them. Nair’s gang pretty thoroughly betrayed me back in Rizhao and I don’t intend on ever forgiving them.”

“Even now?”

“What about now?”

“Well, Hailang, I don’t want to sound too blunt, but it’s not like you're cooped in an Azanian prison. The Sichuanese side, the side that you fought for, is the same side that captured you and forced you into this concrete box. Though I supposed ‘Sichuanese’ is not quite the right word anymore. I know that news tends to move slower in prisons, but just today this nation passed a bill to officially change its name.”

“I haven’t heard about this yet. What are they changing it to?”

“The Republic of New Washington. I find it to be quite tacky, but at least it’s honest.”

“…That’s really the name they’re going for?”

“It’s just another step in the desinicization process. They’re trying to scrub away every aspect of the old order and replace it with America’s corpse. They’ve already decreed that English will now be the only language legally allowed in education.”

“That all seems rather strange.”

“It shouldn’t be strange, Hailang. This has been happening ever since Sichuan let itself get sold to some fleeing American businessmen in the name of petty nationalism. It was happening to Rizhao too up until their revolution.”

“Don’t bring that up.”

“The Rizhaonese people were being exploited. You saw their exploitation with your own two eyes.”

“It was an unfortunate bout of poverty which was about to be overcome.”

“It was a poverty which you never had to deal with because you were one of the few who benefited from the Lockeite order. Your paychecks came from people whose paychecks came from those stray, ruthless, exploitative Yankees.”

“Why are you trying to make me out as some horrible person?”

“Hailang, I’m not, or at least that’s not my intention. What I’m simply trying to communicate is that you were a part of a horrible system. But here’s the good part: you’re not anymore. You literally don’t have a choice anymore. The system you were once a part of has kicked you out and thrown you behind bars so there’s really no need to side with them any longer. And here’s the second good part: I’m not mad at you. I may dislike your actions, I may think you did some horrible things, but so did I. You saw what I did, but you also saw that I decided that, with the rest of my mortal life, I would try to make the world better instead of just ending that life prematurely. Hailang, you have a chance to be like me, to mop up some of the shit you caused. All you’ve gotta do is join up with Theta and I’ll get you out of this prison in no time.”

“…You know a way to get me out of here?”

“Yes, Hailang, I do.”

“But this is supposed to be a super-secure facility. They told me that there hasn’t been a single successful escape attempt.”

“It’s only secure if the guards follow their orders. And your departure won’t be seen as an escape. All you’ll have to do is walk out by my side and I’ll tell them that there was a court order that said you’re free to go. Normally, they would obviously ask to see such a document, or question if such a document could even feasibly exist, but under the trumpet’s suggestion, they won’t find anything unusual in what I say and they’ll let us stroll out of the facility scotfree.”

“…Holy shit. So all I’ve gotta do is follow your command and I’ll be free?”

“Well hold on now. If you wanna get out of here you first need to promise that you’ll participate with Nair and that you won’t engage in any acts of sabotage against her.”

“Oh, I almost forgot about that part.”

“Additionally, you’ll need to promise that you won’t engage in contact with the Lockeites, GüdTek corporate, or any stray remnants of the Confuscian Republic of Rizhao.”

“I can’t even speak to the patriots of my own country?”

“You can always make acquaintances with the new, proletarian administration. I’m told that a friend of yours by the name of Hong Zainan has been appointed to the position of Minister of the Youth.”

“Don’t… mention Zainan. Just… stop mentioning Rizhao entirely. It was my only nation, but now that it’s a pile of rubble I have nothing to do but accept the role of a person with no nation.”

“…It’s not a ‘pile of rubble.’”

“It may as well be, though, admittedly, regardless, your offer still sounds quite intriguing to me.”

“So you promise to switch sides?”

“If that’s how you want to phrase it, then yes.”

“Great. Now just climb over the divider and onto my side of the room. Don’t worry, the guards are still soothed and will think the whole stunt is completely normal.”

Shui Hailang, a little weary, a little worried that they might be being tricked, abided by Aisha’s suggestion and slowly, carefully stood on top of their chair, grabbed the top of the transparent divider, and heaved themself over to Aisha’s side. They nearly fell directly onto their head but were able to switch position in time so that only their back was bothered. Regardless, the fall still hurt.

Aisha was just about to help Hailang to their feet when a guard, one which Aisha did not recognize, ran into the building with a face blush with irritation and a gun in his hands.

“Get back on the other side!” The guard shouted unsurprisingly before pulling out a walkie-talkie and barking “we’ve got an escape attempt,” into the speaker.

Aisha’s charm, evidently, had not affected every guard in the prison, and the prospect of simply walking out no longer seemed possible. Still, though, Aisha figured she could at least manage the most present threat quite quickly. She turned over to the startled Shui Hailang and told them:

“Cover your ears. Now.”

Hailang did as they were told and Aisha summoned her trumpet into her arms before blowing on it with such a passion as to totally incapacitate the red-faced guard. Despite this quick thinking, Hailang did not seem impressed.

“Well, it doesn’t look like I’ll be leaving here afterall,” they commented before attempting to climb back to the other side of the divider, “but I suppose it was nice of you to try your best to free me.”

“What? Hailang, please don’t go. We’re really not that far from the exit. It’ll just be a quick jaunt out of here.”

“Aisha, I’d really rather not get killed by a firing squad, and if I had to get killed, I’d rather have it be at the hands of my enemies, and not the hands of the allies who I’m presently betraying.”

“Hailang, I saw you in Dakahlia. I know what you're capable of. You don’t seem like the kind of person who’d die from a simple bullet wound. Can’t you just wash all the guards away with your water powers?”

“Not with these cuffs on,” Hailang raised their wrists, revealing a thick band of metal around each, “these things can detect if I’m tapping into my connection with Mazu, and will electrocute me if they do. The voltage on them is so strong that, after only a couple seconds of activity, I’d likely be entirely fried to a crisp.”

Aisha, upon hearing this information, decided to pin Hailang to the ground.

“What the hell are you doing?” Hailang, understandably, screeched in response.

“Well,” Aisha politely explained, “if you have no way to utilize your affinity with water, then you don’t really have a way to fight back. And without any way to fight back, then there isn’t really any reason for me to approach this situation with polite conversation. I am trying to do Theta a favor, and you are a part of that favor, and to be completely honest, I don’t really care about your opinion on the matter. If you will not cooperate and run out of here with me, then I’ll simply have to carry you.”

“Fuck. Thabr trained you into a pretty good fighter. I’m having trouble breaking free.”

“I suppose he did. Though I’d really prefer if you could refrain from speaking that name.”

Aisha hoisted Hailang over her back and started bolting out of the room. On cue, alarms began blaring in every corner of the building, and every guard was called to mobilize against the attempted escapee. Not a single prisoner had ever been able to sneak out of the Adams City Municipal Prison alive, and the warden of the ACMP had every intention to keep things that way. Unfortunately for him, Aisha Abdulaziz was willing to face any challenge he might throw at her.

Though, truthfully, it wasn’t actually that difficult to get out of the building itself. Hailang had already done most of the work of escaping by moving from their cell to the visitor room, seeing as there was only one hallway separating said room from the nearest exit. The guards didn’t prove to be much of an issue, as most of them in the immediate vicinity had already been soothed by Aisha’s music. The only real issue when it came to getting out of the facility was the fact that, between the building and the open road sat a rather large moat. Now, Aisha did know how to swim, so the simple act of traversing the trench wasn’t much of an issue, but unfortunately for her, upon hearing that there was an escape taking place, the rather sadistic warden released a shiver of sharks into the open water, one which he apparently kept on hand for this exact purpose.

“Well, fuck,” Aisha commented upon viewing the snapping jaws of the sleek marine creatures, “there can’t be a safe way to swim through there.”

“Then I suggest you just give up, Aisha. I didn’t even really want to leave here in the first place.”

“Even if that is the case, and even if I were to abandon you, I can’t help but suspect that, if they catch us, I’ll be sent here too. So I’m afraid the only option left is to press on, sharks or not.”

“What? Aisha, you’ve gotta be kidding me. Be realistic here, you are not a faster swimmer than a shark. And even if you somehow were, my presence on your back would add a lot of extra weight. So, truly, it would be physically impossible for you to get across that moat unharmed.”

“…Fair. But also, aren’t sharks, like, not actually all that harmful in real life?”

“Aisha…”

“I know there’s a statistic about this somewhere; I think it was something along the lines of there being more yearly deaths from cows than from sharks.”

“Aisha Abdulaziz.”

“So maybe if this moat was filled with cows there’d be a real issue.”

“Aisha, please, let it go.”

“But as it stands, I really doubt that there’d be too much danger in going through waters filled with such a peaceful animal.”

“Aisha! It’s not fucking worth it, okay? A life spent in prison is a much better deal than some stupid, ignoble death via shark-bite!”

“I would not consider my cause to be ‘ignoble.’”

“Well I would, and as it stands, you’ll need my approval to engage in such a stupidly dangerous idea as swimming through shark-infested waters.”

“To be frank, Hailang, you haven’t been able to break out of my grip even a little. Your approval is not really influencing my decision. However, I will admit, I’d rather avoid the sharks if possible. Luckily, there is a way to get past the moat without entering the water at all.”

“And what would such a way entail?”

“Well, I’d need you to tap into your connection with Mazu. All you’d have to do is part the water for enough time to let me traverse the width of the trench. I’m a quick runner, so it shouldn’t take long, and you’ll only be getting zapped for a moment.”

“It seems like both of the options you’ve laid before me involve my life being put at risk. But I’d have to imagine a shark bite is the more painful of the two deaths, so I guess I’ll go with option two.”

Aisha heard a loud noise suddenly sound out behind her. She turned around and saw what had to have been at least a hundred guards all simultaneously storming out of the building, ready to attack.

“Hailang,” Aisha spoke with a strong urgency, “I’m gonna need you to activate that power right now.”

Hailang’s eyes went dark as they dug into their mind, tunneling into their cerebral connection with the water goddess. For a moment, they were completely silent, and Aisha worried that she was about to be sent to prison for life.

Then, in a great and powerful instant, as if Hailang were Moses parting the Red Sea, a corridor of dry air appeared within the moat, a corridor entirely devoid of sharks. Aisha, true to her word and quick on her feet, immediately started sprinting through this newly formed pathway, all while Hailang, who hadn’t been lying about those cuffs, endured an incredible, hair-standing amount of pure voltage.

It was, ultimately, a rather thin moat, and Hailang, to their great relief, was able to survive the shock with only intermediate burn wounds. However, the moat was just wide enough that a good handful of guards had been able to follow the two escapees into that corridor of dry air, though, by the time the escapees reached the other side, it stopped consisting of dry air and became fluid once more, trapping those guards in the shark-infested water.

“Do you think they’re gonna be okay?” Aisha wondered aloud.

“According to you they should be,” Hailang quipped back at her, “afterall, I don’t see any cows in that water.”

“Then I suppose they’ll do just fine.”

Joey Axelrod was having difficulty falling asleep. Every once in a while he’d get close to unconsciousness when, all of a sudden, a sharp, unplaceable pain would singe through him, shocking his eyes back open and making him grip the sweat-soaked mattress. It wasn’t even that the pains from the glass shards his face had been assaulted with were preventing him from grasping sleep, as he had already had all of them removed by a surgeon who also doused half of his face with a numbing agent. Rather, it was the memories of those shards, and the memory of those who hastened their arrival, that kept him so on-edge. No matter where he went, it seemed, he could never escape Vraxi Nair, and Zapata Tochihuitl, and all those other little devils who had hauled away his invention and insulted his existence. Joey Axelrod just couldn’t get a break, but he was hoping that he could at least get some sleep. Those horrible interlocutors were always invading his waking hours, but surely, he thought, he could escape them in his dreams.

Joey Axelrod closed his eyes.

When he opened his eyes, he was positioned on a different bed, a red bed, in a red room with red curtains and carpet and walls. Joey only knew one individual with such particular tastes.

“Lucifer?” Joey called out, “are you trying to summon me again?”

The room remained silent, save for a growing, inhuman, inorganic noise above the ceiling. It was a sloshing, a great turbidity, an uncontainable tempest which, in a sudden catastrophe, instigated a total collapse of the aforementioned ceiling, soaking Joey and the room around him in a river of blood. Joey, rather urgently, swam up to the surface, and when he finally got a breath in he saw the old rickety house of Satan on his dry, grassy hill. Joey waded over to where the blood-water met the blood-mud and began his slow climb up to his master. Joey had a feeling that this would not be a pleasant meeting.

Joey dealt a few reserved knocks onto the dusty old door.

“Hello,” he announced himself, “it’s Joey Axelrod, at your service. I’m presuming you need some kind of service if you’ve sent me here.”

The door opened to an empty room, entirely bare save for Lucifer himself, who looked a good deal more distressed than usual.

“Sit down,” he declared in a booming, resounding, wall-shaking voice.

“…Do you have any chairs?” Joey felt the need to ask.

“You can sit on the floor.”

Joey obliged, not wanting the volume of the cabin to creep any further into upper digits.

“Um, Lucifer,” Joey paused, trying to phrase things correctly, “may I ask why exactly you’ve summoned me here today?”

“You are my avatar, Axelrod. I gave you access to my tremendous powers and with those powers I also made you beholden to my bylaws. One such bylaw is that you must arrive in the underworld whenever I believe it to be necessary. Another bylaw is that you’re not supposed to complain about your duties to your master, Joseph.”

“I apologize, sir, I didn’t mean to offend or disrespect you. I was just presuming that, if you brought me here, there would probably be some broader reason behind that choice, right?”

“Correct. While I do have the privilege to summon you whenever I’d like it, I do not find your presence enjoyable enough to summon you any more than what is absolutely necessary. I have summoned you today due to a great collision of major issues which will require your interference to prevent from snowballing further.”

“That doesn’t sound good…”

“That’s because it is, in actuality, bad. As it stands, all ten members of the Decadeum have avatars on Earth. That is enough to summon the greatest catastrophe the world has ever seen. There are two possible avenues to avoid this catastrophe. The first one involves you killing yourself.”

“What?”

“I figured you’d react like that. The fact of the matter is that at least one member of the Decadeum’s avatars absolutely must go, and you are one such member. Killing you would allow us to all avoid a terrible fate.”

“Hold on. Didn’t you say that there was a way for you to revoke my avatar status. Why not just do that?”

“I’m afraid that the method for revoking your avatar status does involve taking your life as well.”

“…Oh. Well that’s not great to hear. What about the second option?”

“Fair enough. Now, the nice thing about Option 2 is that it doesn’t require you to kill yourself—which I imagine you’ll see as quite a relief. It does, however, still necessitate that you kill an avatar, specifically the most defenseless avatar, a young man by the name of Miras Umarov.”

“…Where could I find him?”

“Somewhere in the city of Kollam.”

“Well, I’m aware of the name, and I know he worked with Nair at one point, so I suppose I can justify taking his life.”

“Also the entire world could be put at risk if you don’t take his life.”

“That too.”

“It’s a morally justifiable killing.”

“You know I don’t feel super great taking moral guidance from a guy with a name like Lucifer.”

“I am neither the representative of good nor evil. I am merely an adjudicator. You must look inward when evaluating my judgments.”

“I know, I know. It’s just that centuries upon centuries of depictions have framed you as being of the tricky, duplicitous sort.”

“I’m well aware. Though I hope that your lived experiences with the real me have altered your interpretation of my true character. Now, I suppose we should forge our words into a solid deal. You, Joseph Agbayani Axelrod, will either kill Miras Umarov or, if that proves impossible, kill yourself.”

Lucifer pointed a big open palm in Joey’s direction. Joey freezed. He had shook this man’s hand before, he had placed his trust within that man’s wicked heart, and, while he hadn’t ever been rewarded for it, he had managed to keep on living. His first interaction with Lucifer was one where that devil saved his life, and the powers that he granted him had saved his life further. Joey Axelrod wanted to live, and while any agreement with a clause regarding his death had the tendency to frighten him, he truly believed that Lucifer had proven that he had Joey’s best interests in that wicked little heart of his. So, Joey, disregarding Faust and all the poor souls before him, took and shook the fallen angel’s hand with a smile.

Vraxi Nair sat in a damp subterranean room. The PAAS had very generously opted to host her and her fellow interlocutors, but, being a communist guerrilla faction in a nation actively trying to stamp their presence out, they didn’t have the needed budget to give said interlocutors the greatest accommodations. Vraxi had been ruthlessly apologized to by a young party official as they led her further and further down into the basement floors of an inconspicuous Krungthep sporting complex and to her room. Vraxi insisted that the official didn’t have to worry but she could see in their face a deep fear of incompetence that no amount of soothing could extricate.

Regardless, Vraxi actually quite liked the dingy living space. It was a good few degrees cooler than the ground floor and possessed a certain lived-in quality that made it feel much more like a home than many of the other temporary bedrooms Vraxi had bounced through in the weeks prior. Also, Theta was staying in that same room, which always made Vraxi a little excited.

“Are you feeling better?” Theta asked her.

“Better from what?” Vraxi asked as she ladled some complimentary soup into a small bowl.

“Joey Axelrod pointed a gun at you. He very nearly shot you.”

“But he never pulled the trigger.”

“The human mind has the tendency to swell and fracture in any stressful, life-threatening situation, even those where the life in question leaves unharmed. I understand that your body is safe—and I’m thankful for that—but I do still worry about your mind.”

“Oh, Theta, I appreciate it but, really, you don’t have to worry for me. Afterall, it’s not like this is the first time that Axelrod’s pointed a gun at my head.”

“I’m just worried about your stress, Vraxi. For me, stress is an entirely quantifiable subject. I experience it in stressful situations, but when those moments pass, I can just delete all the lingering stressfulness and return to a static calm. But, as far as I’m aware, human stress doesn't work like that; it clings to the folds of your brain and stays there, building up over time until it’s impossible to push down.”

“Well,” Vraxi took a long sip of the soup, “I wouldn’t say you're wrong. I’ve definitely felt my stress snowballing a little. But, at the same time, I don’t think that that feeling will last for long.”

“…Why’s that?”

“Because we’re almost done with what we need to do, Theta. We’ve gotten Patcharee on our side, Aisha’s snagged Hailang, all we really need to do now is that favor for PAAS in Roi Et and-”

“Get Joey to work with us.”

“You finished my sentence.”

“I suppose that, despite everything, we have similar minds.”
