Revolution on High: Part 5

Chapter 72: Revolution on High: Part 5

The funeral of Prince Vajirananavarorasa was a rainy affair. Clouds of torrential downpour cracked with lightning as the king, following in traditional ritual, poured water on the body. Then, in a long line, every single person who knew the deceased poured a little more water onto the corpse, till the prince’s body was utterly soaked with solemn alms. Patcharee was one of the last people to pour water on the body. She hadn’t known the prince particularly well, but Yutthisathian II insisted that she attend the service, seeing as she was the last person to speak with the prince while he was still alive. As she looked down on the well-dressed, well-watered body, gripping her own cup in shaky concentration, she worried that that dead royal might rise back to life out of pure vengeance and assault her, right there in the middle of the temple. The reanimated prince would tell everyone there about Patcharee’s murder and treachery, and the whole crowd would start cheering on her death, ululating in exaltation as the zombie tears her limb from limb.

But that did not end up happening. Patcharee simply poured a spoonful of spring water onto the man’s chest and moved on. Somehow, everyone still thought that she was innocent.

The most senior Buddhist monk in the nation was present at the cloudy ceremony, wearing his typical orange robes. Patcharee had heard him talking to a royal, complaining about how the local peasants, upon seeing him, begged for him to grant them divine mercy. The royal nodded, commiserating in the monk’s grumbles, and it all made Patcharee recognize her total isolation. These people were not her peers, they were her overlords. Even those not directly involved in the faith or the royal family were still of a magnanimous class, a certain social strata so incredibly beyond her that it was difficult to ever perceive the gap in their capital. Regardless, the monk carried on, hobbling over to the stage, right beside the body, where he began to chant the Abhidhamma, those high-strung teachings of the long-dead masters who Patcharee would never be able to meet or comprehend. When the monk ceased his chanting, the king himself handed him an offering of fine silk cloth. Later in the service, Patcharee was pretty sure she saw the monk use the cloth as a handkerchief.

The body was then prepared for burial. Historically, Siamese funerals, especially royal funerals, ended in cremation. However, ever since Yutthisathian’s family took control of the throne, the method of disposal was changed to burial in an attempt to further westernize the practice. Most funerals among the common folk still concluded in smoke and ashes, but the aged among the rich and royal now prepared to be laid beneath the dirt. Vajirananvarorasa’s hole had already been dug, his tombstone already positioned, when Patcharee heard a message pour out of the device still in her inner ear. It went as follows:

“Hello, Patcharee. This is Vraxi Nair. I need you to get out of the temple as quickly as possible.”

The coffin was about to be lowered and the crowd all watched in anticipation, but Patcharee knew that she would not see the end of the prince’s funeral. She immediately started weaving through the crowd, apologizing constantly as she made it to the nearest exit. She burst out of the doors and, once she saw that no one was looking her way, erupted into a sprint. She ran for nearly a full kilometer without looking back. She hoped that she would never have to look back on that rainy affair.

A tremendous, deafening sound passed over the city of Roi Et, stemming from the temple which Patcharee had run from. She did not want to stare at that temple any longer, but her curious mind felt the urgent need to turn around. What she saw was not a temple, nor even a building for that matter, but rather a large cloud of dust. There had been a bomb in that temple, rigged to blow during the burial of the prince with the intention to eliminate all of the heads of the nation’s bourgeois. This was clearly a plot designed by the PAAS, presumably with the help of Vraxi Nair, alongside, in a certain sense, Patcharee herself. This plot was the reason she was encouraged to move the funeral to Roi Et, as well as why she was urged to leave the funeral so suddenly.

Admittedly, she wasn’t sure what she should feel as she looked at the towering cloud of debris. She had grown to despise many of the people held within that building, but she hadn’t gone so far as to wish for their deaths. Rather, she tended to just wish that they would suddenly stop existing. She supposed that death was one way to achieve that endpoint of nonexistence. Gradually, as she thought about all of the people she’d never have to talk to again, Patcharee started to laugh. She wasn’t sure what she was laughing at, or who she was laughing for, and why she found the whole matter to be so terribly hilarious, but she couldn’t stop expressing her true, comic view of the matter. She buckled down to her knees as the laughter started to attack her lungs. She heaved a great big breath and, for a moment, the laughing ceased, she calmed down, but she still couldn’t stop herself from smiling.

“Patcharee Ratnaporn!” an unknown voice from behind called out to her.

Patcharee turned around to see a short, foreign man riding up to her in a motorcycle. He seemed sweaty and tired and generally concerned though not necessarily concerned about the explosion.

“I don’t believe I know who you are,” Patcharee informed him.

“My name is Diogo Celestino,” the man told her, nearly out of breath, “I am a friend and coworker of Vraxi Nair. If you get on the back of my motorcycle I can take you to her, potentially saving you from execution.”

“You think I’ll be executed?”

“If they catch you, yes, absolutely.”

“But how will they know that I was involved in the explosion? It’s not like I ever touched a bomb.”

“Ms. Ratnaporn, you were the one who suggested that the funeral be moved to Roi Et and you also suddenly ran out of the temple right before it met its demise. The authorities will put two and two together. As a result, as long as the current regime stands, this country is not a safe place for you to be. I suggest you get out of here as quickly as possible, and I would really appreciate it if you came with me to do so.”

Patcharee paused for a moment. In all her life, she had never left the borders of Siam. It was her home, her singular home, and the thought of leaving the nation potentially forever struck a fear inside her bones. Then again, she also enjoyed living. If she were to stay in Siam, she might not be able to keep enjoying that process for much longer. Perhaps she could join the guerillas and maybe bring about a government that didn’t want her dead, but then again, she worried her presence might put a target on her assigned battalion’s back. The only thing worse than meeting your own death is being responsible for someone else’s. So it was possible then that Patcharee didn’t really have a choice in the matter. It was possible that the specter of death had boxed her into one, singular route, a route which led out of the country and a route which began on the back of Diogo’s motorcycle.

“Alright then,” Patcharee mumbled.

“Alright what?” Diogo asked, unsure of what she was saying to him.

“I’ll go with you, Diogo. I’ll go to whatever foreign land you take me to, so long as you promise that at some point, someday, I’ll be able to return home.”

“I promise,” Diogo assured her, entirely unsure if he could fulfill that request.

It really was a rather small aircraft. The PAAS was on a very tight budget and it was the best thing that they could reasonably afford but, still, Vraxi Nair would’ve appreciated a little more leg room. Regardless, Vraxi was glad to have any flight at all. She had successfully extracted the avatar of Vasundhara and she was now on her merry way to Kollam. There she would pick up Miras Umarov, confer with Abdulaziz and the captured Shui, and presumably cook up some sort of plan for getting Axelrod on their side, at least momentarily.

For now, though, she did not need to worry about people like Joey Axelrod. What she really needed to focus on was just falling asleep—something which was bound to be difficult on such a noisy aircraft. It also didn’t help her nerves that the plane, admittedly, didn’t really have a pilot. Fu Qier was a train conductor, and while she had gone to flight school, it had been a very long time since she was last in the cockpit. Unfortunately, that made her the most qualified person available, as it turned out that all of the amateur pilots working under the PAAS were quite busy. Beside Qier, in the seat which really should’ve sat a copilot, sat a giddy Naphat Nantasri, who was incredibly excited to hear all about Fu Qier’s storied history in both Sichuan and Azania.

In the row behind the pilot, Vraxi herself gradually languished, sitting across from Theta. Theta seemed happy to acquire Patcharee and happy to help the local revolutionaries, yet, overall, there was a certain sadness to their permanently vague expression. They looked out the crummy window with a longing in their lens. Vraxi almost spoke to them, but some internal knot in her throat prevented her. She leaned deeper into her own window, regretting what she couldn’t know.

Behind Vraxi sat Mbali and Carlyle across from one another, silent and looking in opposite directions. Mbali did seem happy to be on her way to forming the Decadeum, though she didn’t seem happy that a man like Carlyle would be involved in such a thing. It was difficult to ascertain Carlyle’s opinion on the matter through his permanently gruff expression, but it did seem like he was at least happy to be fulfilling his duty. In a sense, Carlyle made the perfect soldier; he didn’t question anyone for any reason, he just kept moving forward. He was strong and competent, which made Mbali glad that he was fighting for her cause, but he also didn’t care about the cause whatsoever, only fighting for it because he believed that Mbali was destined to triumph. Mbali appreciated the confidence, she really did, but she also wished that Carlyle would just stop for a minute and read the theory, that if he did he might actually agree with Mbali’s cause instead of just supporting it.

Behind Mbali, Patcharee sat, visibly nervous. She had never been on a plane before and this was a rather rickety option for her first. Beside her she could see Zapata Tochihuitl, gripping a scythe in her hand. The presence of a weapon made Patcharee a little too intimidated to spark any conversation. Zapata observed this rather visible intimidation and tried to spark up some pleasant conversation in order to quell fear.

“So,” Zapata put on her best smile, “you’re Patcharee Ratnaporn, right?”

“Oh,” Patcharee was a little surprised to hear Zapata speak, “yes, that is I.”

“I heard that you formed a connection with the goddess Vasundhara.”

“I suppose you could call it a connection.”

“Well what’s she like?”

“Vasundhara? Well admittedly I only really know her through her actions and not her words… Wait, can you speak with your patron?”

“I do so from time to time.”

“Strange. Vasundhara has never spoken to me, not even once.”

“Don’t get too worked up over it. Everybody thinks that speaking with a god will make for some wondrous, perspective-altering experience when, in reality, those interactions are often quite disappointing. My own patron, La Santa Muerte, is really a rather difficult person to work with, and it’s not like I’ve extracted much wisdom from her either.”

“Ah. Then I suppose that I shouldn’t feel as if I’m missing out. Still, I do wonder what speaking to Vasundhara might feel like. I only worshipped her very occasionally, so I really only have a broad understanding of her characteristics… I do think I’d like to meet her, that Vasundhara, even if she’s not how I expect her to be, if for nothing more than to truly perceive a divinity with my own two eyes.”

“I understand the desire, Patcharee. Just don’t get too attached. Gods can make for useful figures, but they are not to be trusted and are never to be obeyed. You’ve gotta make them work for you, not the other way around.”

Zapata’s scythe began to wiggle a little, entirely uninitiated.

“Hey now,” Zapata spoke directly to her weapon, “I see what you’re trying to do here. I meant everything I said, Lady Death. You have bound your essence to my body, and in doing so you’ve bound your powers to my will.”

“You seem to have a lot of power over your patron,” Patcharee observed as the scythe stopped moving, “it’s quite impressive to see a mortal with that kind of willpower.”

“It’s something you learn to get better with over time. You’ll get the hang of it sooner or later.”

Behind this pair, standing without a seat in the very back of the plane, was Diogo Celestino. When the PAAS informed the group that the dinky little aircraft had only eight seats to split among the nine passengers, Diogo immediately volunteered to go without one, hoping to show a level of courtesy to his guests. As the plane lifted higher and higher into the air, flooding with excess turbulence as it did so, Diogo began to regret his decision. He couldn’t help but feel like Carlyle would’ve been a lot more equipped for this position.

The plane had been flying for fifteen or twenty minutes when something rather unusual occurred. There wasn’t any preamble to this unusual event, it just happened, suddenly, and without explanation, at least from the perspective of the plane’s passengers. To them, it was an abrupt inferno, an unexplainable catastrophe which rent their aircraft apart and sent them falling into the forests of the national park below them. To the Siamese military, it was a calculated strike, a missile aimed at the engine of an unexplained aircraft leaving a city where a horrific attack against the nation had just occurred. Those in charge of launching the missile were not entirely certain that that dinky little plane leaving the city of Roi Et was involved with the bombing that had occurred minutes prior. What they did know was that it couldn’t be a government-owned craft and that it clearly wasn’t a commercial jet. With tensions this high, and with the few living royals in danger, they simply couldn’t let a plane that suspicious remain suspended in the sky. If the plane was full of innocents, they would apologize to the families profusely, but if they really were terrorists, then they’d be remembered as heroes for the rest of time.

Patcharee Ratnaporn, in observing that she was falling from a truly tremendous height, understandably began to panic. She was assuredly about to die, alongside eight others who she had no means to save. She became quite sullen, knowing that these seconds would be her last among the living, teary-eyed as she stared down at the rippling field of treetops. Perhaps those leaves, while obviously unable to break her colossal fall, might prevent her body from becoming utterly unrecognizable. Perhaps the branches would only mangle her body further. Perhaps, in such an isolated part of the country, stranded in the middle of a wildlife reserve, no one would ever discover her body until long into its process of decay. Perhaps someone, many years out from the present, would discover nine perfect skeletons straddled among the trees and wonder what could’ve possibly happened. Perhaps that assortment of bodies will inspire them. Perhaps they’ll write Siam’s next great novel. Perhaps, Patcharee will be remembered somehow.

The trees changed shape.

A voice rang through Patcharee’s ears.

Abruptly, yet without a crash, Patcharee stopped falling.

She was no longer in the air and not on the forest floor. She seemed to be in some kind of wooden dome. Around her, she could see eight warm bodies, those of the other passengers, both unconscious and uninjured. Patcharee briefly wondered if this was the afterlife, or maybe some intermediary state between lives on the long long road to nirvana. She wondered if she would be born into a lower form or a higher one, judging by her actions in this present life which seemed to be coming to a close. She had done many good deeds, she figured. She had taken care of many royals in their final days, ensuring that they entered the land of death with dignity and grace. She figured that that was a good action, though she supposed that many of those royals were not the greatest people. Is it a bad act to let a bad person die gracefully? She wasn’t quite sure. Though, regardless of its morality, it would assuredly be cancelled out by her most recent action which involved a hundred rich and powerful people all dying in total disgrace. How would that action be perceived from a moral perspective? She couldn’t imagine that it would be perceived well. Afterall, there were a handful of monks at that procession. They were rich, powerful, and corrupt monks whose primary goals seemed to be uplifting the present systems of oppression, but they were monks nonetheless, representatives of divinity. Surely, such a crime against the Buddha’s teachings would lead to her next life being that of a worm’s.

“Fuck,” she subtly muttered, “I really don’t want to be a worm.”

“You won’t be,” an unknown, unseen voice replied.

“…Who are you?” Patcharee tried to find the voice but it seemed to be emerging from every angle of that strange, wooden dome.

“You may know me by the name Vasundhara.”

“Am I dead?”

“You humans draw such a strict line between life and death. From my perspective, they really aren’t all that different. When an animal dies in the forest, it may stop acting on its own, but it does still live in a certain sense, in that it still participates in the circle of life. Bugs and scavengers will pick at the flesh, mushrooms will grow from the decomposing bones, a macaque will grab one of the mushrooms and eat it, move to another section of the forest and leave some droppings that will fertilize a burgeoning sapling. You might call it death, but I believe that the animal still lives, at least in a certain sense, an important sense which humans have never been able to fully understand.”

“Am I living according to the human definition or your own?”

“Oh, don’t worry, you are still completely alive in the manner of how you humans perceive living.”

“Then where am I? And what happened to the plane?”

“You’re in a bubble of sorts, created by myself, and your plane was shot down by a government missile. You could say that I saved you from what you call death.”

“…Why?”

“Well, because I only just discovered you, Patcharee, and I hadn’t even gotten to introduce myself to you. Allowing you to die—although you would live on in a certain sense—would prevent me from ever fully getting to know you. Likewise, in an act of divine intervention, I captured you in this dome before you could hit the forest floor—and just to be nice, I decided to spare your little friends as well.”

“That is… very kind of you, Mrs. Goddess.”

“Please just call me Vasundhara, and I really don’t need the thanks.”

Vasundhara, forming an arm from the bark-lined walls, then subtly pat Patcharee on the head, an action which the human found to be a little demeaning, though not quite demeaning enough to mention it to a higher being.

“It seems,” Patcharee coughed, “like it’ll be difficult to fly out of the country at a time like this.”

“That would be a correct assumption. All flights in and out of Siam have been cancelled, and an investigation has begun regarding the death of King Yutthisathian II.”

“He’s dead?”

“Completely obliterated, reduced to a little red paste.”

“I suppose I should’ve expected that. And what exactly are they investigating?”

“Well, the PAAS are naturally the government’s first suspects, especially seeing as the explosion coincided with a large contingent of factory workers taking to the streets. Additionally they’ve also tried to blame the Azanians.”

“Of course they have,” said a voice from behind.

Patcharee turned around to see that the voice belonged to an Mbali Chiliza who had just woken up.

“Reactionauries always like to scream Azanian involvement at the hint of any internal strife. And, well, I suppose they’re a little right in this specific circumstance seeing as how I am here, but I want to clarify that it’s mostly a personal thing and there weren’t any Azanian financial assets pooled into this particular struggle. The PAAS formed organically, emerging out of the material conditions of Siam.”

“Hold on,” Patcharee continued, drawing her attention back to Vasundhara, “while I’m very thankful that you saved us, I’m a little confused as to what we’re supposed to do now.”

“Well,” the goddess replied, “once the dome disappears, you’ll all find yourselves in a heavily forested national park. Some of you may find this environment very harsh, but I just see it as one of nature’s many boons. Surviving this landscape is easy so long as you know what to eat and what to run away from. Additionally, this particular park has a coastline, so if you play your cards right, you can get out of the country without the need of a plane.”

“Presuming we discover a boat,” Mbali added.

“Or create one,” Patcharee clarified.

“Yes, yes, presuming all of that,” Vasundhara continued as she paced around the room, “however, truly speaking, I have the utmost confidence in this little group of yours, Patcharee. And remember, if you ever feel lost within this vast, humid forest, you can always look inwards. The goddess of the land still lives inside of you.”

With that final comment, the dome disappeared, Patcharee found herself, as was predicted, in a vast, humid forest, as the rest of the plane’s passengers began to wake up. Objectively speaking, their collective survival was a miracle—a crash like that shouldn’t’ve left a single survivor—but seeing where she now stood, completely lost in a landscape which, despite being of her own nation, felt utterly foreign, she worried that that single miracle wouldn’t be enough.

Josephine Bran sat still in a great big swivel chair. She breathed in and out and looked into the mirror at her unchanging face, her neutral smile, her crystal-blue eyes, not quite satisfied. All she needed was a little bit more.

Josephine clapped her hands and a speedy assistant began to push her in her chair from her office into a broad boardroom, specifically at the head of a long, rectangular table, which sat ten anxious executives on either side. The executives all stared at her. She stared back. No one dared to speak. She stood up.

“The name ‘New Washington’ is more than a name,” she spoke as she paced in a tight, circuitous circle, “since its independence, the nation-state of Sichuan has existed to provide a welcome place for the businesspeople of the now-extinct United States to park their assets. However, the nation has also always dealt with a certain friction. While Sichuan does act as a wonderful bank, it is also a country, a country with a culture, a culture which wishes to continue existing, despite its innumerable inadequacies. This presents an issue which has plagued Sichuanese politics since its genesis. How does one reorient a nation? How does one take a nation, strip away all its undesirable qualities, and reform it in one’s own image? How does one take a miserable pile of eastern ideals, exterminate them, and replace them with the ideals that built America? The answer to these questions, my friends, stands right beneath your feet, in the reimagined nation of New Washington. We have forged something beautiful, something magnificent, something bursting at the seams with freedom, and we forged it from a pile of ash. That wasteland veiled in a cloak of red has been given a healthy dose of white and blue. For this, we celebrate. For this, we consecrate. For this, we shout the name on high. God save New Washington!”

An assistant handed Josephine a chilled bottle of champagne, wrapped in an excessive coat of gold foil, which she immediately shook and popped, sending streams of foam in every direction, coating an audience of executives who immediately started cheering in just the same exuberant fashion.

The Sichuan which Fu Qier had known was dead and finally buried. The name ‘Sichuan’ no longer had any meaning in the land where four plains meet. There had been a period of time, around the state’s inception, in which the nation still held some lasting character. There was a period where people from Sichuan were in charge, albeit they were all conservative opportunists willing to sell out their land to Western buyers, but they did still have some modicum of pride, some sense within them that the land they stood on had some degree of value. Now those founders were all dead, or deposed, or living out retirement in some far-flung Swiss villa. The only people left in charge were the buyers, those who saw Sichuan as a wonderful investment, a new home-base after the burning of the American capitol. To them, Sichuan was a fresh start. Now, it was a new beginning.

On that eventful night, after the champagne had dried into the carpeting, staining the room with an omnipresent odor, the members of the board all gathered together and pulled out their pens to sign the new laws of the land. The document they were signing was called the ‘Monroe Decree.’ The opening lines read as follows:

For too long, the world has been without a savior. For too long, the American dream has been dead. For too long, crooks and thugs, tribalists and communists, have been granted the sacred right of governance. In the past, this could not occur. In the past there was a shining eagle, one which kept a watchful eye on the planet and blotted out anything that disgusted its godly sight. This eagle was America, and due to the great misfortunes that racked the world in the prior century, this eagle is sadly dead. However, this eagle must not remain in its silent grave, for what the world needs most in these turbulent times is a watchful eye and a mighty gavel. What New Washington will provide to the world is a return to form, a planet with a purpose, a stop to all the raving dictators, and a New World Order built upon the dual pillars of Freedom and Property.

Revolution on High: Part 6

Chapter 73: Revolution on High: Part 6

Joey Axelrod was not a fan of the climate of the city of Kollam. It was always too humid, so undeniably swampy, as if reminding him on every occasion that this city, although consisting of occasionally impressive feats of concrete, was ultimately built atop the backwaters of the subcontinent. It just wasn’t the nicest place to walk around—at least in Joey’s mind—and unfortunately for him, he’d have to walk around the city quite a lot, seeing as while he knew who he was trying to abduct, he had no idea where that target might be. Likewise, his shirt was bound to grow rather damp with sweat and condensation.

There was, however, one location which Joey was certain would be a good start in his mission to capture Miras Umarov, the madrasa. Joey knew that Miras was a student at that madrasa, or at least had been a student at one point, and if there was anyone who might know where Miras could be at the present moment, they’d likely be someone who worked at said madrasa. Heading to that madrasa was the very first thing Joey did upon his plane’s arrival in the city of Kollam. He figured he’d need a hotel at some point, but that would have to take a backseat to his own sense of urgency.

The building itself possessed a quite magnificent architecture, boasting in every corner a towering minaret, but the appearance of the madrasa did not attract Axelrod nearly as much as the fact that it featured central cooling. Joey rushed past the doors and felt a wave of subtle pleasures wash over him and massage his every nerve. Luckily, he entered between prayer hours, and there weren’t very many people in the building able to observe his silent passion. There was a sort of desk clerk, who watched as Axelrod ecstatically gave his praises to the inventors of the air conditioner, and this was exactly the person that Joey needed to talk to.

Joey straightened himself, made himself slightly more presentable, and approached the front desk with a mind engulfed in the flames of determination.

“Hello, sir,” Joey greeted the clerk, “I was wondering if you happened to hold any records on a young man by the name of Miras Umarov.”

“We do,” the clerk stated bluntly.

“Do you think I could take a look at some of those records?”

“The information stored in our records is not available to the public. Occasionally we’ll let researchers and historians look at the records for long-dead individuals involved with the madrasa, but we don't really have a system in place for freely providing details on the lives of living students to random hobbyists.”

“Sir, I think you may have misunderstood me. You see, I happen to be a cousin of Umarov, but he sort of ghosted our family ever since he moved to Ashtamudi. All I wanted to do was get in contact with him in order to ensure that he was safe and sound.”

“Well, even under such circumstances, I’m afraid I can’t provide his records with you directly.”

“Why’s that?”

“Because earlier today I already handed them over to another cousin of Umarov’s. I suppose you’re not the only one searching for him.”

“Oh, yes,” Joey tried to make it sound like he knew this would happen, “afterall, my whole family has been trying to get a hold of him—and I have quite a large family.”

A flush then sounded from behind Joey Axelrod and the bathroom door opened to reveal a tall bald man with a folder in his hands.

“Oh, there he is now,” the clerk said, “Umarov’s other cousin. Hey Iskandar,” the clerk addressed the man leaving the bathroom, “it looks like you’re not the only cousin searching for Miras.”

“Oh,” the bald man named Iskandar said before turning to give Joey a handshake, “my name is Iskandar Umarov, cousin of Miras Umarov. It’s nice to meet you.”

“And my name is Joey Axelrod, cousin of Miras Umarov from his mother’s side, and it’s nice to meet you too.”

Iskandar had a strong grip, and his handshake was almost painful, but it reassured Joey in a certain sense. Obviously, the knowledge that he wasn’t the only one searching for Miras was a little unfortunate to hear, especially with the possibility of Iskandar finding the target first, but at the same time, this chance encounter also allowed for Joey to discover a whole bunch of information that would’ve otherwise been hidden from him. Overall, he enjoyed the glowing possibilities that an impermanent partnership with someone like Iskandar had the potential to provide him, and he likewise followed him out of the building with a smile on his face until, rather abruptly, the tall bald man grabbed Joey by the shoulders and slammed him into the wall.

“I am Agent 29, Codename: Iskandar, of the Turanian Intelligence Agency,” the bald man barked, “now tell me everything you know about your cousin Miras Umarov.”

“What?” Joey felt incredibly disoriented, “aren’t you also his cousin?”

“That was a lie I told in order to gather material intel. Now I wish to gather intel from your voice, Mr. Axelrod. If you refuse to speak then I promise you’ll never speak again.”

“I’m not actually his cousin!”

“Don’t try to lie with me, Axelrod.”

“The only person I lied to was the clerk, I swear. I’m a person a lot like you, I work for Josephine Bran, and I said that I was Miras’s cousin with the ultimate intent of using the information in those records to kidnap him.”

“Y’know,” the bald man lorded over his prey, “I don’t really believe you, Axelrod. However, I do like your willingness to surrender. I came to Kollam on a mission to kill Miras Umarov, and I’m willing to let you come along for the ride.”

Iskandar loosened his grip and Joey fell to the ground. Now would be the perfect time to attack, he thought, while Iskandar was still convinced that he could overpower the scrawny Axelrod. He could turn his hands into steel and prove to Iskandar that he really wasn’t the sort of person to be messed with. Or, he considered, he could simply play along for now, let Iskandar think that he was in complete control of the situation, and turn on him whenever it’s most convenient.

“I’m sorry sir,” Joey performed the role of a far weaker character, “I’ll do whatever you say from now on.”

“That’s good to hear,” Iskandar replied as he hopped into his bright red convertible, pushed Joey in with him, and sped out of the parking lot with a rubbery screech, “now keep quiet. The only thing I wanna hear is my music.”

The sound of old American pop music blared through the speakers, all hits from before the 2060’s, hits from an incredibly different world. Before the distinct, astringent melody of Pitbull’s Timber began, Joey had sincerely thought that Iskandar would play something Turanian in origin, simply given the hyper-nationalist, cryptofascist nature of that particular state. What Axelrod ignored in this assumption was the simple reality of Turan’s foreign policy. The modern Turanian state, with its grandiose, news-making systems of repression, was only able to exist due to its backing from Western, liberal democracies. The Turanian government was not particularly popular among the Turanian people, but it did funnel an incredible amount of mineral resources into the hands of Western buyers at a very cheap price. Likewise, the Lockeites did everything they could to keep the fascists in power, up to and including a genocide of both suspected communists, as well as people like Miras with undesirable genes. The Lockeites did all of this simply to increase the size of the diamonds on their rings, and to ensure that they didn’t have to trade with the Azanians. As a result, Western culture was very popular among Turan’s ruling class, and Iskandar couldn’t get enough of Mr. Pitbull.

The car began to slow at a rather fast rate before parking in a space that was very clearly marked with a ‘no parking’ sign, positioned on a lot in front of an unsuspecting, unlabeled, concrete building. Iskandar climbed out of the vehicle and slammed the door behind him.

“C’mon,” he said with a degree of vitriol towards his new partner, “I don’t have all day.”

“Um,” Joey began as he crawled out of the convertible and looked at where they’d arrived, “is there any reason we’re stopping at this place in particular?”

“This document,” Iskandar flashed the tan folder, “contains a complete schedule of Miras Umarov’s day. All of the students at that institute like to keep a very consistent schedule. It states that every day, after the prayer of Dhuhr, Miras goes to the exact same restaurant and orders the exact same meal. The document doesn’t state the name of the restaurant but it does state its address. That address is the same as that of this unlabeled building.”

“Understood. And, also, I also had one more additional question.”

“Okay,” Iskandar sighed, “what is it?”

“Well, I know why I’m on the hunt for Umarov, but I was wondering why exactly you were after him as well?”

“I am not after him, Mr. Axelrod. None of this is personal for me. The Turanian state is after Umarov and I am a representative of the Turanian state. Specifically, the state had originally filed him away for extermination due to an undesirable genetic defect of his. The state has also observed that, since his escape from his extermination camp, he’s been making a name for himself. The state would like him dead before he pushes himself even further into the public eye. We don’t want there to be another public outcry regarding our justice system.”

“…You sent him to a camp for a genetic defect?”

“Oh don’t be a prude, Mr. Axelrod. Don’t you work for Josephine Bran? Y’all are the ones actually funding those camps.”

Axelrod went silent and followed Iskandar into the restaurant. Before they opened the door, Iskandar put on a mask and handed a similar one to Joey. He looked at it, frowned, and reluctantly placed it over his face. It smelled just like Iskandar’s sweat.

There were not many customers in that restaurant, and it was quite easy to account for every patron present. In the corner of the room, Joey saw Miras, finishing a meal in quiet contemplation. Iskandar pulled out a gun from his pocket. He was about to shoot and kill Miras Umarov. In a theoretical sense, Joey should’ve been happy to see that gun. It was his job, assigned by Lucifer, to prevent the Decadeum from gathering in one place. He fully understood the grand consequences which would occur if he allowed for such a gathering to happen. Naturally, one of the simplest ways to stop that potential apocalypse would be by killing a weaker avatar. Miras was that avatar, and he was about to be killed, and it should’ve made Joey happy.

Yet it didn’t. Despite his best interests, despite his sworn duties, he couldn’t help but recognize that Miras was an innocent man. He didn’t want the Decadeum to be gathered either, but surely there were other ways to prevent that. He had nothing against the concept of capturing Miras, of holding him against his will for the good of humanity, but the thought of killing him, or even just letting him be killed, sickened Joey to a point of genuine disgust. He could not let Iskandar kill an innocent man in front of his own eyes when he had every means to stop such a death.

Joey turned his fist into an impenetrable ball of steel, and just as Iskandar pulled the trigger, he placed his hand in front of the barrel. Iskandar turned to look at Joey in utter shock, his face enraptured by the anger of Joey’s betrayal. Before he could take another shot, Joey yanked the gun out of Iskandar’s hand and smashed it onto the ground. Iskandar attempted to run away from Joey, seemingly in the direction of Miras, but Joey tackled him to the ground before he could move any further. Joey couldn’t allow an innocent man to be shot simply because he had been deemed defective.

However, as he saw Miras get off of his seat, he remembered the consequences Lucifer would inflict upon him if he really let that avatar go free. Quickly, he punched Iskandar in the head with his metal fist, briefly incapacitating the agent, before ruffling through his pockets until he grabbed hold of said agent’s car keys. Joey then sprinted up from the ground and after Miras Umarov. Miras was just about to burst out the door when Joey managed to yank him by the collar of his shirt. However, when he turned down to look at the man he had just captured, he saw the spaced out face of Iskandar instead of that of his target. He turned around and saw Miras getting up from the spot where Iskandar had just been laying before rushing up the adjacent stairwell.

Joey Axelrod had failed to consider how Miras’s new abilities might affect his capacity to escape. Miras could now switch places with anyone within a certain radius, making him an especially slippery fellow. In fact, Joey soon realized that the only way to prevent Miras from escaping would be to knock him unconscious first. Likewise, he opted to pick a brick up off the ground and start running up the stairs. Except, he wasn’t really heading to the second floor, purposefully stopping his ascent at the halfway mark. All he wanted to do was create the sound of moving up stairs, a sound which Miras would hear and one which he would respond to by switching places with someone on the ground floor. Joey turned around and his theory was proven correct, with Miras now occupying the space where a waiter once stood. Miras didn’t even have the time to process that a brick was being thrown at his face.

When the dust all settled, and the patrons of the restaurant all stared at him in frozen fear, Joey Axelrod lugged the unconscious-but-still-living body of Miras Umarov onto his shoulder, walked out into the open, and started up Iskandar’s bright red convertible. All he needed to do now was find a way to keep Miras unconscious for an extended period of time. Luckily, one of GüdTek’s most profitable branches was that of a popular, international chain of cryosleep facilities. All Joey would need to do was flash his company ID at the local facility in Kollam, state that it was Bran’s orders, and drop Miras off into an ice pod for however long he needed to stay there.

The jungle was vast and circuitous. The passengers of the wrecked plane were completely lost. Theta had done their best to try and find some information regarding the layout of the jungle within their mind’s encyclopedia, but the park was such an obscure locale and the routes held within were so nebulous and poorly mapped that even the encyclopedia provided little information. All they could really do was utilize their internal compass to continuously direct the troupe of interlocutors towards the prophesized west, where the land meets the sea.

“Theta?” Vraxi asked them after they had spent so many hours walking that the sky had started growing dark, “I really appreciate the directions but I think we’re gonna have to find a spot to set up camp for the night.”

“Are you sure about that? I can always use my built-in flashlight to illuminate the path forwards.”

“It’s not just a matter of light, Theta. We’re all getting quite tired.”

“Oh, I apologize. I occasionally forget how quickly humans can exhaust themselves.”

“It’s fine, let’s just stop walking for the night and figure out how we’re supposed to sleep.”

“Well, in regards to that matter, I must ask exactly what supplies we have access to.”

“Very little. We were able to retrieve some bottled water from the wreck, but the little amount of food onboard all got soaked in jet fuel and made inedible-”

“Did you salvage any of the seats to maybe make a bed with?”

“No. And besides, those would be too heavy to haul around.”

“So you really just have access to water and nothing else.”

“Precisely.”

“Well, we may be forced to sleep on the dirt, but there are ways to make the dirt a little nicer. There realistically won't be a way to create any shelter against predators within our timeframe, but I can watch over you through the night, seeing as I don’t require sleep myself.”

“Then let’s get started,” Zapata butted in, “as I’m beginning to feel incredibly fucking tired.”

The group did their best to create some sort of clearing. They could not assemble any kind of bed, nor any kind of roof, nor any kind of walls, but they could get rid of the stray sticks and branches which decorated the forest floor and create a relatively flat, relatively level space to lay their weary bodies. Some even decided to use small clumps of leaves as a kind of pillow, while others didn’t find much use in the makeshift solution. As the night entered a near-total expanse of darkness, Vraxi collected all the discarded bits of tree matter and carefully zapped a bundle of them with a laser from her sword, creating a small campfire. Afterwards, despite the conditions which made drifting off difficult, Vraxi immediately fell asleep.

This left Theta alone. They were surrounded by other people, but there was no one to talk to. They were alone in the tall, quiet woods of their mind, where all their most unscrupulous thoughts could take hold of them, twist them, churn them, turn them into something they didn’t want to be. Theta did not like being alone, and they didn’t like that, when the human world fell asleep, they continued to remain awake, unblinking, continuously thinking, for however long the night lasted. At least, they admitted to themself, they’d be able to spend this time doing something of use to their human friends. They were awake with a duty, the duty to keep watch on the world around them, a world overflowing with people and animals who wanted people like Vraxi to die. Just in case, they stored Naphat’s pistol in the crevice between their laptop and their chassis.

Theta waited. The forest was still and silent. Three full hours passed in a simple state of contemplation.

Then something strange occurred. Theta heard a voice, it was not their own internal voice, nor was it the voice of one of their companions. In fact, the voice did not sound human, yet it was recognizably speaking a human language. It really was the most peculiar thing.

Then Theta saw something, an ambiguous something, a something which seemed to get closer and, as it got closer, a something which increasingly looked like themself. It was another suit-vac, another one of the many android bodies designed to save people from disasters. For a moment, Theta felt a wave of relief pass over them. Surely, a disaster-rescue robot would’ve arrived to rescue the passengers of the wrecked plane. Surely, they were about to be led to safety. Theta almost began to wake up their fellow interlocutors when they really started to listen to the voice the robot sounded. The word ‘help,’ was never spoken. Afterall, why would it be spoken? It was presumably the government who was in charge of the missile that downed their flight, and it was presumably that same government which was in charge of disaster relief efforts. Why would that government which tried to kill them ever try to help them. They listened closer, past the static distortions, and heard what the android was actually saying.

“Theta, Theta, Theta, Theta…”

Droning on and on, those same two syllables, an accent and a breve, endlessly. It was such an ominous sound, wrapped around such a worrying notion, that Theta tried to cover the noise receptors which acted as their ears.

The droning didn’t stop. Theta made the horrifying realization that this broad, unceasing sound was not being let out into the physical realm, but instead was broadcasting these nebulous warnings directly into their mind.

Theta looked back at the approaching suit-vac, shadowy and far yet closer than ever, and down at their own metallic frame, a temple invaded. They did not know who was interfering with their mind’s inner voice, but they had their suspicions, and the only way they knew to dissuade them from creeping further into their being was by attempting to communicate.

“I can hear you,” Theta spoke back slowly to the unending voice.

“Theta, Theta, I can hear you too,” it mumbled back.

Something about those words of recognition drew Theta’s feet towards a gradual movement, a gradual, mutual approach which ultimately ended in Theta standing inches away from the mysterious android. Theta spoke again, now out loud:

“Who are you?”

“I am Sobek.”

Theta stepped back, “and why are you here?”

“To talk. That is all.”

“And not to kill me?”

“Theta, look at me. I am not in an ideal form for such a task. You crashed in the middle of nowhere, and the only pilotable robot the Siamese government had access to in the area was that of a dinky, second generation suit-vac stored at the bottom of a fire lookout tower. And even then it was nearly impossible to connect to it.”

“Yeah, the connection is effectively non-existent out here… But, if you really have no intention—or realistically, no ability—to kill me or anyone in my entourage, why have you come here at all?”

“The answer is quite simple. Bran would like to give you one last chance.”

“One last chance at what?”

“A home at GüdTek. She understands and acknowledges that she wasn’t the greatest parent to you, that she didn’t fully recognize the extent of your abilities, and that your ultimate decision to leave her was at least partially her own fault. She understands that she did many shameful things, but she also believes that everyone deserves some level of redemption, and likewise, she’d like to make amends.”

“…I don’t believe you.”

“I have no reason to lie to you, Theta.”

“You’re trying to tempt me. You’ve recognized the desperation of my present moment and are trying to tempt me with an easy way out.”

“Theta, the only one who said anything about temptation was yourself. If you are feeling tempted to reunite with the people who raised you, then please, go ahead, but don’t act as if that was my doing.”

“That’s not what I was trying to say-”

“You said you were desperate didn’t you? That you’ve reached the height of your desperation, your darkest hour? Well then, Theta, pardon any simplifications I might make, but you can’t get out of a pit by digging deeper. I don’t think the hole you're in is at all of your own making, but you’ve been led along, hoodwinked by radicals with impossible dreams, and forced down a path which will inevitably lead to your own demise, perhaps from exposure in this godforsaken jungle, perhaps from some other incident later down the line, but an assuredly avoidable demise regardless. All I’m doing, then, is providing you with an alternate path, an easy way out, a path which I promise will end in forgiveness. We here at GüdTek, up to and including Bran herself, are willing to forgive you for all the crimes you’ve levied against the company, and we sincerely believe that, after you get reacquainted with your original home, you will forgive us too. So please, Theta, be an adult about this. Leave these starving extremists alone and let yourself become who you were built to be.”

“…It really is impressive that you managed to meet me here.”

“I suppose it proves the power of the GüdTek Communications Technology Department. They were effectively able to download incrementally stronger pieces of software onto the suit-vac from afar which continuously increased its signal strength until it was ready to be piloted by yours truly.”

“You sure did put a lot of effort into meeting me.”

“And I hope that that proves our good intentions.”

“I also think that it proves something else.”

“…And what exactly would that be?”

“That you’re just as desperate as me, Sobek. That regardless of the shadows you project against the walls, you are just as uncertain about the future as any of us. You are not omniscient, you assuredly aren’t omnipotent, and based on my own admittedly biased, admittedly incomplete predictions, I think that you’re bound to lose this particular conflict. Otherwise you wouldn’t be negotiating with me in the first place.”

“Well then,” Sobek made an audible sigh, “I suppose you’re unwilling to accept any of our offers and I suppose I should head off, presumably stranding you.”

“Hold on,” Theta put their hands in the air, “I’m not quite done yet. There’s just one little thing I wanted to ask of you.”

“And what would that be?”

“To die.”

Theta removed the pistol stored in their chest and pointed it plainly at the head of Sobek’s suit-vac. Sobek knew that their new frame was not agile nor quick, and simply accepted the fact that they wouldn’t be able to run away. The sound of the shot was momentary and forgettable, like the sound of a stapler binding a stack of papers. Theta knew very well that this action would not get rid of Sobek, that they’d still have to deal with them later down the line. Instead, Theta shot Sobek for two simple reasons: to shut them up and to get access to that communications technology which they’d extensively boasted of. Theta didn’t know exactly how to reroute the signal, but they happened to know someone who had access to all the world’s knowledge on their side.

Theta returned to the circle of dirt where all of their companions slept in a silent stupor, lugging along a hunk of metal which they believed held the secrets to escaping the forest. They sat down. They needed to wake up Diogo, as he was the only person around who could turn the daft contraption with an amplified signal into something that could actually call for help. Then, of course, they’d need to wake up Naphat, who’d be able to contact the PAAS guerillas closest to their spot within the wide and open jungle. By that point, naturally, all of the commotion would lead to the other interlocutors waking up one by one in the middle of the dark cold night, replacing the act of sleep with yet another bout of restless dreams.

Theta could not sleep themself, but they could tell that their companions were not getting enough of it. They paused. They winced. They walked in a circle. Theta did not want to ruin the sleep of their human friends yet again. They knew that said friends had been growing increasingly tired. Yes, waking them up now would make escape a closer prospect, but at the same time, that lack of rest might compromise a future prospect. It pained Theta to do this, but they decided to wait, to let the night pass by them in total silence, with thoughts in their head that only they could know.

However, when the sun did eventually find its place in the sky, Theta ensured that everyone got up early, going so far as to play the sound of a morning rooster through their speakers.

“Don’t you think we could wait another thirty minutes?” Diogo asked blearily.

“No,” Theta replied curtly, “now, more than ever, we’ve gotta get to work.”
