Revolution on High: Part 7

Chapter 74: Revolution on High: Part 7

Theta laid the deactivated suit-vac in front of Diogo Celestino.

“This is the body which Sobek approached me in. As you can see by the hole in the head, I shot it. Now that obviously didn’t kill Sobek, but it did give us access to what I believe might be an incredibly important piece of technology. Sobek, from some far away location, was able to communicate with and control this automaton despite the non-existent signal in this jungle. Ergo, if we were to jailbreak this machine and use that same communications technology to our own advantage, we might just be able to communicate with the outside world and find a way out of this jungle, a way out that’s a lot more efficient than just wandering aimlessly.”

“But,” Zapata interrupted, “how would we actually get the machine to work in our favor? That sounds like a pretty complex process.”

“And that’s where Diogo comes in. While I presume that he doesn’t have an answer to that question offhand, I am certain that there’s an answer somewhere in the Library of All Things.”

“Fair,” Diogo admitted, “but even then, if we do get the communication device to function, who could we possibly call that would both be willing and able to help us?”

“I’m glad you asked, Diogo, because that’s where Naphat comes in.”

“…What do you want me to do?” Naphat asked, still half-asleep and not fully aware what the conversation was about.

“It’s true that you’re a member of the PAAS who has recently become quite important, right?”

“Correct.”

“And it’s true that many of the PAAS’s guerilla fighters operate in heavily forested areas around the country.”

“That would also be correct.”

“So all I’ll need you to do is contact one of your higher-ups and have them get some guerillas to guide us to the coast and also have a mid-sized boat waiting at said coast.”

“That’s not the easiest ask at turbulent times like these… but with the importance they seem to vest in you folks I’m sure those requests will all be fulfillable.”

“Perfect, now Diogo,” Theta turned to face the man in question, “it’s time for you to enter your mind.”

The library looked just as crowded as usual. Diogo took a deep breath and took in the smell of old literature and not-quite-rotting wood. It was a stale place, the library, an inherently still and tepid place given the static nature of books, but it was, at the same time, a location brimming with life, a land which constantly readjusted itself on the fringes, too far away to notice from the center, but if one were to stay in the library for a century, they’d watch as it gradually evolved. It was the sort of place that accumulated dust, but purely the visual kind of dust that one might drag their finger over, not the excessive kind that gets into one’s system and forces one to cough their lungs out. It was, without a doubt, a beautiful location, and Diogo wished that he spent more time in it outside of the urgent scenarios which forced him to enter it in search of solutions.

And where exactly would he find the solution he needed now? Well, he considered, his question was a matter of communications technology—that was well established—and the Dewey Decimal System placed matters of technology in the 600s range. He walked, quick but not hurried, into the corridor marked with a colossal number six. At the next junction, he figured, since it was a machine he was after, that he would have to head towards the 620s range, which was established for matters of engineering. He continued his unhurried walk towards a somewhat smaller corridor with a slightly less colossal number two affixed to the entrance.

Now, up to this point, navigating the library had been rather easy, so easy in fact that Diogo had grown dangerously confident, so confident in fact that he began to forget that the library was not a forgiving beast. When he analyzed the next junction, he immediately realized that none of the options seemed to have anything to do with communications. ‘Mining and Related Operations’ clearly wouldn’t help him get out of the jungle, nor would the books on ‘Hydraulic Engineering.’ The only section which seemed like it might provide any modicum of help was the one marked ‘621– Applied Physics,’ a label so vague that it could potentially be fitted over every known process in the universe. Regardless, it seemed to be Diogo’s only hope, so with a much less confident gait, he passed through the stricter, darker corridor.

At the end of the corridor was a room, a warm room, with even more corridors spliced into the walls, floor, and ceiling. Garish signs with phrases like ‘Steam Engineering’ and ‘Pneumatic Machinery’ only further contributed to the sense that Diogo Celestino was utterly lost. The fact that the room was actively filled with hot steam shot out from a plethora of pipes and the clanging sounds of metal against metal did nothing to help mitigate Diogo’s growing unease. However, he did find one sign, placed atop a trap door with a ladder to a lower floor, which, while vague, did seem to point into the direction where he was headed. It read ‘621.3– Electrical, Magnetic, Optical Communications, Computer Engineering; Electronics, Lighting.’ It seemed to Diogo like a very broad category, but he supposed that Melvil Dewey was composing his system long before the advent of many modern technologies. Mr. Dewey had been unable to predict quite how important electricity would be to the history of humanity beyond him, a rather forgivable mistake which would, centuries down the line, ultimately lead to Diogo’s predicament, his need to go further and further down the tight, cramped rabbit hole of the decimal system’s oversights.

Luckily, the next few rooms were a little bit easier to slink through. He could assume, simply from Theta’s specifics about the technology in question, that he’d have to take the pathway labeled ‘621.38– Electronics, Communications, Engineering,’ and that from there he’d need to head through the tunnel labeled ‘621.382– Communications.’

It was the Communications room that really stumped Diogo Celestino, precisely because he did not know how Sobek’s communications technology actually worked. This gap in his knowledge was precisely why he had come to the Library in the first place. He could really only make presumptions from here on out, educated guesses that had the potential to lead him astray. He tried to cross out potential paths based on the little bits of information he knew. ‘621.3827– Fiber Optics,’ that couldn’t be correct, as the communications were all happening wirelessly. ‘621.3825– Satellite Communications,’ there could have been a satellite involved in Sobek’s communication system, but it’s not like Diogo would’ve been able to detect that. ‘621.3824– Antenna Systems,’ now that was something that might just work.

Every suit-vac, or at least every suit-vac which Diogo had ever seen, possessed a little dark antenna which jutted out from the back of the torso. He had seen this little feature on Theta a plentiful number of times—effectively whenever he was walking behind them—and he had also seen one on the deactivated suit-vac which had previously belonged to Sobek. It would therefore make some modicum of sense that, if antennas were universally affixed to suit-vacs, then Sobek likely communicated to the suit-vac via an antenna.

The door which was marked with the ‘621.3824– Antenna Systems’ label was quite small, only a little bit taller than a meter, and even the rather short Diogo Celestino had to crouch down in order to pass through it. He had expected that, after making his way through the pin of a needle, the ceiling to the adjoining room would be at a standard height, but he instead entered a tunnel which was just as compact as the door and seemed to lack any sort of lighting. Diogo had to admit that it was a little freaky, but he supposed that these distortions were only the natural consequences of going a little too deep into the recesses of the library. He continued walking forward, crouched the whole time, bending his knees more and more the further he progressed, an attempt to compensate for the increasingly small amount of space in the corridor. Eventually, he was forced to switch to a crawl, and he still couldn’t make out the end of the tunnel. Just as the hallway got more and more compact, it also got darker the further Diogo traveled. He could no longer see his own arms. It all made him feel like a dumb blind mole, aimlessly digging in a direction he couldn’t name, to a destination he didn’t know, further and further away from the concept of safety. He began to feel lonely in that vertical hole.

Then Diogo heard a sound. It was the indefinite gibberish of radio static, a plight to the ears and a further plight to the mind, because Diogo could not tell from where the static was coming, and he began to worry that it was all in his head.

‘If only I had an antenna myself,’ Diogo briefly thought, ‘then maybe I’d be able to decode this noise.

Before Diogo could finish that thought, the tunnel very suddenly began to slant downwards. Diogo tried to put his hands against the walls so as to prevent himself from falling forward, but the walls in this sector proved to be covered in an odd sort of oily substance that denied his grip. Quite quickly, Diogo began to slide downwards, in a direction he couldn’t see, at a velocity he couldn’t quantify, towards an end that could very possibly be a brick wall. Diogo felt a pang in his chest, a little urgent internal message that begged him to pull out now, to close his eyes and wake up, leaving the library and returning to the forest. He was tempted, without a doubt, but he was equally frightened by the prospect of coming back empty-handed. He had to keep going, no matter how much this dark slide scared him shitless, no matter how many times he failed to slow himself down.

Then Diogo saw a light, and before he could process where it came from, he noticed that there was no longer a floor beneath him. The slide had shot him out into a large room filled with books, specifically into a large wastebasket filled with paper shreddings that slightly broke his fall. He stood up and crawled out of that dismal bin, sore but not dead, and attempted to acquaint himself with his new environment. It was a room without any doors, meaning that the system didn’t get any more detailed than this. The room he stood in held the entirety of humanity’s knowledge regarding the field of antenna systems.

‘It’s rather beautiful,’ Diogo thought to himself, ‘it’s admittedly a rather specific subject, but it’s everything about that subject. Every possible detail, every minor nuance, every offhand fact about antennas, it’s all here, compiled neatly within this room in alphabetical order…’

Then Diogo identified his next major roadblock. Since this rather large room held all the knowledge regarding antenna systems, he could not make his subject any more specific. The only way he could narrow things any further was via the names of authors.

But who wrote the book he was looking for? He knew he was looking for a book about complex forms of communication with suit-vacs, a field he knew very little about besides that it was possible. He tried to wrack his brain for literally any knowledge he had about people involved in the development of the suit-vac androids. He strained himself in order to peer far back into the crevices of his crepuscular mind, many years back in time to a menial day in the Sao Luis Hebepod, on some late night in the little gameroom where he had mastered the art of table tennis. He remembered staring at a wonderful little ancient television, in a room devoid of anyone but him, listening to the calm and stoic voice of a graying documentarian. Then he heard a name, a distinct trochaic name, a clear identifiable name which frayed the longer he thought about it. Simon. That was the name of the person who designed the antenna system affixed to the suit-vac. But what was the context of that name? Was their name Simon Something? Or Something Simon? No, that wasn’t right, it was something more complex than Simon. There was something at the end of it. Simonson? No. Simonov? No, but perhaps Simonova? Yes, Simonova! He could hear it in full definition now: Something Simonova. Somethinga Somethingich Simonova. He couldn’t actually remember the first name or the patronymic of that marvelous engineer's name, but none of that really mattered in a library order by surname.

Diogo, finally operating with a pep in his step, rushed over to the grandiose line of bookcases marked with the letter ‘S.’ He practically ran through the aisle, brimming with excitement, making far more noise than would usually be allowed in a library, all because he knew that his actions were about to get his crew out of the jungle. He sprinted past the ‘Sa’ names, slowed to a jog when he spotted the ‘Se’ names, and finally slowed to a walk when he saw the name ‘Adit Si’ printed along a book’s binding. Immediately, his eyes started looking for his salvation, and they found it in the name ‘Klementina Simonova.’

Diogo immediately pulled all of the books with Klementina’s name on them off of the shelf and spread them on the ground in front of him so that he could read their titles clearly. Could his answer be in the article titled ‘Suit-Vac Antenna Design Blueprints’ or maybe in the larger one titled ‘The Creation of the Suit-Vac, Part 16: The Antenna?’ No, a brief glance at the forewords of these works made it obvious that they were much more focused with the physical construction of the antenna than any of the fancy communicative techniques the Sobek must’ve utilized in order to control the suit-vac using said antenna. Luckily, there were still more books and journal articles by Simonova, but after checking over all of their titles he realized that only those first two works were about the suit-vac specifically. All the other articles were about much broader topics in antenna communications, relaying information which might, in the long run, be useful to Diogo as it could tell him how exactly this suddenly important technology actually works, but not useful in the sense of containing the specific set of knowledge he was after. Unfortunately, Diogo had to admit that Simonova wasn’t getting him anywhere, that he was just as lost as before.

Diogo fell to a slump as his voice fell to a mumble, allowing himself to aimlessly stumble through those narrow halls of books stacked on books. But, before he could leave the S section, something nearly glinted in the corner of his eye. He saw an awfully short name, a tiny little mononym which, for a novel, might be appropriate but for an academic paper was exceedingly odd. It didn’t leave his mind that he was in the section for authors whose names started with ‘So.’ He backed up to see the full title of the miniature tome and was truly astonished by what he read:

Complex Communications with Suit-Vac Systems, a Guide by Sobek

Diogo nearly fell flat on the ground, and he did end up falling to his knees. This had to be it, his ticket out of the jungle, his ticket to a beautiful beach with a beautiful boat which would ship him to Ashtamudi and from there to total gnosis. He grabbed the tome, held it tight towards his chest, and let the thin neural string of his being pull him out through section and subsection, to the very center of the library, and eventually into the land of the real. He felt the soft dirt beneath his feet and the clothes on his skin and the metronomic beat of his steady little heart and he breathed and he gasped and he let the group all stare at him and finally he dissolved his expression into a smile.

“I found the book,” he announced.

“That’s fantastic,” Theta said as they grabbed the book from Diogo’s hands. They immediately put it down on an improvised table made of loose branches and detritus before rapidly flipping through every page, scanning all the information directly into their mind.

“They’re quite a fast reader,” Patcharee commented in a restrained astonishment.

“That’s always been a talent of theirs,” Vraxi responded, almost proudly, “I suppose that’s just an advantage of a computer-based mind. Things tend to run quicker.”

“Alright,” Theta closed the book, “I’m done, and I’ve got a pretty good idea of what I’ve got to do to effectively rework this machine into a functioning telephone. Do any of you have a wrench?”

Nobody responded.

“I suppose that makes sense. Carlyle, do you think you could wrench some of the screws out of this thing with your hands?”

“I can do my best,” Carlyle said, with a slight smile that seemed to reveal his gladness in the opportunity to display his physical might.

Theta and Carlyle quickly got to work disassembling and reassembling the mechanical guts of the abandoned suit-vac. Theta worked with an unbreakable precision, a tightly honed focus which let them go through the process of remaking that machine as if it was something they had always known and not something they had just learned minutes prior.

Theta could not smile, lacking the necessary implement of a mouth, but when they were done, Vraxi could tell that they were beaming. Even as others struggled to detect the emotions of Theta past the glossy flat glass of their lens, Vraxi had an almost innate ability to peer through that glass and into the heart.

“It’s ready,” Theta announced with a glee undetectable to most, but obvious to Vraxi, “now get over here, Naphat. I’ll need your help.”

It was clear by Naphat’s wobbly gait and mixed expression that she wasn’t super comfortable with playing the role of the savior. Her job was to contact the highest-ranking member of the PAAS she knew and demand that they help her get out of the jungle and, further, that they provide her with a boat, expenses paid. It was quite a large request for a struggling army in the middle of a revolution and it was made even larger by the simple fact that, just a few days ago, Naphat was a very low-ranking member of her party. She had really just been an average, perhaps especially invigorated partisan, an individual whose driving forces were the goals of communism and the passions of youth. The only reason she even knew the phone numbers of high-ranking party officials was because she just so happened to be coworkers with an avatar, which just so happened to place her within a covert Azanian collaboration, which just so happened to make her an influential member in the plot to assassinate the king. It was true that she worked hard and it was true that she cared deeply for the stances of her party, but it was at the same time entirely true that she had only ended up in a position of influence due to the sheer luck of her circumstances.

“So, I should be able to get on a call with Comrade Khamdi,” Naphat began, “and he should theoretically be willing to provide us with some help, but also, we’ve all gotta recognize that this is a very busy moment for the party, and because we’ve been separated from the rest of the world ever since we fled the assassination, I have absolutely no idea how busy we might be. It’s entirely possible that every city in the nation has been drawn up into some inferno. It’s entirely possible that Comrade Khamdi is already dead. There really isn’t any way to know until I call him.”

“Then call him already,” Zapata said, “we’re in a bit of a hurry here.”

“I was about to do that. I was just trying to give a bit of preamble to set expectations,” Naphat started dialing a number on the improvised suit-vac-telephone, “now everyone get ready, and don’t be mad at me if he doesn’t respond,” she waited for a moment as the phone let out a neutral tone into the ear before, all of a sudden, it stopped, and played the noise of an air conditioner in a room across the country, “Hello. This is Naphat Nantasri speaking. Is this the office of Comrade Khamdi?”

“You’re speaking to him, though I’m not in my office.”

“Oh, great, and where exactly are you then?”

“Cooped up inside something between a bunker and a barrack.”

“So I’m presuming that things are pretty rough out there.”

“Have you been living under a rock for the past day?”

“Close. You see, after the assassination, which I’m presuming was successful, I got on a small plane which was almost immediately shot down. Me and my crew, miraculously, all survived, but we’re all sorta trapped in the middle of a national park. According to Theta, we’re at the coordinates 15.00664° N, 98.43428° E. There are no paths, we are completely lost, and we desperately need to get to Ashtamudi.”

“Are you asking for my help with that?”

“Yes, very desperately so.”

“Comrade Nantasri, you’ve got to understand that we’re really stripped for resources right now. I mean, I’m pretty sure we have some guerillas in that region, and they might be able to form a search party for you all, but how would you get out after that? Are you expecting us to finance a boat for you all?”

“I was hoping you’d be willing to.”

“Comrade Nantasri, surely you understand how much of a strain that would be on our already strained budget.”

“I understand that, Comrade Khamdi, but I also believe that the importance vested in this particular mission is of a grand enough scale as to justify that admittedly large expense.”

“Comrade, if you were the on the ground you’d understand my qualms with-”

“Hold on,” Mbali interrupted the party official and stole the speakerphone from Naphat, “Hello, comrade, this is Mbali Chiliza, representing the People’s Republic of Azania. I would like to inform you that we, the Azanians, are deeply invested in Naphat’s escape to Ashtamudi as well. Accordingly, if you provide our crew with some guerillas to guide us to the coast, along with a boat waiting for us at said coast, the Azanian government would be very willing to pay you back triple-fold for the price of the boat itself.”

“…is that really so?”

“Yes, it is so, it is fully and entirely so.”

“Then I’ll do my best to fulfill those requests of yours. I’ll try to get things organized quickly, but please, have a modicum of patience and understanding. People like me, in times like these, can die at any moment.”

Only about three hours had passed before Vraxi heard a rustle in the leaves. Admittedly, those hours passed slowly as, unlike during the previous day, the crew could no longer attempt to move forwards since they had already provided the guerillas with a precise set of coordinates. Moving forwards would only confuse the people tasked to rescue them, and as a result they were forced to stay still, with nothing to focus on besides their increasing hunger. None of them had eaten anything in over 24 hours, and the strenuous work they had done on the day prior made it difficult for Vraxi to think beyond her stomach. Likewise, when she did hear those rustlings amid the leaves, and when she saw the heads of a pack of water buffalo, all of them ridden by her uniformed saviors, she did not think about the future, about her ultimate destination or even the journey there, but instead she hoped against all other odds that that the guerillas had packed some food with them.

“Thank you so much-” Vraxi attempted to say before being interrupted by the head guerilla who immediately shushed her.

“Be quiet and be quick,” the guerilla told her and the larger crew in a heavily hushed tone, “we’ve detected the signals of government-controlled drones here in the forest. They have a sonar system that can very easily detect human speech. Now, there are nine of us and nine of you. Each of you can get on top of one of the water buffalo, behind one of us. We know the way to the coast, and we’ll try to get there as quickly as we can. Yes, there is a boat waiting there. And before you ask, while the sonar can detect the sounds of the water buffalo, if all of us are completely silent, the drones will pass them off as standard wildlife. Now hurry up and get on the animals and please don’t ask any questions.”

“…do you have any food with you?” Vraxi attempted to ask in a very quiet voice.

“There’s food on the boat,” the guerilla replied curtly, “you’re gonna have to wait.”

Somewhat disappointedly, Vraxi climbed onto the back of the water buffalo helmed by the head guerilla. While she was thankful to have any ride at all out of that godforsaken forest, she really thought the guerillas should’ve come with a more stable vehicle. Vraxi Nair had never ridden a horse in her life, let alone a water buffalo, and the awkward geometry of the animal’s spine was discomforting to say the least and often threatened her falling off entirely. After the third near-fall within the first fifteen minutes, the pilot of the beast finally broke and told her directly:

“Please, wrap your arms around my torso or something. I really don’t want you to fall, especially when there’s eight more animals behind you that would all be very willing to step on your body.”

Vraxi, immediately folding to any authority she respected, wrapped her hands around the pilot’s stomach in a position which was rather embarrassing and a bit straining in the long run but at least could prevent an untimely death.

Four hours later, as Vraxi neared the beach of her salvation, the spectre of untimely death came near her once again. The guerillas all relayed some hand signals to one another and stopped the hulking animals in their tracks. The whole forest went silent. Vraxi felt inclined to ask a question, to ponder why the group had stopped so suddenly, but feared being reprimanded for excess noise. Then something cut the silence, a whirring, buzzing sound like that of miniature helicopter blades. Vraxi looked up and saw a sea of drones. She opened her mouth to scream but the guerilla in front of her immediately shoved a meaty hand in front of her mouth, as if demanding silence of her in the most silent manner he could think of. She tried to calm down. After all, the drones weren’t attacking yet. They were a school of blind piranhas, ready to shred their prey if they heard a human voice, but in that moment when she saw them they were still entirely docile. She held her breath and one by one the drones all left the sky, flying off to some other corner of the forest.

The final leg of the journey was completed in total silence, the only voices coming from the mouths of the water buffalo. Vraxi was far too frightened to even open her mouth.

They managed to reach the beach unscathed and Vraxi saw a mid-sized boat—enough to fit nine passengers—waiting for them. She hopped off the animal and was about to thoroughly thank its rider before remembering that, even here on the edge of the forest she wasn’t permitted to speak. The guerilla looked at her and smiled and nodded, but Vraxi felt that she still needed to show her appreciation. Slowly and quietly, she moved toward the rider, and brought them into a great big hug. The rider reciprocated, and when the two were finally done, the rider gave her, Naphat, and Patcharee a spirited salute before riding back into the forest.

Silently, in a controlled order, all nine passengers got onto the boat. Fu Qier, while not especially experienced in maritime travel, was once again still the by far the most experienced, and took on the role of the designated driver. Gradually, the boat accelerated from the coast, entering the wide open ocean in its journey through the Bay of Bengal.

Before the boat could even leave the beach, Vraxi had already raided the admittedly limited pantry, sating her appetite on saltines and tinned fish.

Revolution on High: Part 8

Chapter 75: Revolution on High: Part 8

The Indian ocean was wide and blue, wider than the horizon and more blue than the peacock’s coat. Vraxi climbed out of the sleeping quarters and onto the deck to observe the splendor of a morning at sea. It was a rather fast-moving vessel and it was supposed to get to port in Ashtamudi before the end of the day, but despite the present level of urgency she should’ve possessed, Vraxi almost wanted to stay for a day longer—or at least she would’ve if Diogo hadn’t already gotten seasick. There was something very tranquil about being alone atop a body of water like this, finally separated from the world at large, finally arriving in that place which—while not untainted from economic activity—was mostly unseen by all. It really was a beautiful sunrise on the water.

“Vraxi!” the distinct voice of Fu Qier called out to her from the pilothouse, “Vraxi, is that you? I need your help!”

“Coming,” Vraxi rushed to the impromptu captain, “what’s the issue?”

“Well I’ve been driving this boat for the past sixteen hours or so and I desperately need to sleep. The only issue is that I’m not sure if you know how to safely pilot one of these things.”

“Uh, well, Theta might be able to. That information’s probably somewhere up in their digital encyclopedia.”

“Could you please drag them over here then? Otherwise I might just collapse on the job.”

“I’ll do that right away,” Vraxi quickly assured the woman before sprinting over to the room where Theta hadn’t been sleeping but had been going through the motions.

“Theta!” Vraxi bust open the door, “Captain Fu desperately needs your help. Are you available?”

“Very much so. What’s the issue?”

“She really needs someone to take over the job of steering the ship. Would you be capable of taking on that role?”

“It doesn’t seem like that’d be too hard. Afterall, we’re in some rather calm waters. If we were in a storm I might hold back, but I’ve got a solid enough knowledge of marine transportation to get us from Point A to Point B in the present conditions.”

“That’s good to hear. But let’s try to get over to Fu quickly as she sorta sounded like she could doze off at any moment.”

Right as the two interlocutors rushed out of the little dark room, a third figure, that of Zapata Tochihuitl, intercepted them in the adjoining hallway.

“Where are you two heading,” she immediately asked before they could pass her.

“To the pilothouse,” Vraxi speedily replied, “we’re trying to switch out captains so that Qier can get some needed rest. Theta will be taking command of the ship shortly.”

“Would you mind if I tagged along with you two? I don’t want to be cooped up in that little bedroom with a Diogo Celestino who vomits every hour.”

“Sure, just, make sure he gets some fluids in him.”

When Vraxi arrived in the pilothouse she was met with a captain who was already three quarters asleep. Luckily, there weren’t any icebergs in the Bay of Bengal and Fu had avoided all accidents during their tenure as captain. Not wanting to wake the exhausted pilot, Vraxi simply pushed Qier on her swivel chair out of the pilothouse, across the deck, and onto a small, secluded mattress where she could hopefully finally rest. When Vraxi returned to the pilothouse she saw Theta already pasted over the control board, presumably memorizing its various complex functions, while affixed to their head was a dapper white hat with the word ‘CAPTAIN’ printed on it in three languages. Theta seemed to have already gotten used to their new role.

“You seem to be taking to the job quite well,” Vraxi complimented Theta’s competence, “we should get to Ashtamudi in no time.”

“And, speaking of which,” Zapata began, “what exactly are we supposed to do when we get there?”

“Well, if the timing all works out, Aisha Abdualaziz should meet us at the port with the recently freed Shui Hailang in tow.”

“That’s really a rather dismal collection of people. I don’t like the thought of meeting Aisha once again.”

“Zapata, I understand your concerns here, but for our plans to work, we need every single avatar present in the city of Rhapta. That includes Aisha, and besides, she’s become a much nicer person ever since she broke away from Thabr’s curse.”

“She murdered my brother.”

“And she also saved my life in Rizhao. She’s a complicated figure and I don’t expect you to suddenly make amends with her. At the end of the day, revolutionaries do not have to be friends with one another, we simply have to possess a shared cause. With Thabr no longer in the picture, Aisha has her mind in the right place and is willing to help us, and in that sense she’s still doing a better job than Carlyle, who doesn’t care one bit about our cause and is only here because he’s convinced that history will favor us.”

“Well, if you’re unconcerned about Abdulaziz, I’m naturally inclined to ask how you feel about Shui Hailang, someone who has never proved themself to be willing to change.”

“Well… I admit that the matter of Shui is a fair concern, a concern which I myself have been turning over in my brain. Shui has actively worked against our cause and, unlike Flanders, is still driven by an ideological purpose. Then again, GüdTek has also wronged them. They put them in jail after their tantrum in the Maldives. It’s entirely possible that such a punishment could instill in them a change of heart.”

“Well,” Zapata sighed, “I just hope that you keep a close eye on them. I can only imagine how royally they could screw our plans up if we allowed them to.”

“Anyways, gathering Shui and Abdulaziz should really be the easy part when it comes to our mission in Ashtamudi. After that, we’ll need to head to the madrasa and pick up Miras before attempting to figure out where in the world Joey Axelrod is.”

“…We need him as well?”

“We need every single avatar on our side. That sadly includes Axelrod, regardless of our feelings about him.”

“It’s true,” Theta added, “I have a long history with Axelrod and I don’t like him either, but he’s still unfortunately needed.”

“But,” Zapata clarified, “assuming we actually find him in the first place, how would we ever convince him to join us? It’s not like Shui’s case where we broke them out of prison and they had a real reason to realign themself.”

“Admittedly,” Vraxi admitted, “I don’t really think we’ll be able to convince a man like Joey of really anything at all. We may have to take him by force, tie him up, and take him to Rhapta in a bound position.”

“So we’re basically just kidnapping him.”

“We’ve done worse in the past.”

“I was just trying to clarify. And so what exactly is the plan when we actually make it back to Rhapta?”

“Well, presumably we’ll have all ten avatars plus Theta in our group, so all we’ll have to do is go down into the underground, stand on the circle with the names of our patrons, and opt to summon the Demiurge.”

“And what do you think we should do once we’ve summoned it?”

“We ask for its help, I suppose,” Theta answered, “we ask it to save us from the issues that plague us and the world at large.”

“So we’re asking for a deus ex machina?” Zapata surmised.

“Effectively, but what else would you ask for when face to face with the most powerful being in existence? Getting help from the Demiurge is our best chance at moving forwards as a society, as a planet, of moving past the dreadful economic phase we find ourself in, into a world without forces like GüdTek and the Lockeites controlling every aspect of human life and constantly pushing us back into the past. The future stands behind a guarded gate, and the Demiurge holds the key. For the sake of the planet and its people, we must open that gate, and ensure that no one else destroys it before we can get there. I can only imagine what someone like Bran would do if given access to the power of the Demiurge.”

“Yikes,” Vraxi shuddered, “I’d rather not think about something like that.”

“So that’s it then,” Zapata confirmed, “just nab the last four avatars, two of which are already waiting for us, head over to Azania, jump back in the hole, stand on the circle, and tell the greatest god there ever was that we want it to eliminate the system of capitalism.”

“Realistically,” Theta clarified, “the wish will be a lot more complicated than that. I imagine that it will require a struggle not just inside the cave, but outside, in the wider world itself. There will still need to be a global proletarian revolution, but the wish should help to spark it, and maybe even weaken the forces preventing it.”

“Truthfully, it’s just good to have a goal in mind.”

The ship captained by Theta, being of the unregistered sort, was not actually able to anchor in the port of Kollam. Instead, Theta sailed to one of the less populated coasts of Ashtamudi, specifically to one of the many swamps that waterlog the country. Theta had some difficulty when it came to properly bringing the ship to harbor, and it sort of ended up in the position of a beached whale, but they were too delighted by the sight of Aisha Abdulaziz, alongside Shui Hailang, to care very much about maritime concerns. Zapata, noticeably, was not as delighted by the sight of those two.

“Hello, fellow avatars,” Vraxi called out from the window of the ship, “we have arrived on land with a mission to save the world. Are you ready to join us?”

“We are!” Aisha answered proudly.

“I suppose we don’t have a choice,” Hailang conceded.

“Are you really sure that we want to associate with people like them?” Zapata asked after hearing Hailang’s response.

“We literally have to,” Vraxi spoke back, “and if we need to we can drag them along, but no matter what we need Theta and all ten avatars gathered together for any of this to actually work.”

“Fair enough then. I concede.”

All nine passengers quickly departed the sandy ship and approached the two newcomers. Theta immediately opted to hug Aisha.

“It’s really nice to see you back to being yourself,” they admitted mid-embrace, “you can be a really helpful person when you don’t have a demon in your brain. Genuinely, thank you so much for rounding up Hailang.”

“It’s really not a big deal. It was an in-and-out endeavor.”

“And Hailang,” Theta moved to shake their hand, “I’m glad to see that you’ve changed your mind on some things, perhaps not all things, but enough things to not immediately reject my handshake.”

“You’re welcome,” Hailang replied with an expression that read disappointment, “I must admit that I never imagined to be working with you after what happened in Rizhao, though I suppose there are certain aspects of the Lockeite method which aren’t the most ideal, such as the justice system which led to my imprisonment.”

“Well, it’s good to see some self-reflection from you, no matter how it surfaces. I’m glad to know that I’ll have you on our side in the coming missions.”

“Speaking of which,” Naphat interjected, “from what it sounds like, I must say that this particular mission seems to mostly concern the efforts of avatars. I myself am not an avatar, and I was wondering if you’d be okay if I excused myself from the latter half of your mission and sailed myself back to Siam? As I’m sure your aware, Siam is in something of a pivotal moment in its history, and I’d hate to not be aiding the nation at a time like this.”

“Well that’s completely understandable, and I appreciate you feeling the need to ask for my permission first. But, before you go, I just want you to be aware that you have been incredibly helpful in assisting us. After all, we never would’ve gotten out of the jungle without you. When the Demiurge is released and its effects are felt around the world, I want you to know that you were responsible.”

“Thanks, Theta, and thanks for, albeit inadvertently, helping me get a big promotion in the party. You’ve been a big help, even if you’ve gotten me into some trouble along the way.”

“Additionally,” Fu Qier chimed in, “it seems fit that at this time I should also submit my letter of resignation. While I’ve appreciated working with you, Theta, I also admit that I am not an avatar, and the struggle of Siam has invigorated me. I was too naive to help fight against the counterrevolution in Sichuan, the conflict that fractured my nation into little pieces, but I am still alive to assist the revolution happening today in Siam. Furthermore, I imagine that Ms. Nantasri will need some help when it comes to steering the ship back home.”

“Thanks for that, Qier. I have no idea how I would’ve gotten back to Siam by myself.”

“Well, Ms. Fu,” Theta began, “I’d like to sincerely thank you for acting as our chauffeur. Without you, we wouldn’t’ve physically gotten anywhere. You have acted as the engine which keeps the revolution running.”

Theta watched as the two revolutionaries climbed back into the boat and got ready to sail the ocean that led them here. Unfortunately, the boat was still beached, and Fu Qier ended up needing the help of all eight avatars present to push the awkward machine into the open waters. With moistened cuffs the group of potential saviors watched the tugboat brave the seas once more, to a land that needed help more than ever, and away from themselves, who could’ve used some help as well. When the boat finally dropped over the horizon line, Vraxi turned around to face her awaiting audience, ready to speak to them with stern determination before a sudden phone call interrupted her plans.

“Hold on,” Vraxi said as she saw the important name attached to the message, “let me get this real quick.”

“Vraxi, where the hell have you been?” Suravinda Gambheeram asked through the phone line.

“Um, well, a lot of places, actually. But I was in the middle of a jungle for a while, and I couldn’t take any calls there, and then I was at sea, and my cell plan doesn’t really cover that either-”

“Do you have Miras with you?”

“What?”

“Miras Umarov, is he with you?”

“I suppose not yet. We were planning on picking him up from the madrasa as we try to gather all of the avatars. Believe it or not, but we were actually able to get a hold of Shui Hailang.”

“Miras Umarov is not at the madrasa.”

“What? Where is he?”

“I have no idea. I called the madrasa and they told me that he left for lunch one day and then just disappeared, though they also said that some family members of his had been looking for him.”

“Fuck, do you think they took him back to Turan?”

“Maybe, except, well, there was one thing I found interesting about the description of the cousins of Miras that traveled to the madrasa.”

“What do you mean by that?”

“Well, it’s quite likely that those individuals demanding information about Miras, individuals who did so right before his disappearance, were not actually members of Miras’s family but instead individuals who kidnapped Miras with the direct intent of preventing him from joining up with you all. It’s very possible that those who kidnapped him were working under Bran in some capacity, and had insider knowledge of your intentions to gather up all of the avatars and venture off to Rhapta. With that in mind, I naturally asked the clerk at the madrasa who talked to those ‘cousins’ for their physical descriptions. The first man he described didn’t stoke my interests, that of a nondescript and hairless fellow, but the second man’s features caused my mind to whir. He seemed to hold the exact description of one Joseph Agbayani Axelrod, all the way down to his glinting, metallic eyes.”

“So you think Joey’s kidnapped Miras?”

“I think that it’s very possible.”

“Fuck, that’s quite distressing to hear.”

“Well… look on the bright side. If Joey was able to kidnap Miras, then there’s a good chance that he might still be in Ashtamudi. You might not be all that far from him and it’s my understanding that you’ll need him on your side as well.”

“I suppose in the long run.”

“Well, I’ll have to leave you to it when it comes to actually finding where Joey is. Perhaps some of your avatars will have some leads when it comes to where he’s traveled to.”

“Thank you for the information, Professor Gambheeram. I’ll talk to you later. Bye.”

Vraxi hung up the phone and brought her hand to her brow in utter frustration.

“Did you get any good news?” Diogo asked her, unable to fully see her face from his angle.

“No. Nothing good,” she sighed and tried to heed the professor’s advice, “do any of you have any meaningful connections within the city of Kollam?”

“I mean,” Mbali offered, “I’ve got some connections at the Azanian embassy. Why do you ask?”

“Well, unfortunately, it seems that Miras Umarov is missing, and there’s a quite high chance that he was taken away by Joey Axelrod, and there’s a quite high chance that Joey is still in Kollam. Now, not only will we need Joey because he’s an avatar, but also because he’s seemingly the only person in the world who knows where Miras is. The reason I ask if anyone has connections in the city is because we’ll presumably need to sweep the whole metropolis if we want any chance of actually finding Joey.”

“Well, I suppose in that case I could check the CCTV footage the embassy tracks by its entrance. It’s a rather popular road it looks out on, and knowledge of whether or not Joey crossed it could theoretically be useful.”

“That could potentially be helpful. We should keep that in mind.”

“I think I have something in my own mind that could prove more helpful,” Hailang spoke up, “as unlike any of you, I actually once worked beside Joey in the city of Kollam. I happen to know where his favorite places to drink were in this city and I have a good feeling that that’s where he’d choose to hide out.”

“That could also be helpful. Thank you, Hailang.”

“Um, sorry,” Patcharee interjected, “but who exactly is this Miras Umarov we’re all speaking about? I wasn’t really present among you all until quite recently. He seems to be quite important but I really know nothing about him.”

“Oh, about him,” Vraxi responded, “well he’s an avatar like us, representing the god Aldar Kose. He’s also quite young, but very devout regardless. We first got in contact with him back when we first visited Ashtamudi, and, after a bit of convincing, he was quite willing to work alongside our cause. Now, he used to live at the local madrasa in Kollam, and while he’s not very online, it should’ve been easy to acquire him, simply a matter of knocking on the madrasa’s door. However, it seems like Axelrod’s meddling has prevented any chance of an easy acquisition.”

“Speaking of acquisitions,” Aisha added, “I have my own idea of how we might be able to track down Joey.”

“And what would that be?”

“Well, when I first struck an agreement with my patron Israfil, it was agreed that he would help me track down any mortal whom I had wronged before. This was because I had wronged many, many people back when I was possessed by the demon Thabr, and hoped to track down those people so that I could try to make things better. This is how I tracked down you, Vraxi, back in Rizhao. Admittedly, the tracking isn’t an especially straightforward process and it requires a lot of messing around on my trumpet, but it’s also the case that Joey is one of the many people I’ve wronged, seeing as I arguably wronged him when I broke free of Thabr’s curse and broke the deal he shook with me.”

“Well then, it seems like we have multiple manners up our sleeves of potentially catching Joey. Now all we need to do is start searching for him. Personally, I suggest that we split into groups so that we can maximize our potential of actually finding our target.”

“With that in mind,” Theta added, “I think I have one more idea when it comes to tracking down Joey Axelrod.”

“Oh really? What would that be?”

A loud, buzzing noise interrupted Theta’s response. Vraxi looked up and saw a large, unmanned drone. On its bottom, she could just make out the lettering of the GüdTek logo. Before she could even verbally identify the aircraft, a little chemical canister dropped from its basin and into the air. Theta immediately recognized the object’s destructive potential.

“Everybody run!” Theta shouted as loud as they could, “Split up!”

Vraxi wished she could’ve received an explanation, some prior forewarning, or something, anything other than a blind command to start sprinting. Her feet grew lethargic, her legs shaky and unprepared, but she began to run regardless, as fast as her sore appendages could let her, to a location she couldn’t recognize, but a place she knew was far away from both the coast and the drone.

She didn’t look back, even as she heard the sounds of her fellow interlocutors running in other directions, even as the time she spent running installed a veil of safety above her mind, even as the raucous noise of the canister exploding eliminated that sense of safety, and even as she felt a singe of heat tickle her backside, proving that the bomb was far larger than she could’ve known.

Vraxi continued running until she made it to the swamp’s edge, in the outskirts of a town on the suburban circle that surrounded Kollam’s metropolis. Exhausted, she opted to sit beside a telephone pole and finally turned around. In doing so, she saw the silhouette of Theta, and her face lit up accordingly. She also saw the silhouette of Carlyle Flanders, and her face had no real reaction.

“Thank god you're okay!” Vraxi shouted as Theta approached her.

“I’m glad you’re doing well as well,” Theta replied as they embraced her, “I know it put me closer to the blast, but I’m glad that I ran behind you. I’m glad that you were in my vision.”

Vraxi blushed for a moment, happy to hear how much Theta cared about her wellbeing, though her mind soon drifted to the wellbeing of everyone else.

“What about the others? Are they okay? That was a really big blast.”

“I was the last one to start running. I made sure I was the last. I wanted to do the best I could to ensure the safety of the group. Our victory necessitates we all be present. I did the best I could to ensure that presence without dying.”

“So you think they’ll be okay?”

“I think so. We all went in different directions. It’s hard to guarantee anything in a situation like this one.”

“And you’re sure that you’re okay as well, right?”

“I am. Thanks for asking.”

“Um, in case anyone was wondering,” Carlyle added, “I am also okay.”

“That’s good to hear, Carlyle. But with all of that established, I think that we shouldn’t waste any more time. My plan for capturing Joey Axelrod is as follows…”

Zapata couldn’t believe it. After running far away from the sudden explosion, to a bus stop on the very edge of Metro-Kollam, she had managed to end up next to the one person she least wanted to be forced to interact with alone.

“Are you okay?” Aisha Abdulaziz asked her, panting a little from the impromptu 5k.

“I am fine, at least physically,” Zapata slumped onto a bench as she spoke, “did you follow me here or something?”

“…I was just trying to run away from the blast. I saw you sprinting and I figured that if I ran behind you you would eventually lead me to safety, which you did, and I really, sincerely appreciate that.”

Even just the sound of Aisha’s voice stirred the bubbling disdain in Zapata’s soul. The fact that Aisha could just talk to her so casually, as if nothing had ever happened between the two, caused thin white lines of rage to form at the edge of her vision. Zapata was already strained physically, and the simple act of being beside the woman who murdered her brother in cold blood, who murdered him directly in front of her eyes, only strained her further.

“Y’know I still don’t forgive you,” Zapata announced, breaking the silence between them.

“Emiliano was a great friend of mine. I regret what happened to him immensely.”

“It’s wild that you haven’t gone to court for your crimes against him.”

“The police never discovered my identity, and besides, Zapata, you know that I was possessed.”

“Possession has never been a valid defense in any court that I’ve been to.”

“I am incredibly sorry, Zapata, and I want to make things better for you, I want to make things better for everyone I wronged.

“You just want to be absolved, Aisha. You want me to say that I forgive you and break out into tears and hug you until it’s as if my brother never died.”

“…It’s more complicated than that.”

“No it isn’t! It really isn’t. The simple fact of the matter, that fact which you refuse to accept, is that I, Zapata Tochihuitl, sister of Emiliano Tochihuitl, will never, ever forgive you. We will always be at odds, we will always be opposed, even if we fight on the same side.”

“…You don’t even think that the revolutionary struggle will help bring us together?”

“We are coworkers in the revolution, Aisha, not sisters and not even friends. We are united by a shared cause and nothing more. Now, speaking of that revolution, can you please start fiddling on that trumpet of yours? We still need to find that bastard Joey Axelrod.”

Revolution on High: Part 9

Chapter 76: Revolution on High: Part 9

Shui Hailang couldn’t believe the timing. Just as they were being thrust into the endlessly embarrassing position of total surrender, just as fate was forcing them to ally with the scoundrels that trampled their fatherland, a final little gift was dropped from the sky from their former employer, a sudden chance to get away. That bomb was like a holy messenger, a word from the divine which told Hailang that their journey wasn’t over yet, that they wouldn’t be forced to endure the tragedy of teaming up with someone like Vraxi Nair, that escape would be possible and they wouldn’t even have to fight for it. After all, once the canister hit the ground, the whole group of people began running in aimless directions. All that Shui Hailang had to do was ensure that they ran in a direction nobody else chose, then some time later they’d have to hop on a plane or a boat to some neutral country that doesn’t like to extradite its prisoners. It was the perfect plan, and what made it even more perfect was that it was literally just handed to Hailang, without a struggle or anything. It was so perfect in fact that when Hailang did reach civilization in the form of a little roofed bus stop, they allowed themself to sit on its bench, lean on its translucent walls, and rest for a moment, after a long and gruesome period of extended wakefulness. This rest was only supposed to last a minute, but it ultimately rolled on for closer to an hour and likely would’ve gone on longer if it weren’t for a sudden, unexpected feeling that caused their dreary mind to stir, as if something cold was brushing up against their leg.

When Shui Hailang opened their eyes they saw the nervous face of Diogo Celestino, one of the last faces they wanted to see, but perhaps not the worst. It seemed to them that he had managed to catch up to them, an unfortunate and preventable tragedy, but they also suspected that they could outrun him if they were to start dashing. Likewise, they immediately got up to run, though their leg seemed to catch on something and they rapidly fell to the ground.

Hailang, spread across the pavement, looked down to their foot and saw that, connecting their ankle to the pole of the bus stop, there was a strong pair of metal handcuffs.

“I thought that you might try to run,” Diogo narrated, “considering how you don’t really seem fond of the rest of us, but luckily, almost offhandedly, I had already borrowed a pair of handcuffs which Aisha nabbed from the prison she also nabbed you from.”

“Fuck you, Diogo.”

“I apologize for the inconvenience, but it seems to be of the necessary sort. Theta is very invested in the gathering of the Decadeum and-”

“But is what Theta wants the same as what you want?”

“It is, and don’t try to do this whole song and dance with me again. You convinced me to shed my loyalties once but it’s not gonna happen again, especially when you're splayed on the ground, not really in any sort of bargaining position to begin with.”

“Fair enough. It was worth a shot.”

“Anyways, in order to gather the Decadeum, I still require your assistance, which means that I’d appreciate the opportunity to let you go from the cuffs without you immediately running away or punching me in the face or something like that.”

“And what’s in it for me in this whole prospect of assisting you?”

“Well, I don’t intend on hurting you, nor do I really have the means to, so I don’t have a stick but I do have the carrot of potentially inconveniencing Joey Axelrod. After all, he’s sorta the reason you ended up in prison, isn’t he? Wouldn’t you like to get back at him for that?”

“Admittedly,” Hailang’s face soured, “it was quite a surprise to hear that, after our incident in the Maldives, Joey was able to walk free while I was forced into the indignity of incarcerated life.”

“And isn’t that a little messed up? After orchestrating the plans which led to your imprisonment, it was ultimately your enemies that got you out. Instead of paying back all of the favors you accrued from him, he simply left you to rot.”

“I suppose that’s all true, and I suppose I should be allocating some resources into making his life worse. How about this? You can uncuff me and I’ll lead you to a certain drinking establishment which I believe that Joey might be hiding out at as we speak, an establishment he truly adored back when we were working together against you.”

“Well, I like the second half of your proposal, but the first half just won’t stand. I can’t imagine any world where I uncuff you and you don’t immediately start running away from me.”

“Well I’m not sure of any alternative you could suggest. Afterall, how am I supposed to lead you to Joey if I’m stuck in one place?”

Rapidly, Diogo removed one end of the cuffs from the pole and linked it around his own right leg.

“There’s our solution,” he proudly announced, “now you have enough freedom of movement to leave this bus stop, but not quite enough freedom as to move in any direction that I’m not also already headed in. The beauty of the linked-leg system is that we can only move if we both agree to move in the same direction.”

“But then couldn’t I just stay put and prevent you from moving?”

“But you won’t, because while you’d rather get away from me than do anything else, you’d also rather displease Axelrod than do nothing.”

“A fair psychoanalysis. I guess we should start moving then, just please make sure to keep your steps in line with my own. I don’t want us to topple over.”

Joey Axelrod was drinking again. In fact, he was on his third glass of Old Monk rum on the rocks and it was barely afternoon. The fact that he had safely transported Miras into cryosleep really should’ve eased his stress, but in reality, his stress had only stewed and expanded. Yes, he had managed to hide Umarov, and yes, he had done so while avoiding the moral dilemma of killing Umarov, but he increasingly worried that the ice pod wouldn’t be enough to keep the avatar away from Theta’s eyes. He began pacing, which could’ve been awkward in a more crowded establishment, but there happened to only be one other customer at that hour. He simply wasn’t sure if Ashtamudi was secure enough. It was true that the ice pods were under the domain of GüdTek corporate, but the employees themselves were all Ashtamudians, people who might not be willing to uphold his theoretically criminal act of placing an unwilling subject under cryosleep. Joey also didn’t think that those employees would necessarily figure out that he had forged Miras’s signature, and he was nearly certain that they’d all be fired if they dared disrespect his corporate authority, but still, he worried that they might already be conspiring against him, that they might have already contacted Vraxi Nair, unintentionally triggering the end of days.

He just couldn’t let Miras stay put in a place like that. He had to relocate him to somewhere safer, somewhere in the heart of New Washington, where people like Vraxi Nair couldn’t stand for a single minute without being efficiently escorted to court and then the gallows. Then again, it was also true that the act of transport could expose him. If he were to grab Miras and take a train to Lockezhou, Vraxi Nair could try to infiltrate that train, or hijack his plane, or commandeer his boat and steal Umarov from his fingers. There just wasn’t a reliable way to avoid the increasingly observant eyes of that increasingly large horde of avatars.

What he really needed to focus on, Joey finally concluded, wasn’t about Miras at all. Miras was as secure as he could reliably be, but Joey himself was still out in the open. What he needed to do was hide himself, as the enemy could be slinking around any given corner.

Just as Joey came to that conclusion, he heard an odd sound start playing from outside the bar. It sounded like a repetitive pattern of footsteps and clanging metal chains. He moved to peer through the cloudy window, and was immediately frightened and confused by what he saw. On one end was Shui Hailang, a former ally and presently rogue agent, and on the other end was Diogo Celestino, one of those particularly dangerous avatars fully committed to the summoning of the demiurge. Just the sight of them was enough to make his knees go weak, but before he could collapse to the ground, an odd particular of the pair’s appearance made him stare. The two avatars were not walking side by side out of choice, but rather due to mere physicality, as a pair of handcuffs had turned their four legs into three. This odd limit to their dexterity caused Joey to pause for a moment, but the simple fact of their presence informed his mind that he had to flee. Quickly, Joey tried to summon a portal, however, instead of a door to a location across the city, a matte, solid circle formed instead, one with text that read:

Due to your failure to successfully eliminate any of the presently living avatars, I’ve made the sad, executive decision to presently limit your use of certain abilities, such as those of portal-making. If you wish to regain some of these withheld abilities, then please, begin killing.

-Lucifer

Joey immediately started panicking at the sight of the message while the metallic sound of the approaching pair of avatars only grew louder. He had no choice but to run.

“Mohan!” Joey shouted to the bartender, “I need to use your backdoor!”

“What?” Mohan replied, but before he could even fully process the request, Joey had already scaled the bar and rushed out the back of the establishment, leaving a significant sum of money on his tab, never to be actually paid.

Moments later, Diogo and Hailang awkwardly opened the door to the bar and hobbled inside to look for Joey.

“This place seems pretty empty,” Joey commented.

“Well,” Hailang assessed the environment, “there seems to be a guy in the corner.”

“A guy who is distinctly not the guy who we are looking for.”

“Hey now, I never said that Axelrod was guaranteed to be here. I said he might be here, because I know that he’s been here before and I also know that he’s a bit of a day-drinker. I think it was a fair assessment from the knowledge I had available. There are also some other bars that we can check, and if he’s not at any of those, then you might as well give up and unchain me.”

“I’m definitely not doing that last bit and I also don’t think we’re quite done here. It’s true that he isn’t here at the present moment, but he could’ve just left. I’m going to ask the bartender for some information regarding the matter.”

“Fine then, go ahead, just don’t expect a miracle.”

“Hello, good sir,” Diogo addressed the bartender, “my name is Detective D. Celestino and I’m here with my apprentice, Shui Hailang.”

“Apprentice?”

“Um, hello,” Mohan replied, “…Why are you two chained together?”

“We had an altercation with a gang of sadistic teens. Luckily, we made it out alive. But that story is irrelevant to the question I have for you, good sir.”

“Okay then…”

“In the past couple of days, have you or have you not encountered a repeat customer by the name of Joseph Agbayani Axelrod?”

“…I’ve encountered a guy named Joey. I imagine that could be his full name.”

“Interesting. Now, would you be able to tell me if this Axelrod character has been inside of this bar within the past hour or so.”

“Well,” Mohan considered the question. The truthful answer was an obvious yes, but he wasn’t quite sure if he should be truthful. After all, Joey had sunk a significant sum of money into his product, and Mohan had a feeling that outing Joey to the police could risk losing a profitable customer. Then again, it was also the case that Joey had just left the bar without paying, an act which frustrated Mohan immensely, especially since he didn’t know whether or not Joey would show up to actually pay him back. In that case, it was possible that the only way for him to ever see that money again would be by letting these plainclothes policemen apprehend the thief, forcing Joey to pay back the money he owed while in prison. He continued, “actually, he just left.”

“He just left? What sort of timeframe do you mean by ‘just’ and what direction did he head?”

“I mean, it was probably about a minute ago… he looked out the window, saw something, presumably you two, and then immediately dashed out the back of the building.”

“Dang, Hailang,” Diogo turned to his ‘apprentice,’ “it seems like we’re hot on the criminal’s trail.”

“I’m surprised to say that we are,” Hailang agreed before turning to Mohan, “and thank you, good sir, for your help in this matter. And by the way, just so you know, ‘apprentice’ is really an inaccurate description of my title. We have equal qualifications, he just has seniority and an ego problem.”

“Alright then, officers,” Moahn began to segue, “just also be aware to check if that Axelrod has some money on him. He left without paying.”

Diogo and Hailang exited the bar without responding, not wishing to spark the man’s hopes.

Joey Axelrod had simply started running into traffic. He had no real direction or destination in mind, only a goal to get away from the enemies he knew were after him. The fact that Diogo and Hailang were seemingly chained together did ease his consciousness somewhat, as they were assuredly less mobile that way, but he also had suspicions that the cuffs were a ruse, detachable at any moment and designed to make him think that he was safer than he really was. He simply could not take any chances, for he knew that he, along with Miras, was all that stood between the world at large and the summoning of the Decadeum.

He took another left, onto an especially busy road, in the hopes that the throng of bustling people would make it impossible for someone to track down any individual. He veered to one side of the street, against a host of towering office buildings, then to the opposite side against the gilded fronts of various embassies, before going back into the middle of that swarming lunch-rush crowd and pushing forward until he made it inside the one building he recognized as a safe place, yet another bar, one which was a fair bit more expensive than the last, the tragic cost of a downtown location.

Joey slumped onto a booth, put his face in his hands, before finally trying to catch his breath. He was thirsty in more ways than one, and decided to order the day’s fourth glass of rum.

Like the rest of the group, when she saw the bomb planted, Mbali Chiliza started running in an aimless direction away from the blast. Patcharee Ratnaporn, unsure of the situation, decided to follow Mbali, the nearest person who seemed to know what they were doing. It was only when she heard the tremendous noise of the explosion she was nearly consumed by that she realized the severity of the situation she had landed in.

Ultimately, however, she arrived, as many did, at a bus stop on the outskirts of town. She saw Mbali already there and waved.

“Oh, Patcharee,” Mbali ran up to her, “it’s good to see that you’re alright. Do you know how any of the others are doing?”

“…I was hoping that you might know that.”

“Well, that’s just unfortunate, but not so unfortunate as to ruin absolutely everything. After all, both of us were able to make it out of the blast zone in time. I don’t see any reason why they couldn’t as well.”

“…Mbali, I’m worried about our futures.”

“Why is that, Patcharee?”

“It’s just, well, even if everyone survived that assassination attempt, doesn’t that mean there will just be another, and another, until eventually we all die? I thought that getting out of Siam would put us in the safe zone, but it seems like, regardless of physical location, there are always people trying to kill us.”

“…I must admit I understand your concerns, Patcharee. This is a thankless job that often tries to kill us. However, I think that a very important word in that sentence you just spoke was ‘trying.’ They are trying to kill us, that much is obvious, but they have not managed to succeed. Yes, we’re being hunted, but we’re still not stuck between the enemy’s jaws.”

“But… aren’t we just prolonging the inevitable?”

“No. In fact I’d say that that’s what they’re doing. The reactionaries of the world are attempting, with all their might, to push back the inevitable revolution. By summoning the Decadeum, we make their fight against the inevitable infinitely more difficult.”

“But… assuming we’re all okay, we’ve been split up regardless. How are we supposed to fight as a unit now?”

“Theta already suggested that we split up to look for Joey. I suggest that we continue with that plan as if nothing unusual happened.”

Likewise, Mbali and Patcharee took the very first bus to the Azanian embassy. It was a somewhat bumpy ride but didn’t take especially long and ended with a very warm welcome for Ms. Chiliza.

“Ms. C.,” one of the higher-ups spoke with an air of surprise, “it’s always nice to meet you, but I worry that our meeting implies that something has gone very wrong. Why are you back here in Ashtamudi?”

“It’s a bit of a long story, most of which is confidential,” Mbali answered with ease, “you’ll probably understand what I mean in a week’s time, though. I have to imagine it’ll be all over the news. Luckily, at the present moment, the one thing I need from you is very simple: do you think you could lead me to whoever reviews the security camera footage of this place?”

“Right away, Madame,” the higher-up replied, before guiding the pair through a nest of corridors.

“You seem to be a rather big deal here, Mbali,” Patcharee covertly whispered to her partner.

“Azanian embassies are sorta the only place where I’m a big deal. I fulfill a very private but very important position in the Azanian government. Likewise, places like these provide me with the respect I feel that I’m denied in the majority of locations.”

“Right here, Madame,” the higher-up stopped and pointed to a door.

“It’s madames, plural. There are two of us.”

“Is this… woman-friend of yours cleared?”

“Look at my own clearance,” Mbali flashed her ID in front of the higher-up, “I can let her in if I’d like to. I’m here for a matter above your station and my partner’s presence is inextricable from that matter.”

“…Very well then. You may proceed.”

Mbali and Patcharee entered a small, private room with a singular camera operator surrounded by a field of buzzing screens.

“Good afternoon, Ms. C.,” the operator greeted her, surprised that she would even show up to such a place, “I heard that you needed something from me.”

“Yes, I do, and it’s something rather urgent,” Mbali breathed in as she tried to recollect Joey’s appearance, “now, I’m not sure if you’d know this offhand, but I was wondering if, within the past hour or so, you’ve seen the visage of a certain foreigner pass by the outside of the embassy. I’ll avoid using his name for confidentiality’s sake but he’s rather pale, with dark, curly hair, somewhat short as well, and with a certain… metallic attribute to his eyes. I know it’s not a great description but I thought it might be good to ask.”

“Hmm,” the operator muttered for a moment before pulling up a clip which featured a person passing by who looked exactly like Joey Axelrod, “could this be who you’re looking for?”

“Holy shit,” Mbali exclaimed, losing face for a moment, “that’s him!”

“So that’s what he looks like,” Patcharee spoke softly to herself.

“This is great,” Mbali said before trying to temper her expectations a little, “but when did the camera record that moment? 30 minutes ago? An hour?”

“Oh, um,” the operator tried to phrase her words correctly, “well that’s actually a live feed.”

“…So he just passed by us?”

“It would seem so.”

“Patcharee, we’ve gotta get out of here, now. And Madame,” Mbali turned to the operator, “I thank you immensely.”

The two rushed down to the front door of the embassy before rushing out into the crowded street, hot on Axelrod’s tail.

Zapata felt the sinking suspicion that she was running in circles. She had been forced by circumstance to work alongside Aisha Abdulaziz, and unfortunately, Aisha was the only one of them who had a method of actually finding Joey Axelrod, further forcing Zapata to abide by her enemy’s whims and ways. To make matters worse, Aisha’s methodology didn’t even seem to be especially effective.

“Are you sure that this strategy actually works?” she asked Aisha bluntly, “a while ago you were saying that the trumpet implied he was at a certain bar, then we went to that bar and it was empty. You then said that he must’ve moved elsewhere, but that elsewhere you tracked was also empty. It’s really starting to seem like you don’t have any idea what you’re doing.”

“He’s moving, Zapata,” Aisha admitted, “and the trumpet strategy really works best on static targets.”

“The famously static targets known as human beings.”

“Likewise, I usually tend to track down people in their sleep.”

“Oh I’m sure that’s reassuring. ‘Look, honey, the woman who killed our son has just broken into our home in the middle of the night. I’m sure she’s here to make amends and not to finish us off.’”

“Admittedly,” Aisha paused to blow on her horn again, sending yet another sonar signal, “there have been some confusions in the past. But I’m really quite quick to erase those confusions and do my best to make things better.”

“Has anyone actually forgiven you?”

“I beg your pardon?”

“Your whole deal now is that you run around to your many victims and beg them for forgiveness, but have any of them actually forgiven you for your crimes.”

“Well, there was Vraxi, after I saved her life.”

“Was there anyone besides her?”

“…I saved a woman from a fire once. It was in the middle of the night and she was fast asleep while her isolated house was being consumed by flames. Back when Thabr was controlling me, I had killed her husband. I succeeded in saving her life and she forgave me.”

“So people only really forgive you if you save their life first. I suppose that tracks, since for you to be there you had to kill someone close to them first. It’s sort of an eye for an eye in that sense. Though honestly, at that rate, I can’t imagine any world where all of your victims choose to forgive you.”

“I’m not seeking forgiveness, Zapata. I don’t even forgive myself, and I completely understand that there is simply no world where everyone I’ve wronged turns around and says I’m alright,” Aisha stated before taking another blow on her horn, “what I’m trying to do is make things better. I do not seek anything in return. I’m trying to be as good of a person as possible to do whatever I can to make up for all the horrible things my hands have committed. The end goal of my initiative is not forgiveness. The end goal, ideally, is a slightly better world, one in which my presence on Earth was not a total stain. I’m trying to make my life worth something, Zapata, because even if I end up being remembered as the butcher of Mansoura, I’d still like to prove that I’m at least multifaceted.”

“…Admittedly, I could definitely describe you with the word ‘multifaceted.’”

“Thank you.”

“That’s not a compliment.”

“But it’s not an insult either, and that’s enough for me.”

“Well, regardless,” Zapata tried to change the subject but her eyes were caught by a little, running, recognizable figure, somewhere three blocks ahead of her, “holy shit. I think I see Axelrod.”

“What? Where?”

“Straight ahead. Now start running.”

Joey Axelrod couldn’t believe it. He had truly received the most wonderful voicemail in the history of the medium. He hadn’t been expecting it—not in the slightest—but the information held within was enough to get him off his feet and running in the flick of a dime. The message went as follows:

“Hello, Joey. It’s me, Theta, your creation. I’m sending you this message as a form of apology. I’m afraid Vraxi Nair has gone too far. She and the rest of the group have started killing without remorse in order to fulfill their goals, and I’m beginning to think that they might not have the best intentions. On paper, the world they envisioned was magnificent, a world without strife or class or suffering, but I’ve since learned that these dreams come at a cost. Joey, they’ve gone too far, far beyond where I’m comfortable sitting, and I think that I’d like to come home. I heard that you’re in the city of Kollam and so am I. Please, hurry and meet me at the Monument to the Fallen Sailors. If you don’t get here soon, Nair might start getting suspicious. Once we get home, we can take the first flight to the Novaplex. There, I think we’ll be safe. And, one more thing, I’d just like to say that I’m sorry for how difficult I’ve made the past few months for you. I promise that, starting today, things will start turning around.”

Joey had been expecting this message for a long, long time. He knew that, eventually, Nair and her cronies would cross a line and Theta would come to their senses. Even then, he still couldn’t believe it, and he could barely keep his emotions under control. Little streams of teardrops poured from his dampening eyes as he ran with no reservations towards the person he adored the most in the world.

He passed over a little hill and the monument came into view. At its base was a little android with arms outstretched, waiting for him.
