Revolution on High: Part 10

Chapter 77: Revolution on High: Part 10

At the bottom of the obelisk dedicated to all the nation’s dead and missing sailors, stood a little, unassuming robot, waving at Joey Axelrod.

Joey adored the sight of his creation. It was a sight he had longed to see for a long time, and now, fate was finally coming together to serve him what he deserved. He had had his tussles with Theta in the past—after all, Theta was the one who shot him in Tahiti—but he was willing to put that all aside after hearing the android’s earnest apology. Yes, the past had been rocky, and yes, the future was still unseen, but in the golden hour of the present he could still dream of a much more pleasant world, one where Theta was finally returning to his arms, returning to the person who cared for them the most.

Then, as Joey reached a point only a few meters away from Theta, he felt a touch on his shoulder, which soon devolved into a tackle, which soon saw him prostrated flat on the ground. Joey looked up, and he saw the face of Vraxi Nair. Just as he was about to grasp what he had always deserved, that wicked woman swooped down from nowhere to steal all his hopes away and cast them into the fire, just like she had always done, time and time again. He couldn’t accept this fate.

“Vraxi,” he spoke in a gritted voice, “I’m not gonna do this bullshit all over again. I am taking what’s mine.”

“Theta constitutes a fully conscious life,” Vraxi rebutted, “they do not belong to anyone other than themself.”

“You idiot! They just sent me a message telling me that they want to return to me. This is what they want too. They’ve finally come to their senses and realized that you’re an untrustworthy and volatile and needlessly violent person and that they’d rather not associate with you for the rest of their existence.”

“That was a ruse, Joey,” Vraxi’s grip grew tighter as Joey attempted to break free from her hold, “it was a made-up story, crafted by me and Theta to goad you out of your hiding place. Theta did not believe in anything that they sent you.”

“It’s true,” Theta added in monotone, “it was all a lie. And while I do not like to lie, I found it necessary in this particular circumstance. It was the only reliable way to get you to come to us, to get you to join the Decadeum whether you want to or not.”

“…How could you, Theta?” Joey asked with utter dismay, “I really thought that this time was different. I was really willing to believe that you had finally changed your mind. But it turns out that you only sunk deeper into your own depravity.”

“Don’t call them depraved,” Vraxi replied with a harsh tone, “they were simply being pragmatic.”

“You don’t get to decide what I say to my own creation, you tyrannical temptress!” Joey’s hands shifted to steel as he spoke with added anger, “you don’t get to decide a single thing about me, Vraxi Nair. You are a lucky little shitstain who happened to meet Theta at the most impressionable time in their life. You may have them hypnotized, but you don’t know the first thing about them, and you don’t know anything about me either, because if you did, you wouldn’t lead me to Theta in the first place with no one to defend them but yourself.”

Joey’s metal arms grasped onto Vraxi’s back tightly, nearly breaking it, before picking her up and throwing her towards the nearest building.

“That’s what happens when you try to mess with me, Vraxi! You get pummeled into the fucking dirt!”

Vraxi was in a state of half-consciousness after getting slammed into the hard brick wall. Her eyes drooped, her tendons reeled with every little movement, and she could feel a colossal bruise beginning to formulate on her back, dipping deeper into darker and darker shades of purple, an undeniable mark of what Joey was capable of. She tried to get her feet on the ground, an attempt at standing straight after the tremendous shock, but she immediately doubled over and vomited on the ground, too exhausted to move and too dizzy to think.

“It was a good trick, Vraxi Nair, a nasty, immoral trick, but an impressive one nonetheless to lure me into your domain. Your issue, however, stems from the fact that you don’t know how to defend yourself, and in how you continuously forget that I am not an opponent to be passed off as an afterthought.”

Vraxi tried to respond, but she could only pant. She tried to summon her sword, but she could only summon the thought of it.

“Now with that out of the way, I suppose that it’s time for me to take what’s mine,” Joey announced before grabbing Theta by the waist and slinging them over his shoulder, “and hop on the first flight to New Washington.”

“Joey, I don’t want this,” Theta stated defiantly.

“Theta, trust me, I know that, deep down, you do.”

“You don’t know what I want, Joey. You don’t know what I truly believe in.”

“But I do, Theta, because I made you. I know you better than you know yourself, and I know that these horrible people have brainwashed you, tricked you into thinking things which will only ever harm you. Luckily, I’ve come to save you from their influences, and while you may dislike my intervention now, trust me, a year from now you’ll thank me for it.”

Vraxi was beginning to lose hope. She was beginning to suspect that after all this time and all this effort, her chances were finally being squashed. She supposed that it had been a long time coming, that it was surprising that she had even made it as far as she did. Perhaps, in another couple of decades, or another century or so, someone might complete the work she started, summon the Decadeum, and direct the world down a better path. Perhaps, she considered, that path could even be reached without the use of any magic. However, for now, she couldn’t help but accept the fact that her fate was already decided. She was really regretting the fact that she had told Carlyle to look out for Joey at a position further down the road, for if she had just had some backup, she knew that she could’ve avoided her dismal, present condition. She looked out with teary eyes at the remnants of the Decadeum laid before her: herself in paralysis, Theta being carted away, Miras trapped for the rest of his days, and everyone else potentially maimed by that explosion. For just a moment, to ease the pain, Vraxi allowed her eyelids to rest, a gesture she knew would signal her acceptance of defeat. However, just as her vision went black, an interesting sound brought her back to a state of wakefulness, the characteristic sound of clanging metal chains. The sudden disturbance piqued her curiosity just enough to lead her to search for the sound, and when she finally managed to crane her neck to the left, she saw a truly phenomenal picture.

“Diogo… and Hailang,” Vraxi spoke excitedly through her dilapidated throat as she saw the pair enter the square, still cuffed together, “And Mbali and Patcharee too, along with Zapata and Aisha, and even Carlyle Flanders… They all made it… There’s still a chance.”

Vraxi Nair was too injured to fight, but she still had people who were willing to fight for her. The battle was not yet over.

“Hey Mbali,” Diogo asked as he peered at the increasingly distant visage of a running Joey Axelrod, “do you think you could reach that kidnapper with your fishing rod.”

“Well,” Mbali mulled it over briefly, “I can try, and my chances will only get worse the longer I wait.”

In a flash of light, a large metallic, maritime instrument materialized in the hand of Mbali Chiliza. She checked the hook, reeled the rod back, and flung the tip into the distant sky. There were many factors to be considered in that fateful throw, both the grandiose distance of Joey himself, the fact that he was actively moving, and the fact that there were still throngs of citizens abound whom she did not want to hit by accident. She had to be simply perfect in her aiming, but luckily, she had spent a lifetime practicing.

In a momentary, glinting instant, Joey Axelrod saw a particle of light enter the top of his vision. While he hadn’t turned around, he knew by audio alone that Vraxi had acquired some backup, and he furthermore knew the agent Mbali Chiliza by name. He understood the danger that that little hook could hold. After all, he saw what it had managed to do to Shui Hailang once before. However, unlike Shui, Axelrod could see that horrible weapon coming, and knew how to get out of the way. The hook could only tap into the mind of its victims if it managed to hit said victims in the temple. All Joey had to do was dip down his head and let the hook pass by him. Quickly, he directed his neck downwards, removing his brain from the range of the hook’s arc, but as he made another step forward after avoiding Mbali’s assault, he felt a strange, powerful tug begin to emanate from his upper back.

In reality, Mbali hadn’t been aiming for Joey’s temples at all. She knew that he would see her hook and adjust his head accordingly. What Joey couldn’t account for was all the space on his body beyond his field of view. Drawing on this, Mbali instead aimed for the back of Joey’s shirt collar, hoping to clamp on to his clothing and drag him back to her in a very physical manner.

Theta could sense a sudden shift in the odds. They were no longer being forced forward atop Joey’s shoulder, but were in fact moving backwards, along the path of an ethereal string. In a matter of moments, they were airborne, shooting across the sky towards a group of interlocutors they never thought they’d see again. They could also feel Joey’s anger rise in real time. In a certain sense, they could understand his anger. He had gotten incredibly close to achieving the object of his dreams, but then a tiny, minuscule misjudgment on his part caused all of those dreams to start shattering. He assuredly must’ve felt incredibly lost in the world. It was a feeling that Theta could almost sympathize with, and likely would’ve if those dreams didn’t directly harm them. Even as his fate became clear as day, he still harmed them, gripping tighter and tighter around Theta’s frame until the metal started to warp. While it wasn’t really a feeling they could possess, Theta imagined that if they were more biological they would be feeling very queasy, a malady only heightened by the fact that they were over twenty meters up in the air.

Then, suddenly, that strangely biological feeling departed them, and all the tightness in their frame finally began to relax. At first, they weren’t sure why all that stress had faded so rapidly, but as they allowed their camera to take in the surroundings, they ultimately realized why. Joey had let go.

Theta wasn’t exactly sure why Joey had made such a decision. After all, Joey had often sworn to protect Theta with their life, and while that ‘protection’ often went directly against Theta’s wants, Joey had never gone so far as to purposely place them in harm’s way. However, with that sudden, unexpected drop, that attitude seemed to have finally changed. Joey’s anger with his creation had finally reached a tipping point, and he had given up on the prospect of ever teaching Theta to be like him. As it became apparent that Theta could only continue existing as an accomplice to Vraxi Nair, it must’ve become obvious to Axelrod that the only way to prevent the Decadeum from being summoned was by letting Theta fall to their doom.

That twenty meter drop seemed to last a lifetime. Theta simply couldn’t wrap their head around the idea that the man who had been instrumental in their creation was now responsible for their impending destruction. They knew that Joey didn’t like the way they’d grown since their initial parting, but they never thought that Joey would try to throw them away. It was the ultimate separation between parent and child, that of an infanticide.

The crowd of interlocutors watched as Theta fell, and the happy faces they put on after watching Mbali’s hook successfully capture Joey all quickly began to sour. It was the kind of tragic incident that was too quick to react to, too fast-acting to even really process, the kind where the tragic end is accepted before the ending even occurs. After all, it’s easier to mourn a dynamic figure in freefall than it is to mourn a pile of loose screws. A corpse’s visage can only ever pale in comparison to the lively poses of a body approaching death. In that moment, Theta became that artistic body, that abstraction of themself, representing all they ever lived for more efficiently than their approaching corpse ever could. It conveyed a message of dwindling hope, affecting every interlocutor in their own way, but always holding some kind of deeper impact. Even Patcharee, who barely knew Theta, was impacted by the sight of their approaching death, but unlike those surrounding her, her view of the hope that Theta represented seemed to outshine their tragic fate, and she felt, internally and undoubtedly, that this didn’t have to be the end for the world’s savior.

A sound of rumbling emanated from the ground beneath Theta, but it wasn’t the sound of them crashing to the ground. In fact, it was not the sound of their fall to the floor, but rather the floor’s fall to them. Emerging through the asphalt was a verdant shade of green, one which flowered and expanded into a colossal bush, at least ten meters in height. In the end, Theta did not fall to the hard pavement, but rather their fall was broken by this sudden growth of plant matter.

Theta was alive. Vraxi Nair, from her deeply bruised and compromised position, put on the widest smile she could, while Joey Axelrod was enraptured by a feeling of total disbelief. However, before he could even express that emotion, the fishing line met its end and he was placed in the den of his enemies. Before he could make a move, Carlyle removed the handcuffs connecting Diogo and Hailang and placed them on Joey’s wrists, trapping him.

“Congratulations, Axelrod,” Mbali spoke smugly, “you’re officially a member of the Decadeum now. First, we’re gonna tend to the wounds of Vraxi and Theta which you rudely, needlessly inflicted, and then you’re gonna tell us where you hid Miras Umarov, alright?”

“What if I don’t want to tell you?” Joey bluffed, “Are you gonna torture me or something.”

“Honestly, Joey, I don’t really believe in torture. Oftentimes, it leads to false confessions, and we simply don’t have time for any bullshit like that. Instead, we’re just gonna give you an ultimatum. If you refuse to tell us where you hid Miras Umarov, we’re gonna make you have a simple conversation with Theta, specifically regarding the reason as to why you chose to kill your own creation.”

“Um,” Joey gulped. That was truly the last conversation he wanted to have. He wasn’t even sure himself why he decided to drop Theta and he could only imagine the guilt he’d feel in explaining his psyche to his victim. It was a fate he simply had to avoid and he likewise responded as such, “I’ll do it, Mbali. Once everyone’s gathered, I’ll tell you where I hid Miras, and before you ask, yes, he is alive.”

“Good. If you had killed him, well, I can only imagine what we’d have to do to you. Anyways,” Mbali turned away from Joey, “Diogo, do you think you could help me carry over Vraxi and Theta? And Aisha, do you think you could book a hotel room? We’re gonna need some beds for the injured.”

Vraxi and Theta sat alone in the quiet hotel room, splayed out on two parallel beds. The pain emanating from all of her bruises was still rather excruciating, but more than any other emotion, she was glad that Theta and herself were still alive.

“Are you feeling any better?”

“A little, but I’m counting every second until Mbali comes back with some painkillers. How are you feeling?”

“Mostly pretty adequate. I do not feel pain in the same ways which you humans do, though I can still detect when I’ve been injured. Luckily Patcharee saved me for the most part from any serious harm, but I could still use the help of a screwdriver to keep me in an ideal position.”

“I like how you’re always looking on the bright side in these sorts of circumstances.”

“Am I? Right now, positivity only seems natural. After all, we successfully captured Joey and all of us survived the process.”

“Well, I suppose we succeeded as a group. It’s just that, on my own, I failed spectacularly.”

“Don’t say that, Vraxi. You played a vital role in the process.”

“I was barely able to hold on to Joey. He almost immediately threw me aside. I overestimated my own abilities and I was deservedly punished for it.”

“Vraxi, you’re being needlessly negative. Everything worked out in the end, didn’t it?”

“I suppose. It’s just that, if the rest of the group hadn’t suddenly shown up at such an opportune moment, Joey could’ve hauled you away right then and there, and it would’ve been my fault for not stopping him.”

“Vraxi, it would’ve been my own fault. I was the one who came up with the idea of using myself as bait.”

“Regardless, it feels like I failed you.”

“Vraxi, I appreciate you more than you could ever know. Please don’t be so hard on yourself.”

Vraxi paused for a moment to consider Theta’s words. They really did appreciate her, but in reality, only Vraxi could know to what extent. Afterall, Theta had been purged of the memory of that single beautiful moment where their heads collided in a romantic embrace. Vraxi could not rid her mind of that kiss, no matter how much she tried. She almost wished she could, like Theta, enter her own mind and extract unwanted memories, just to put them on an even playing field. At the same time, she wanted more than anything to recreate that perfect moment, but she worried that the timing would never be right, that she would never again enter a situation where a kiss between her and Theta would be natural. However, before she could push down the thought of that kiss yet again, her weakened mouth started to move on its own.

“Hey, Theta, do you remember how you had to lose part of your memory back in Azania.”

“I do. It was an unfortunate necessity to prevent Sobek from killing us. Luckily, you informed me afterwards that I didn’t forget anything important.”

“Well, um,” Vraxi adjusted her position on the bed to face Theta directly, “I may have been obscuring the truth somewhat back then.”

“In what way?”

“Well, um,” the logical part of Vraxi’s mind tried to stop her from speaking the truth, “it’s actually not all that important-”

“No, Vraxi. I want to know what happened. I’ve always suspected that you didn’t tell me the full truth back then. In such a dire moment as then, I didn’t want to push you into saying anything you’d regret, but now, in our relative safety, I desperately want you to tell me what really happened.”

“We kissed.”

“…Oh, Vraxi, why didn’t you tell me sooner,” Theta got up from their supine position, walked across the room, and slumped onto Vraxi’s bed, staring deep into her eyes, “Don’t worry, I’m not mad that you hid that from me, Vraxi, I understand why you’d be embarrassed to speak the truth, but I also need you to understand that I love you, Vraxi Nair, and I figure that we should make up for lost time.”

Theta locked their metallic legs around Vraxi’s fleshy torso before leaning their sheer steel face into a spot only centimeters away from Vraxi’s lips. Theta didn’t have a mouth, but Vraxi could tell that they were smirking.

“I don’t know how the kiss was initiated the first time,” Theta admitted, “but I figure that it’s time for me to take the reins. But first, I still must ask, Vraxi Nair, would you like for me to kiss you?”

“Um…” Vraxi was blushing profusely and could barely speak straight. Her bruises were still bothering her but all her desperate mind could think to do was to blurt out “yes, please!”

Vraxi dropped their metallic faceplate down to Vraxi’s soft countenance and leaned into every movement, approximating a florid make-out session to the best degree they could. It was visibly evident that Vraxi was enjoying that approximation, so much so that it encouraged Theta to lean into things a little bit more, to grind on Vraxi’s bruised-purple body with a little more intensity, to eventually even snake their cold smooth hand under Vraxi’s linen shirt and sensually grope at her tender, slightly bruised breasts. Vraxi squirmed and vocalized her delight as her saliva got all over the smooth veneer of the suit-vac’s head. Theta was ready to take that vocalization as a sign to go even further with their advances when the sound of the hotel door unlocking stopped them in their tracks.

“We’re back!” Zapata announced as she needlessly kicked open the door.

“Oh,” Diogo commented as he saw the position that Vraxi and Theta had twisted themselves into, “would it be better if we waited a bit?”

“Unfortunately, no,” Theta awkwardly slid their body off of Vraxi’s, though only after giving her one final caress on the face, “I can’t have my own personal fancies delay the rescue of Miras Umarov.”

“Well luckily for you,” Mbali added, “Joey here is about to tell us exactly where he hid the kid.”

“Um,” Joey began as he slowly shuffled into the room, his handcuffs slightly hampering his mobility, “hello, Theta, and Vraxi, and everyone else. It seems I have no choice but to temporarily join your forces. Conveniently for you all, I hid Mr. Umarov within the city of Kollam, in a location not too far from this hotel, specifically at a business known as GüdTek IcePodz Kollam, a cryosleep facility. Umarov is currently suspended in a state of cold—but livable—unconsciousness. Additionally, in order to extract Umarov from the facility, you’ll need my own facial ID, as I was the one who brought him there in the first place.”

“So naturally,” Theta replied, “you’ll accompany us to the facility in order to ease the extraction process, right?”

“Um,” Joey gulped as he stared at Theta’s face, and a guilty nail was hammered into his conscience, “yes, I’ll do exactly that.”

“Good. I’m glad that you're being agreeable after that despicable move you tried to play on me.”

“Please don’t remind me of that. I don’t know why I did it.”

“You should be thankful that Patcharee saved me. Otherwise, you’d be reminded of what you did everyday for the rest of your life.”

“Um-”

“Speaking of which,” Theta turned to Vraxi, “why don’t you and Patcharee accompany Joey to the cryosleep facility. I’m afraid it might seem a little suspicious if all ten of us showed up there at once. I trust that you two have it in you to prevent Joey from trying to escape.”

“I supposed we should be able,” Vraxi spoke somewhat warily as she was still incredibly sore but didn’t want to disappoint Theta, “I think that my bruises have healed enough for me to start standing again.”

“I should also be able,” Patcharee admitted, “I promise I won’t let Joey out of my sight.”

“That’s great to hear, Patcharee. Now go forth, you three, we have a world to save.”

The walk to the facility was mostly quite quiet. Neither Joey nor Vraxi wanted to acknowledge the reality of their diametric relationships with Theta, while Patcharee only piped up every once in a while to point out some of the more unique architectural features of the city of Kollam. It wasn’t until they reached the block where the facility sat and stood mere meters from its entrance when Vraxi finally started to speak.

“Y’know it’s really messed up what you did to Theta earlier today. They almost died, and you’re basically their father.”

“Listen, Vraxi, I regret that I did it. It was a needless thing for me to do and it occurred out of pure instinct with no intentional malice. If you’re gonna force me to work with you, the least you could do is not constantly remind me of all of my misdeeds.”

“Some mistakes cannot be forgiven, and you really can’t expect a mistake so dire to be forgiven within the day.”

“…I saw you making out with Theta in the hotel room.”

“What?” Vraxi was surprised that Joey even acknowledged that that had happened, “What of it? Just so you know, Theta was the one who initiated things.”

“I thought so. I didn’t mean to invade your privacy but I suppose I just found the moment too poignant not to acknowledge. Just as my own bond with Theta reaches its most dilapidated state, your bond with them only grows stronger. It feels representative of a larger shift.”

“…I’m not sure what you’re trying to say here, Joey.”

“I’m saying that you win, Vraxi. You’ve done it. You’ve fully ripped Theta away from my jealous hands as I’ve lost all chances of ever winning them back. I’ve finally accepted my fate in this matter. I’m content, Vraxi, content with the fact that Theta loves you, while I’ll only ever be, at best, their complicated father figure. I give you my blessing, Vraxi, though I don’t imagine you want it. It seems that Theta’s path to happiness is by your side, and I don’t have any right to halt you any further.”

“…So you’re not gonna try to kill me anymore?”

“No, Vraxi. No matter how much I’d like to.”

“And all you care about now is ensuring Theta’s happiness, even if it means that you won’t be together.”

“Yes, Vraxi. That’s all that really matters now.”

“Y’know, that would almost sound like a noble sacrifice if you hadn’t tried to kill them first.”

“Vraxi, Joey,” Patcharee interrupted, “I know you have a whole history between the two of you, but I really feel like we should be focused on helping out this Umarov fellow right now.”

Joey, accepting defeat, obliged by Patcharee’s request, went inside the facility, and had the woman at the front desk scan his face. He requested to extract a patient by the name of Miras Umarov, and an hour later, a very frigid figure emerged from the back door. He seemed confused and frightened, especially when he saw Joey, but a warm hug from Vraxi was quick to calm him down. The Decadeum had been assembled in Kollam.

However, just as the scanning of Joey’s face concluded, an image was entered into GüdTek’s central database. It was an image of Joey Axelrod, his face clear and identifiable, while in the background, the equally identifiable face of Vraxi Nair could be observed. It was true that the Decadeum had been complete, that Theta’s forces were stronger than ever, but it was equally true that Sobek was watching, waiting for the perfect moment to attack.

Revolution on High: Chapter 11

Chapter 78: Revolution on High: Chapter 11

Even in the tropics, the night was cold and dark. The newly assembled Decadeum sat in a huddle beside Ashtamudi’s docks. In the center of their circle was not one of their own, but rather one who was especially willing to help. That graceful personage was none other than Suravinda Gambheeram.

“You asked for a covert escape from Kollam,” the professor began, “and I’ve provided as covert of a method as possible. In a matter of moments, an automatic, pilotless submarine will arrive beside the boardwalk. It will rise to the edge of the surface and its hatch will open on its own. The eleven of you are to all, quickly but quietly, enter the vessel and begin your journey to Azania under the cover of both night and the sea.”

“And you said everything about the process is automatic, right?” Vraxi clarified.

“Yes. However, if there are any major, colossal issues encountered on the voyage, the vehicle may force you to engage its manual setting. Luckily, there’s a pamphlet within the cabin to help guide you to safety if something unforeseen like that were to happen.”

“Eh,” Diogo interposed, “I doubt we’ll run into any issues that serious. After all, like the professor said, we’re being incredibly covert here. How would our enemies even find us under so much water?”

“I would avoid being so confident, Diogo,” Mbali felt the need to say, “I have the feeling that too many things have been going our way as of late. It’s only natural that something catastrophic should happen.”

“For once,” Hailang added, “I agree with Mbali. The fact that you all even managed to get me over to your side of this blasted conflict indicates that you all have been operating atop a tremendous amount of luck, a supply of the substance which is due to run out some time soon.”

“Um,” Miras Umarov spoke up as he pointed to a disturbance in the water, “is that it? The submarine?”

“I believe it is,” Suravinda replied as the hatch traveled further above the surface and opened automatically, “likewise, it’s time for us to go our separate ways. Be careful entering the sub, go one by one, and please, be careful when you’re summoning the Demiurge as well.”

“Don’t worry,” Zapata replied as she hurried to be first in line to climb into the sub, “we will be.”

Gradually, the eleven interlocutors all assembled in the somewhat cramped vessel, united by a common, albeit tenuous, cause. They departed the Ashtamudian coastline under the cover of night, where no mortal eye could spy on their activities. However, there was one eye, separate from the world of the mortals, that had never stopped watching them. Sobek had tracked their whole journey, from the cryosleep facility, to the hotel, to the hole-in-the-wall restaurant where they celebrated their reunion, to the train station where they met with Gambheeram, to the docks, to the water, and now to the open sea. Sobek had observed every moment, and was now simply waiting for the perfect time to strike, the situation with the perfect combination of factors as to guarantee Theta’s defeat.

Sobek could’ve struck right as the interlocutors departed Ashtamudian waters, but they had another plan in mind, a more failure-proof plan, that would require some human assistance on the other side of the Indian Ocean. Sobek would wait until Theta had just about reached their destination, and only then would their masterful plan unfurl. But in order for that masterful plan to function, they would first have to wait and simply observe the Decadeum in their natural state.

“It kinda sucks that we had to miss breakfast in order to get to this sub before sunrise,” Diogo commented, “I’d really hate to try summoning the Demiurge on an empty stomach. I don’t wanna get exhausted halfway through.”

“I believe I saw some rations in the back,” Aisha mentioned.

“Was there anything good?”

“…There was some granola.”

“Like in bar-form?”

“No. Just the loose stuff.”

“I suppose I’ll pass on that for now. Though I may have some later if things get dire.”

“I’d love to have some loose granola,” Carlyle spoke up.

“Oh,” Aisha responded, still not entirely sure of what to expect from Carlyle’s character, “I’ll grab that for you then.”

Aisha left the main room and entered one of the supply closets while the rest of crew sat through a dull period of silence, a moment of waiting as the autopilot tugged their sub through a preplanned route beneath the sea. There was still a broad element of tension pervading the group, an undeniable degree of vitriol held between various members of the crew. Vraxi looked down at her feet and then out towards that odd collection of people. She wondered if they’d ever be able to squash their differences and become a bit more cordial with one another. Then she remembered the past, of Aisha’s murders, of Hailang’s betrayal, of the scars Joey left on her body, and of the story Mbali told her about Carlyle. He really was a man with no ideals other than winning, a man who would kill for the mere concept of victory. He was a man that Vraxi would never understand, and never would’ve associated with had it not been for his status as an avatar. Once the whole business with the Demiurge was over, she was certain she’d never seek his presence again. Then that certainty made her think about something she had barely considered, that after all of this was done, this whole grand ordeal, life would keep going, work would still be done, and the world would keep turning as it always had. It was a humbling thought, but one which still encouraged her, a reminder that she wasn’t just fighting for an ideal, she was fighting for the sake of the same Earth she’d known all her life.

Aisha reentered the main room with a tub of loose, unsweetened granola in one hand and some sort of rubber and steel contraption in the other. She tossed the tub to Carlyle who caught it one-handed, thanklessly.

“Uh, Aisha,” Hailang spoke up, “what’s that thing you’ve got in your other hand?”

“Oh, um,” Aisha reread the label to make sure she was correct, “it says here that it’s an inflatable raft. Apparently it can fit up to fifteen people inside in the case of an emergency.”

“But, presumably, in the case of an emergency, you wouldn’t have the time to inflate something that large.”

“Well, I’d assume that you’re supposed to inflate it before the emergency actually happens.”

“But then the raft would be stuck inside the vessel. The only way to enter or exit the sub is through the hatch and the hatch is far too small to let something as wide as a fifteen-person raft pass through unpunctured.”

“Then I suppose you’re meant to inflate it after you’ve left the vessel.”

“On the open sea? In the same raging, turbulent waters that caused the emergency in the first place? That sounds like a fantastic way to accelerate the process of your own drowning.”

“I didn’t design the raft, Hailang, I’m not sure why you’re acting like its issues are my fault somehow.”

“You’re the one who suggested using a deathtrap to save our lives.”

“Can you two please shut up?” Zapata demanded, irritated by the noise of her former combatants, “I had to wake up at 3:15 AM this morning. Some of us would actually like to get some sleep. And Carlyle,” she turned to face the accused, “can you please shut your mouth when you’re chewing? I can hear that granola from across the room. I don’t care if you’ve lived for 300 years, that should’ve been plenty of time to learn basic manners.”

The room got significantly quieter and Zapata finally fell asleep.

By the time Zapata woke up, the vessel was already nearing the coast. She rubbed her eyes and tried to get a better look at the monitor displaying the GPS. Strangely, however, the screen went dark just as Zapata leaned closer to it.

“That’s odd,” Zapata muttered to herself before turning to Theta, “hey, do you know how to turn this thing back on?”

“It turned off?” Theta asked, “that’s the first time I’ve seen it like that… Well, there’s probably gotta be a power button or something like that nearby.”

“I suppose,” Zapata replied with a subtle consternation, but was interrupted before she could speak further by a sudden buzzing sound.

“What’s that noise?” Vraxi asked as she too awoke from her slumber.

“I’m not exactly sure. It seems to be coming from the GPS monitor, which is also refusing to show our location.”

“Well that can’t be good. Is there any way to fix it?”

“Hello,” a voice emanating from the monitor spoke, “does this vessel belong to one Suravinda Gambheeram.”

“…I believe it does. Why do you ask? And also who are you?”

“Why, I am Sobek, an artificial intelligence produced by GüdTek labs. I’m sure you’re familiar with my name by now.”

“We are,” Aisha replied with a bit of a shudder.

“Unfortunately,” Mbali added, defiantly.

“What do you even want from us, Sobek?” Zapata finally asked in frustration.

“Well I’d mostly just like to talk,” the program replied, “I mean, it’s a rather fascinating situation we’ve all ended up in. Truly, who would’ve expected to see Shui and Chiliza, Nair and Axelrod, Abdulaziz and Tochihuitl all fighting for the same cause.”

“Well, to be completely honest,” Joey clarified, “I really do not share a ‘cause’ with any of these folks. I am mostly here against my own volition.”

“Don’t worry, Joey, GüdTek has already noted your betrayal and marked you as an enemy of the company. There’s no reason to try crawling back to us.”

The room stayed silent for a moment.

“Anyways,” Sobek continued, “as you approach Inhaca island, I wanted to warn you all of what is to come, and perhaps discourage the lot of you from going any further.”

The screen turned on again, but instead of displaying a map of the Indian Ocean, it showed what appeared to be a livestreamed video. The video showed a vista which most of the interlocutors could recognize, the landscape of Inhaca island, but instead of a peaceful town with peaceful inhabitants, it was populated by what appeared to be a large, Gibson-backed army. A whole array of fully-armed troops, more than could be counted, awaited the interlocutors on Inhaca island, and in the center of them all stood a defiant, embittered Josephine Bran, ready to halt the revolution at all costs.

“Inhaca is presently under a Lockeite occupation. If any of you step foot on the island, you will be shot on sight. If any militants try to stop our occupation, they will be shot on sight. If any of the locals leave their homes, they will be shot on sight. To be completely clear, we do not want to be doing this, but at the end of the day, it’s truly for the better interests of the world at large. It’s simply our attempt to protect the golden laws of liberty and property.”

“The Azanian government will not let this stand,” Mbali spoke with vitriol on her tongue.

“The Azanian army has manpower in droves, but it lacks the technological advantages needed to succeed in any altercation with a Lockeite regime. The fact that they weren’t able to mobilize fast enough to prevent our occupation should be proof enough that they won’t be able to prevent us from shooting them on sight.”

“Why are you even showing us this?” Vraxi finally spoke up, “to prevent us from going further? We’ve faced plenty of adversity already, and one video won’t stop us from making the final stretch. I mean, for all we know this video could be a fabrication.”

“You may be confident, Vraxi Nair, you may believe in your cause more than anything else, but not everyone in your group is quite so eager to throw their life away for your ideals.”

After Sobek spoke, a loud, grating, high-pitched noise started emanating from the central console. Vraxi tried to turn it off but none of the buttons seemed to be working and the longer the noise persisted the more disoriented she became.

Behind Vraxi, one Carlyle Flanders entered a state of confusion. The sudden, fraying noise had made him dizzy. It became difficult to focus, difficult to think, and especially difficult to think logically. All he really could think about were those parting words that Sobek gave, words that he couldn’t help but feel were directed at him. His vision went dark for a moment, and when it did come back, his eyes were immediately enraptured by the scenes of the TV screen, those of an indomitable army, an unstoppable force, which made the paltry group of individuals surrounding him seem pathetic in comparison. There was simply no world in which this ragtag assortment of interlocutors could overcome the force of capital incarnate.

Perhaps, he considered, it was time to switch sides again. After all, all he really cared about was winning, and it seemed like the Lockeites were unbeatable. Carlyle Flanders had no choice but to turn against the folks who had brought him this far.

The noise stopped playing and the ship went quiet. Vraxi felt a hand grip her shoulder, right over one of her bruises. She turned her neck around to see the avatar of war.

“Carlyle,” she spoke in a weathered voice, “stop that. That hurts.”

“I’m sorry, Vraxi,” Carlyle began, “and though I’m rarely ever sorry, I really mean it this time, but I believe this is the end of the road for our partnership.”

“…What do you mean by that?”

Carlyle responded by grabbing Vraxi’s other shoulder and throwing her into the adjacent wall, intensifying her already brutal bruises.

Vraxi felt like she was moving in slow motion. She had dedicated so much time and energy into the assembly of the Decadeum, and now it was finally falling apart. Carlyle was an avatar, he was a vital piece of the puzzle, but if he refused to cooperate, if he suddenly decided to switch sides, then his presence threatened the fate of the entire initiative. Before Vraxi’s contemplation could go on any further, her back hit the wall, her body bruised further, and she entered a state of dark unconsciousness.

Theta watched in fear and amazement. They could not believe what they had just seen play out before them.

“Why?” they spoke in total dismay, “Why would you do this to us?”

“You saw the video Sobek showed us. It doesn’t seem like you all have much of a chance at winning anymore. Likewise, I’m no longer supporting your cause. It’s a rather simple decision for someone like myself.”

“You bastard,” Mbali declared with hate overtaking her tongue, “I should’ve known that you’d pull some bullshit like this someday.”

“He hasn’t pulled off anything yet,” Zapata announced with a grim, determined expression, “the eleven of us are still all gathered in one place, and Vraxi still appears to be breathing,” a scythe began to materialize in Zapata’s dominant hand, “Carlyle, I simply can’t allow you to go any further.”

“Finally,” he commented with a wide grin plastered on his face, a rather uncommon expression for someone like himself, “a real battle. I’ve gotten tired of all these strategic, pre-planned encounters of yours. Beating up Joey was enjoyable, yes, but he was unarmed, and it was a seven-against-one. I’m glad to finally be faced with a real challenge, Ms. Tochihuitl. Now come at me!”

Vraxi charged at her unbearable opponent and slashed the scythe of her spirit directly at his face. Unfortunately, he ducked at just the right moment and the blade ended up piercing the vessel’s hull instead of his flesh. A subtle trickle of water began dripping from the wound as Carlyle got down to grab Zapata’s legs and engage in yet another judo throw. Zapata managed to notice this maneuver just in time and shoved the tip of her scythe into one of Carlyle’s assailing fingers. The sudden, unexpected pain caused him to wince and draw back his hands for a moment and that golden opportunity gave Vraxi just enough time to jump out of his grasp and slam her knee into his lowered jaw. He briefly hit the ground but rolled back into a standing position before Zapata could take advantage of his fall.

“Not bad,” Carlyle admitted, “but I’m not the only problem you have to consider.”

Carlyle pummeled his fist into the tear in the hull, widening it significantly and causing a large torrent of water to start flowing into the ship.

Theta knew that this would be a major issue. There were a lot of major issues for them to consider at this moment, such as the fact that Vraxi desperately needed medical attention or the fact that Carlyle was presently on a rampage which would be difficult to halt, but what really worried Theta the most was the tear in the hull. The submarine was rapidly filling up with water and if they didn’t manage to bring the vessel up to the surface, every single one of them would drown. This likely wouldn’t be much of an issue for Carlyle, as he couldn’t die so long as war raged on in the world, but the rest of the group was concerningly mortal. In order to deal with every threat at once, they’d have to allocate some responsibilities, preferably to the members of the group who they could actually somewhat trust.

“Aisha, I need you to use your horn to try and calm Carlyle down. Mbali, if you find a chance to strike him with your fishing rod, please take it. Diogo, please relocate Vraxi to somewhere safer. Miras and Patcharee, if there’s anything you can do to help Vraxi regain consciousness, please do so. Joey and Hailang, please just sit back and do nothing, since the last thing I need right now is two more enemies. While you all do that, I’m gonna try and steer this ship above water, okay? Okay. Thank you.”

The moment Theta finished speaking they rushed to the vessel’s control panel and tried to figure out how to work the thing. Miras, who was trembling beside the panel, spoke to them in a trembling voice:

“Are we going to die here, Theta?”

“No, Miras. We’re not going to die, not as long as I’m in charge of things. Now go and try to see if you can wake Vraxi up. It’s gonna be difficult to summon the Demiurge when one of us is in comatose.”

“Okay… but if this is our last real conservation, I want to say that I’ve appreciated what you’ve done, whether or not the plan pans out in the end.”

“Thank you, Miras, now let me get to work.”

Theta rapidly analyzed the control panel laid before them in order to determine which lever would let them safely ascend. As they did this, they could feel water pooling at their feet. It was almost as if their suit-vac system kicked into gear, as their priorities immediately honed in on the prevention of any casualties within this present disaster. Eventually, Theta did find the proper lever, but even as they pushed down on it with all of their might, the ship only rose at a painfully slow pace. It had become apparent that this was not a state-of-the-art submarine, and Theta silently cursed Suravinda for not splurging on something more expensive and well-equipped, though they then immediately took back that silent curse as they were quite thankful that Suravinda had provided them with anything.

Meanwhile, the fight with Carlyle was looking slightly more promising. It wasn’t that Zapata was necessarily beating him, and she had actually gotten hit by him a fair few times, but Carlyle was beginning to appear sluggish in his movements. Typically, the avatar of war would never get tired this quickly, but Aisha’s music had managed to place him in a sort of trance. Unfortunately, while it was directed at Carlyle, Zapata could still hear this music, and her movements started appearing more sloppy as the concept of falling asleep grew more and more delightful within her mind.

“You seem to look a little tired,” Zapata taunted as she tried to keep Carlyle’s fists away using the long-range advantage of her scythe.

“You don’t look much better,” Carlyle honestly replied.

As he responded to her words, Zapata lunged at her opponent and got a solid slash of her blade against his knees. Blood began to splurt out and discolor his pants as he let out an enraged grunt and charged forward at his opponent. Zapata simply stepped to the side and managed to stick her thin blade into his back. He ripped the scythe out of his body with his own bare hands, though when he turned around, he looked more tired than ever.

It was in that perfect moment, that moment of pure exhaustion, when Mbali finally struck. She let her fishing hook soar across the room and directly inject itself into Carlyle’s temple. His pupils went white as he fell to the floor and entered the world within his mind.

Meanwhile, Diogo was trying to bring Vraxi back into the realm of consciousness. He had successfully dragged her away from the realm of combat into a safer corner of the ship, but she hadn’t begun to look any better amid the journey. Miras and Patcharee huddled on either side of him as they tried to think up a solution to get her to wake up.

“Well, surely we could just wait a bit,” Miras suggested, “she seems to be breathing alright, so I can’t imagine she’ll be knocked out for especially long.”

“That simply won’t do,” Diogo retorted, “you do realize that our vessel is actively sinking, correct? Even if she manages to wake up, say, thirty minutes from now, we’ll have already had to evacuate the sub by then, and I can only imagine how painfully difficult the evacuation process would be when we have to maneuver a body in a vegetative state. It can’t be done. There must be another way.”

“I can try slapping her,” Patcharee proposed.

“Eh, that could work. Go ahead.”

Patcharee went ahead, leaned down, and gave Vraxi a light slap across the face. There was a minor reaction, but zero signs of a regained consciousness.

“Hmm,” Diogo considered, “that was clearly too minor of a disturbance, but perhaps if we upped the ante, like with a strong punch to the gut, we could get her to wake up in full.”

“We absolutely shouldn’t do that,” Miras spoke up with an uncharacteristic defiance, “she’s already incredibly bruised, and while she is breathing, she’s only barely doing so. A disturbance like that could be what causes her to stop breathing. I’m absolutely against it.”

“I think Miras is right on this one,” Patcharee concurred, “I really feel like we shouldn’t be risking anyone’s lives right now, especially since we all need to be alive for this whole Decadeum thing to actually work.”

“So what it seems you two are saying,” Diogo synthesized, “is that we need some large disturbance to get Vraxi to wake up, but it can’t be so large as to cause significant physical harm to her.”

“I suppose, though I’m not sure how we’d actually accomplish such a thing.”

“Well, you can produce all sorts of plant matter at will, correct?”

“To a degree, yes, though I’m still getting used to it.”

“Then would it theoretically be possible for you to summon up a plant with an especially potent chemical property which could seriously startle someone without actively poisoning them?”

“…I’m not sure what plant you’re trying to allude to here.”

“Are you familiar with the Carolina Reaper?”

“Oh. I suppose I am. I think I see where this is going.”

“If you were to produce an extraordinarily hot pepper and place it in Vraxi’s mouth, it might be just enough to shock them back into a state of consciousness without inflicting any lasting damage on the body.”

“Admittedly,” Miras admitted, “the idea sounds somewhat cruel, but it may be the only way to get Vraxi awake in time. A high dose of capsaicin is still a much better fate than a watery grave.”

“Fine then, I’ll do it,” Patcharee capitulated and started the process of summoning the pepper. First, she grabbed the tin of granola Carlyle had abandoned as she needed to start with an organic material. Not long after, vines began to sprout from that improvised pot, and eventually, the fruit of the pepper began to form and mature.

Vraxi was immersed in a state of total darkness. It was as if she had already drowned, as if she had sunk down below to the deepest trench in the ocean, as if she was already being eaten by a school of bottom-feeders. Occasionally she heard a noise, but they were all distorted, washed out and waterlogged, echoes from afar. She wondered if her ears were bleeding. She wondered if she’d ever find the strength to open her eyelids.

Then something unusual happened. She felt a searing pain, a new pain, a pain which made her other pains seem dull in comparison. It emanated from her mouth, but it quickly spread to her whole body, and it all felt incredibly, cruelly infernal. She immediately assumed she was being burned alive. Something terrible must’ve happened inside the sub and now everything was falling apart. She was surrounded by a vast and open ocean and she was stuck in a little box being consumed by a fire. It was so embarrassingly ironic she wanted to die right then and there, because at least in that case she wouldn’t have to suffer the thoughts of her own inadequacy. She had made it so far but she just wasn’t good enough, she just wasn’t strong enough to persist. She had made the world depend on her, and she proceeded to disappoint. She just hoped that someday, someone would complete the work that she had failed to finish.

The flames persisted, and in fact they grew hotter, yet the fumes couldn’t manage to knock her out for good. The heat had got to a point where no matter how hard she tried to think of sentimental things, the only thing she could consider was the present pain. She couldn’t believe she wasn’t dead yet. She couldn’t believe the heat. Her instinct for survival began to kick in. If she could just find some water, she could cease this pain and at the very least die in a dignified manner. She wondered if she could still crawl, if she could still move at all. With that sudden boost of adrenaline, that sudden newfound purpose, that drive to live, her eyes started opening all on their own.

“Vraxi, can you hear me?”

“…Yes, I can hear you, but I can’t see you well quite yet. Who are you?”

“It’s me, Diogo Celestino. You got hit really back there but I’m so glad to see you alive. Do you think you can stand?”

“Diogo, the fire, you have to get away from it.”

“There isn’t any fire, Vraxi. Patcharee just fed you a hot pepper in order to wake you up.”

“Oh, that’s good then,” Vraxi noticed all the water pooling on the ground, “but are we just going to drown instead?”

“That’s a difficult question to answer. As it stands, it’s hard to say.”

“We’re not going to drown,” Miras stated, “I trust in both Theta’s abilities and the grace of Allah and sincerely believe that we will make it through this.”
