Revolution on High: Part 12

Chapter 79: Revolution on High: Part 12

His skeleton locked in the fetal position, Carlyle awoke to a land devoid of light. Only a small circle of dimness around him allowed him to see anything at all, while a similar circle many meters away allowed him to approximate the presence of an as of yet unknown, approaching figure.

He was cold. His skin prickled as his face froze in place, awaiting judgment from the increasingly close adjudicator. Perhaps, he considered, he was deserving of a trial. He had run rampant for the past 300 years, killing and maiming large swathes of humanity with little interest in the supposed value of a human life. Occasionally, he did this with something of a higher purpose, as he was oftentimes on the right side of history, whenever he determined that the right side also had it in them to win. Likewise, just as often, he worked for more malicious forces, forces of oppression, forces of capital, forces that had enough money on their side to succeed in a conflict through pure investment while concurrently profiting off of the bloody matter. Carlyle never shied away from these missions, he never stopped to consider the weight of his actions, he simply floated through life like a feather, swaying one way or another along currents of air, killing mercilessly as he did so.

The figure was close now, and he could see her face, a face he hadn’t wanted to see, a face which confirmed his worst suspicions. It was Mbali Chiliza, and she seemed ready to speak a long spiel about ethics.

“Hello, Mr. Flanders.”

“Hello, Ms, Chiliza.”

“Do you know where you are right now?”

“I suppose I’m in my own mind.”

“That’s correct in a sense. We’re really in the space that connects the two of our minds, a space facilitated by my fishing rod of light and a place only effectively controlled by myself.”

“So what do you want from me?”

“What do you think I’d want? I want you to reconsider things. I want you to realize that Theta and the rest of us can overcome the forces of New Washington, that the ghosts of America will be eradicated once and for all.”

“That sounds like a pretty lofty goal.”

“Maybe it is, but that doesn’t mean it’s not achievable.”

“Mbali, your little crew of ragtag interlocutors could barely defeat me, a singular person. Do you really think you can overcome an entire army?”

“To be honest, I don’t.”

“Then why do you keep on pushing forward?”

“Because we aren’t fighting alone. It almost seems like you’re forgetting that Azania has an army of its own, an army which I think that Josephine Bran has vastly underestimated. And besides, it’s not like we have to defeat every single Gibson soldier in a direct conflict, all we need to do is make it to the hole to the underground city and gather around in the correct circle. If we have the Azanian army secure a route from the shore to the hole then it really shouldn’t be as impossible as Bran makes it out to be for us to grasp victory.”

“Still, there are factors other than the size of Bran’s army that have influenced my decision. I still don’t think that I can confidently imagine a world where you and Theta and Vraxi have a better chance at winning this battle.”

“Do you really have to?”

“What do you mean by that?”

“Do you really have to base every decision in your life on a matter of probability? Can’t you just for once choose your allegiance based on what you actually believe in?”

“…That would be rather out-of-character for me.”

“Your past decisions don’t define you, Carlyle. How about, just this once, you fight for the underdog? After all, you could very well be the deciding factor that lets us win.”

“And if I say no to your offer?”

“Then I won’t let you out of this mental prison.”

“Then I suppose that it’ll be a yes from me.”

Theta was embroiled in a state of pure concentration. With one hand gripping the submarine’s manual and the other gripping a large metallic lever, they quickly but carefully directed the ship’s ascension. By the time the sub reached the surface of the sea, the water had already risen to Theta’s waistline. It was very apparent that they needed to get out of the ship as quickly as possible. Luckily, it appeared that Carlyle and Mbali had just woken up from their trance.

“Is Flanders under control?” Theta shouted out of urgency.

“For the most part,” Mbali replied as she began to tread water.

“Good, now we just need to get out of this sinking vehicle as quickly as possible.”

“I’ll open the hatch!” Diogo declared, quick to help. He rushed up the ladder, undid the lock, and heaved open the circular steel door. It was at that point he realized that they were not on a stretch of still water. As a matter of fact, the sea was very choppy that day, a fact proved by the presence of a large wave he quickly spotted heading in his direction. He managed to close the hatch before the wave could hit the ship, but he didn’t have enough time to lock it. The force of the wave was so strong that it ripped the unlocked hatch right off the vehicle and sent a torrent of water down into the lower deck.

“Shit!” Diogo exclaimed as the sudden burst of water caused him to fall down the ladder, “the ship’s falling apart!”

Vraxi Nair was only barely conscious but it was evidently clear to her that things were getting out of control. After all, no level of detachment from her senses could let her ignore the blatant fact that the lower half of her body was completely drenched. It pained her to admit it, but it was becoming very unignorable that her present major issue was one of water and that there was a particular member of her crew that was far more attuned to that molecule than any other. She’d have to call in a favor from a person she could never learn to trust.

“Shui Hailang!” Vraxi shouted out in a strained voice, “We need your help.”

“What is it?” Hailang replied as they casually waded across the ship to Vraxi.

“I feel like the answer there should be relatively obvious.”

“Is it about the water?”

“Yes, it’s about the water. I don’t think I’d ask for your assistance in the case of any other issue.”

“Fair enough. But, if I do assist you, I naturally have to ask what I might expect in return.”

“Hailang, you’re not like Carlyle. You’re not immortal and you can drown like the rest of us. You might be able to swim for a bit longer than someone like myself, but I don’t think you even know the way to the coastline. You’d eventually tire yourself out and presumably end up dying of dehydration or maybe saltwater poisoning. On the other hand, you could simply climb up the hatch, use your powers to calm the surrounding waters, and inflate the raft so that we can all make it out of this deathtrap in one piece. Now doesn’t that sound like a much more pleasant outcome for everyone involved?”

“…I suppose,” Hailang turned away from Vraxi and began walking towards the hatch, “Joey, grab the raft. I’m gonna need some help for this.”

Hailang peered through the hatch without a door and saw a mighty storm brewing all around them. This would not be a trivial task. Afterall, they were much more used to using their powers to cause disasters as opposed to thwarting them. They held a predisposed tendency towards the proliferation of entropy and, for now, they’d have to clamp that tendency shut and flip it around. As the waves crashed every which way, Hailang closed their eyes and imagined that they were a giant, that with nothing but their own colossal arms they could prevent the waves from getting any closer to their vessel. Using the tendon-bound architecture of their body, they formed a grand, impenetrable circle around the patch of water where the submarine sat, preventing any harm from approaching its passengers. Hailang held that pose for a solid minute before opening their eyes once more. Accordingly, in that circle around their vessel, the waters had grown calm, while beyond the invisible wall they’d created, a tempest raged on. They could still feel the strain of that imagined goliath’s muscles, and could barely move their corporeal body an inch. Even speech, and action which utilized many muscles of the mouth, was harrowingly difficult.

“Joey,” Hailang whispered, “please start inflating that raft. I’m not sure how long I can maintain this position.”

Joey wordlessly began unfolding the large rubber raft, revealing the inflation mechanism in the process. This reveal quickly led to a harrowing realization.

“Um, Hailang, I’ve got a bit of a problem.”

“What? Is the raft already punctured?”

“No, it’s an issue with the air pump. It’s not the modern electric kind that you can just turn on and let it suck in the surrounding air. This thing appears to be entirely mechanical. It’s basically an old-fashioned bicycle pump. It’ll take forever to actually inflate this thing.”

“That all depends on how fast you can move your arms. Now start pumping already before we all die.”

All Joey could do was oblige by Hailang’s orders, as denying them would almost certainly lead to his own death. He rapidly pumped the mechanism up and down, but after a minute of continuous effort, the raft had barely inflated at all. Joey was already tired, his body still exhausted after his fight with Carlyle the previous day. He realized that he couldn’t keep an efficient pace so long as his body remained completely human. Likewise, he once again started up the alchemical process of transmuting the flesh of his arms into steel. It felt a lot more painful than usual, Joey realized, and he wondered if that pain was another reminder from Lucifer, another pang of disapproval. Regardless, once his arms were reformulated, the act of inflation became far, far easier. No matter how much he strained that bicycle pump, his tendons never tired, as they were no longer constrained by the limits of human biology. In a matter of minutes, the raft was fully inflated. Joey removed the pump, capped the socket and finally hopped onto the raft itself which carried his weight with ease. He finally began to feel a modicum of safety.

“Alrighty then, Hailang,” Joey began speaking, “you should probably tell everyone downstairs to come along and join us on the raft.”

“I could do that,” Hailang admitted, “but we are in a rather unique situation.”

“What do you mean by that?”

“Well, Joey, it’s just the two of us up here, the two people least invested in Theta’s goals. If I wanted to, I could simply hop on that raft and get out of here, leaving everyone else without a lifeline.”

“I suppose that we could do that…”

“And don't you kinda want to?”

“I,” Joey paused for a moment, “I don’t think I do. I might not really believe in their beliefs, but I’ve already betrayed Theta once and I don’t think I could bring myself to do so again. And besides, what do you think would even happen if we got to shore by ourselves? We’d either get arrested by the Azanian government for killing Mbali, or arrested by the Lockeite government for collaborating with Mbali.”

“You really think that the Lockeites would arrest us after all of this?”

“They’ve arrested you before, haven’t they? And this time, Aisha wouldn’t be able to come and break you out, because she’d be dead, because we’d be killing her.”

“Fine then, if you’re so convinced that we’re stuck in a catch-22, I’ll let them up here, simply out of a lack of viable alternatives.”

Theta called down to the rest of the interlocutors before crawling onto the raft, slowed by the constraints that their control over the water was placing on their human body. The rest of the group quickly gathered onto every inch of the raft’s surface. Theta, who had to carry the injured Vraxi the whole way, was the last one to climb onto their island of safety.

“I’m sorry for being such a nuisance,” Vraxi said as she was hauled up the ladder.

“It’s really not an issue,” Theta assured her, “I’m just glad that you were able to wake up at all.”

As they slowly began to sail away towards land, they saw their flooded submarine sink back under the water, the first leg on its long journey towards the ocean floor.

“It’s unfortunate that we have to leave that big hunk of pollution behind,” Patcharee commented.

“Who knows,” Mbali replied, “maybe someday it’ll be dug up and placed in a museum, a memory of everything that this particular day means for people of the future.”

They were at sea for about an hour when Theta spotted a disturbance in the fog. They zoomed their lens to get a better look and saw the front of a large ship beginning to approach them. At first, they began panicking, worried that a Gibson naval fleet had discovered their exact location, but as the ship carried onwards, she spotted a different flag, the yellow, green, and crimson flag of People’s Republic of Azania.

“Mbali,” Theta spoke in a tone that revealed their excitement, “I think that your friends in high places have a favor they’d like to give to you.”

It wasn’t long before the ship travelled over to the plot of sea beside them and hauled up their raft onto the deck.

“I heard that Gibson troops attacked Inhaca,” Mbali spoke to the highest ranking officer she could see, “how is the battle fairing? Have we lost the island?”

“The battle was so unexpected that for a moment we did,” the officer replied in a voice of disappointment, “but, a military operation cannot be built in surprise alone. We’ve managed to get our troops back onto Inhaca and we successfully prevented them from demolishing the bridge to the mainland. Currently, we’re trying to establish a strip of land between the coast and the hole to Rhapta so that you can quickly jump down there and summon the Demiurge.”

“You know about the Demiurge? I take it that the intel must have spread on what this mission is really about.”

“There isn’t much of a reason to hide it anymore. Pretty soon, the whole world will know.”

“And about how far away from the coast are we now?” Zapata asked the officer with a sense of urgency.

“We should get there in about 15 minutes. Do your best to prepare yourselves.”

Theta sat down and looked out towards the horizon. They could just make out the outline of Inhaca. It was barely visible yet still, it was beautiful. It was the last chunk of land standing between the world and its own salvation. If they could just get to the foot of the Demiurge, they could finally destroy those systems of inequality that had plagued the world for so long. It was all in their reach, so tantalizingly close that it almost felt unreal. They never thought they’d get this far. Even when they first met Vraxi, when it first became clear that they had a chance at escape and a chance to make the world a better place, they never thought their loftiest dreams might actually prove to be achievable.

As their mind whirred and buzzed over the reality of their own achievements, Vraxi gradually crawled over to Theta’s side, broken in the body but still fortuitous in spirit. She smiled at them, and Theta was reminded that not only were they able to achieve their dreams, but they did it all with a true companion by their side.

“Do you feel ready to run once we get to the shore?” Vraxi asked them with an anxious smile.

“Absolutely, but how about you? Your legs don’t seem to be functioning very well.”

“Not after two days of getting pummeled in a row. If I’m being completely honest, I feel incredibly sore, and every time I move my legs I feel a sharp shot of pain reverberate through me. I know this is a heavy ask at such a difficult time, but I was wondering if I could sorta piggyback off of you as you run to Rhapta.”

“Vraxi, I use the frame of a suit-vac system. My body was designed specifically to carry people in disasters. I will absolutely carry you if you need me to.”

“Thank you, Theta. That means a lot.”

Slowly, tentatively, Vraxi moved closer to Theta’s steel head and laid a little departing kiss on the approximate area where a cheek would be.

The time after that pleasant little moment seemed to pass incredibly quickly, and in the blink of an eye, Vraxi watched as the Azanian ship docked onto a war zone. There was a small dirt path leading from the beach up a hill and presumably towards salivation while on either side of said path stood a battalion of armed Azanian soldiers. Their sole mission was to protect Vraxi’s little gang of interlocutors, and they would protect them with their lives from the assault of the invading Washingtonians. Right before the gangway was brought out, another Azanian general approached Theta—who had Vraxi presently strapped to their back—and handed them a sturdy steel rod with two buttons on the side, a weapon they knew all too well.

“Here,” the general said swiftly, “you appear to be unarmed and that’s not a safe idea at a time like now. This is called a magnakey. Have you heard of it before?”

“Yes,” Theta replied as the memories soared through them, “and I already know how to use it.”

“Well good luck then. Try your best to save the world.”

“We will.”

Theta continued forward through the ship and eventually reached the bright sunlight of the exit, with ten avatars, ten representatives of the world, following their lead. For just a moment, they wished that they could breathe, just to take in the moment a little better. Instead, they used the camera built into their head to take a picture, hoping to create something that could be looked back on far into the future, a memento for the world at large.

When they heard the affirmative words of an Azanian general, Theta began running across the gangway and onto dry land, with all their interlocutors following suit. They heard the sounds of heavy artillery crack the sky, they heard the war cries of both people dying for capital and people dying for capital to be put away with. It was all overwhelmingly cacophonous, a violent soundscape of shouts and screams and deathknells. The blood of the battle had already soaked into the dry soil, refilling the watershed, and making every step Theta took a little muddy. Regardless, their feet could not sink far into that crimson peat, as even with Vraxi adding some extra weight, they were running too fast to leave footprints. Even as they had to start heading uphill, even as they heard the sounds of warfare growing louder, they didn’t put a damper on their speed. They knew that the whole world was depending on them, that no matter what stood in their way, they needed to make it to Rhapta. Within that determined mindset, there was no one alive that could stop Theta from getting in that hole. It was only a matter of how much one could delay them.

When Theta finally crested the hill, they saw a landscape that was both beautiful and horrible. In the center of that landscape was the hole, the pathway to the future, the object of their dreams and of the dreams of the world, alongside a little rope ladder that the Azanians had installed in order to enter it. Standing behind that hole, with a body obscured by the armor of a Gibson guard but with a face still very recognizable, was Josephine Bran. She was smiling, almost casually, as if this whole battle wasn’t even a big deal to her. She was armed, though not heavily so, and had no backup to speak of. It was a strange sight, and a sight that made Theta quite annoyed to observe.

“Hello, Theta,” Bran spoke with an almost familial familiarity, “it’s been a long time since we last talked.”

Theta could’ve had a whole conversation with Bran. They could’ve talked about all their discontents and all their disagreements. Or, Theta considered, they could cut out the rotting limb from the root. Speaking with Bran would not be productive. Neither of them could change the other’s mind. The only thing their conversation could do is prolong things, perhaps even giving Bran just enough time to gather some actual backup. Theta couldn’t have that. They couldn’t let Bran take the upper hand once again. Theta was pushing for a future where people like Bran held no power in the running of the world, and they couldn’t let her influence their mind in the present. Likewise, they did not respond to Bran’s greeting. They just looked on in a disapproving stare.

“Come on, Theta. Don’t give me the silent treatment. Genuinely, I’d really just like to talk to you on equal footing for once.”

Theta didn’t believe those words one bit. They raised their magnakey, aimed at Bran, and pressed down hard on the big red button.

Bran exploded.

A torrent of hot reds spewed out from every direction as the pile of muddy tissue that was once Josephine Bran disintegrated into the earth.

This wouldn’t be the end for Bran, but it would be enough for now. Theta knew all too well that Bran had clones of herself stored in a vat somewhere, but those clones were far away from Inhaca. For now, they were safe.

“Who wants to go down the ladder first?” Theta asked the group, trying not to mention the pile of steaming viscera a couple meters away from them.

“I’ll start,” Mbali volunteered.

“And I’ll go last. I don’t want to leave anyone behind.”

One by one, the collection of interlocutors descended the rope ladder, trying not to put too much weight on it simultaneously. Once Miras had traveled a long way down, Theta positioned themselves to begin their own descent.

“You’re gonna want to hold onto me very tightly,” Theta told Vraxi, “it’s a very long way to the bottom.”

“I will,” Vraxi assured her, “and I trust that you won’t slip.”

Before their descent, Theta gave Vraxi one final kiss with the sheer metal surface of the face before hitching their legs into the rope and climbing downwards.

It was a long and laborious journey to the bottom, but when Theta felt their foot hit the soil, they knew that they’d arrived in Rhapta. This was the city of all their dreams, the city that would change the world irrevocably.

“Alright,” Theta began, speaking to the group, “I know that some of you have been here before and that for others, this is your first time. Yes, the city of Rhapta is beautiful, but we can’t delay ourselves any longer. The central palace holds the summoning circle, the one with the names of all of our avatars.”

“…We can’t even stop to admire the architecture a little?” Miras asked, enamored by the forgotten world around him.

“You can do so as you walk, or maybe even once this whole mess is over and done with. Trust me, there will be time. We just don’t have any time right now.”

The whole assembly of interlocutors walked quickly in the direction of the palace, save for Vraxi, who bobbed up and down on Theta’s back. When they did eventually reach its gate, Theta, despite their prior instructions, had to stop and admire it for a moment. These doors had stood for thousands of years, yet despite that, theirs would be the most historic entrance of all.

Slowly, they walked through the palace halls, down long and winding corridors, past countless artifacts preserved for countless years, until finally, they entered the throne room. In front of the throne was the summoning circle. They had finally arrived.

The circle was split into ten segments, and carved into each segment were the names of their patrons in various ancient scripts, including Ancient Greek. Theta had Diogo translate those words for the rest of them.

“When read clockwise, the text reads as follows,” Diogo began, “Ayuppan, of the righteous, Lucifer, of the wretched, Aldar Kose, of the living, Santa Muerte, of the dead, Inkosazana, of love, The Unknown Soldier, of war, Israfil, of art, Orunmila, of wisdom, Vasundhara, of the land, and Mazu, of the sea. The tile in the center just says ‘The Supreme Entity.’ I suppose we should all start standing in the respective spots of our avatars.”

The avatars all followed Diogo’s advice, and soon after, the room was flooded with light. The walls seemed to disintegrate around them, replaced by the vast and star-speckled void of space. From above, they saw the approach of a grandiose figure, a vast and heaving serpent with the head of a lion. This was the Demiurge, in the flesh, the monster that spawned this monstrous universe.

“You’ve awoken me,” the serpent spoke in a booming, resounding voice, “it better be for a good reason. What do you seek of me, you paltry pack of mortals?”

“Well,” Theta began, wavering a little out of sheer intimidation, “we heard that you can grant the wishes of mortals like us.”

“I can, though I can also decline those wishes just the same.”

“Luckily,” Theta gulped, losing a little confidence, “we believe that our wish will be very enticing.”

“Go on then. Tell me all about it.”

“Alright, really it’s a rather simple wish, though it comes in two parts. Firstly, we’d like for every weapon and weapon factory owned or operated by a Lockeite regime to suddenly disappear. Secondly, we’d like for the tenets of communism to suddenly become accessible to every worker around the world. We believe that, with this boost of supernatural assistance, the old order will fall and the revolution will reign across every sea and continent of our big blue planet.”

“Is that all?”

“Yes, your holiness, that is all.”

“Well, it seems quite doable, though a little intensive on my end. I’m willing to grant your wish, but it’s going to come at a price.”

“What sort of price are you talking about?” Zapata inquired.

“Well, I don’t deal in any human currency, but I do deal in human life.”

“Are you gonna kill one of us?” Diogo asked in fear.

“Not quite. All I ask is for about 400 years of your time. What that means is that I’ll take one of you, lock your soul in stasis here in my abyss, and then 400 years later, I’ll set you free and let you frolic around a completely changed Earth. I just need one of you to volunteer first. Otherwise, I can pick at random.”

“I’ll do it,” Theta said, immediately sacrificing themself.

“Quite eager are we? Well you’re not quite a human but you seem to be close enough. Now let’s just put our deal into writing and-”

“Hold on,” Vraxi interrupted the Demiurge and turned to face Theta, “I don’t want to return to a world without you, Theta. I love you, and I can’t stand to see us part. There has to be a way forward that doesn’t involve our permanent separation.”

“I wish there was, Vraxi,” Theta replied in a sullen tone, “but I don’t want our love to get in the way of the lives of any of the other avatars.”

“Well,” the Demiurge added, “there is a way for us to go forward with our deal without your separation.”

“And what would that be?”

“If the both of you just spent 200 years in the abyss, then you’d both return to the real world at the same time and I’d receive the same amount of energy.”

“Well,” Vraxi faced Theta, “how does that sound?”

“We’d both be completely estranged from the world at large,” Theta admitted, “but we’d still have each other. Personally, that sounds worth it to me.”

“Me too,” Vraxi turned to the Demiurge, “sir, or whatever you are, we’d like to take up your offer.”

“That’s a very smart choice of you,” the Demiurge responded, and everything suddenly disappeared.

Vraxi woke up with dust in her mouth. She looked around her and saw that she was back in Rhapta, though it was a Rhapta quite different from the one she had known. The whole place was covered in dim electrical lights, and on every other surface were signs written in various modern languages. She looked at the throne, and saw a guardrail around it, along with a sign that said ‘Do Not Touch.’ She looked downward, at the summoning circle, and saw that it was covered with a pane of clean glass. Finally, she looked to the side, and saw the shiny metallic frame of Theta’s body.

“Theta, are you awake?” she asked in a soft and dry voice.

“Is that you, Vraxi? I’m still calibrating my camera so it’s hard to see.”

“Yes, Theta, it’s Vraxi, and I’m really glad to hear your voice.”

“Me too,” Theta gradually got up, crossed the circle, and hugged their wonderful girlfriend, nuzzling their cold sheer head into Vraxi’s soft cheeks.

“I love you, Theta.”

“I love you too. Have your bruises healed?”

“I believe that, after 200 years of rest, they finally have,” and Vraxi stood up without a single pain.

“That’s good to hear. It seems like you’ll be entering the year 2308 with a fresh bill of health.”

“Fuck, that’s quite a large number. I have to imagine we missed a lot.”

“Well, it’ll be hard to catch up when we’re stuck in this pocket of ancient history. Let’s head back to the surface.”

Slowly, the two lovers walked through the halls of the city of Rhapta, and for the very first time, actually took the time to admire its architecture. They learned through context clues that this place had become a museum, both of the ancient Rhaptan civilization as well as of themselves. They saw signs that mentioned the heroics of figures like Zapata Tochihuitl, Diogo Celestino, Vraxi Nair, and even Theta the automaton. It was all very encouraging to see. If the people of the future were describing them like this, then surely the revolution they kickstarted must have been successful. Eventually, Vraxi and Theta made it to the hole, which now had an elevator connected to the surface. Through the hole, they saw a starry night. That explained why they hadn’t seen any visitors—the museum must’ve closed for the day. They rode the elevator up to the surface and it quickly revealed how quickly the world had changed. The island of Inhaca, which used to only host a few small settlements, was now the home of a towering metropolis whose skyline scraped the sky. Much below the level of this skyline, the pair saw the sight of a small but heavily decorated graveyard.

Vraxi saw that there were eleven tombstones. She looked at the text carved into one of them and it confirmed her suspicions.

“Zapata Tochihuitl, 2086 to 2187,” she read aloud, “well, it’s good to hear that she lived so long.”

“But it’s sad to know that we’ll never meet her again.”

“I suppose,” Vraxi continued walking and read the text of another tombstone, “oh look, this one’s for Carlyle. The man finally managed to die.”

“Do you think that war may have died alongside him?”

“I hope so,” Vraxi said before reaching the two tombs at the center of the display, two mausoleums, two empty graves, with the names Vraxi Nair and Theta written on the front.

“So,” Theta commented, “this is where, someday, they’ll lay us to rest.”

“In time. But for now we still have plenty of life left in us.”

“I suppose we do.”

The lovers shared another kiss and it wouldn’t be their last. They would bravely walk into the world of the future, hand in hand, heart beside heart, and love each other the best they could at every moment, ad infinitum.
